title: [Conductor] Add KV event manager and HTTP API
body:
## Description
Fifth slice of the Mooncake Conductor upstreaming series, on top of the zmq subscriber. Wires the ingest path into the prefix index and exposes the query surface, and produces the mooncake_conductor binary:

- kvevent/event_manager.{h,cpp}: EventManager owns the indexer, the per-service ZMQ subscribers and the coroutine HTTP server. Start subscribes to every configured service concurrently and reports individual failures through the log rather than failing as a whole, so one unreachable publisher cannot block startup. Stop is idempotent. UnsubscribeFromService stops its ZMQ client outside the manager lock, because the client's loop thread can still be dispatching a batch that needs the manager. Registers five routes: /query, /register, /unregister, /services and /global_view.
- kvevent/event_handler.cpp: KVEventHandler implements the zmq EventHandler interface for the three publisher protocols, dispatching each batch to per-event handlers that translate into indexer mutations. Mooncake Store publishes one logical hash as several physical objects, such as separate key and value components, so pool_bindings_ tracks the physical set per logical key and only removes the index entry once the last component is gone.
- Handler lifecycle: MarkUnavailable stops admitting new callbacks and WaitForIdle waits for the ones already admitted, with DispatchLease releasing the in-flight count on every exit path. This is what lets a service be unsubscribed while its subscriber thread is mid-batch.
- kvevent/config.{h,cpp}: reads the static service list from CONDUCTOR_CONFIG_PATH. A missing file warns and yields an empty list; a malformed file is fatal, since silently serving no cache would be worse than failing to start.
src/main.cpp: resolves the log level, parses the config, starts the manager and HTTP server, then waits for SIGINT/SIGTERM.
Two adaptations were needed against the merged common layer, both beyond the mechanical namespace nesting:
  main.cpp consumed a LogLevel enum that no longer exists. https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/3825 replaced it with LogLevelConfig, which already reports glog's own values, so the four-case switch collapses to two assignments.
  Parsing helpers come from mooncake-common rather than being reimplemented: medium normalization uses AsciiToLower (ascii_string.h) instead of a local std::tolower transform, which also drops a locale-sensitive path from a comparison against ASCII literals, and the cache-group check uses TryParseInteger<int64_t> (integer_parser.h). Both substitutions were checked against the previous local implementations over 6470 inputs, including every single byte, the medium spellings the call sites compare against, signed and unsigned int64 boundaries and overflow, embedded NULs, and padded and whitespace-wrapped forms.
  yalantinglibs is guarded with if(NOT TARGET yalantinglibs::yalantinglibs): the top-level build already provides it through mooncake-common, and its config.cmake mutates an imported target owned by the parent scope, so it cannot run twice.

Verified: builds standalone and under the top-level configuration, and conductor_test passes (169 tests across 34 suites, up from 113 across 25).

title: [TransferEngine] Add opt-in NVIDIA Data Direct registration
body:
## Description

Add opt-in NVIDIA Data Direct registration for CUDA device memory in the classic RDMA transport. On supported platforms, enable it with `MC_RDMA_DATA_DIRECT=1` and select compatible NICs using the existing device filter or custom topology.

The option pairs PCIe DMA-BUF export (`CU_MEM_RANGE_FLAG_DMA_BUF_MAPPING_TYPE_PCIE`) with `mlx5dv_reg_dmabuf_mr(..., MLX5DV_REG_DMABUF_ACCESS_DATA_DIRECT)`. It takes precedence over `WITH_NVIDIA_PEERMEM`, preserves shared DMA-BUF exports and per-chunk offsets, and leaves the existing registration path as the default. Unsupported configurations fail explicitly rather than falling back.

Runtime symbol lookup keeps the path available in CUDA wheels built with older RDMA headers, without adding a mandatory dependency on the newer mlx5 symbol. This does not add automatic NIC selection or change TENT/IBGDA registration.

## Description

Under `MC_USE_TENT=1`, `sendNotifyByName()` can invalidate a segment already opened by the caller. title: [TENT] Cover the RDMA context enable failure paths and link-speed events without an RNIC
body:
## Description

`RdmaContext::enable()` acquires a device, a PD, an epoll set, completion channels, data CQs and a notification CQ in order, and #3325 made a failure between any two steps release what had been acquired so far. None of that has been testable without an RNIC. The per-context verbs table from #3777 lets a test stand in for individual verbs, but `openDevice()` still called libibverbs directly for its GID scan, and `ibv_query_gid_ex()` is a header inline that dereferences `context->device`, so a stand-in `ibv_context` crashed inside the library before `enable()` got anywhere.

Two small production changes open the seam:

- `_ibv_query_gid_ex`, the entry point behind that inline, joins `IbvSymbols` with a `QueryGidEx()` helper hiding `entry_size`, and the three GID-scan call sites go through the table. The binary already links the symbol, so requiring it loses no host.
- `kIbvEventDeviceSpeedChange` names `IBV_EVENT_DEVICE_SPEED_CHANGE` where the header lacks the enumerator (the async-event ABI is append-only, so its value is 20, after `WQ_FATAL`), and `applyContextEvent()` switches on `int`. The branch that handles a speed change without a link flap is now compiled and tested everywhere instead of sitting behind `#ifdef`. A `static_assert` pins the fallback to the real enumerator on any build whose header has it, so a header that ever broke the append-only rule fails to compile rather than misroute an event.

On that seam, a `FakeRnic` stands in for a whole device with live counters of what is currently held, and 19 cases cover:

- every fakeable exit of `enable()` and `openDevice()` — unknown name, open failure, `ibv_query_device`, port out of range, no usable GID, `ibv_alloc_pd`, a later completion channel, a later data CQ, the notification CQ, the final port query — each asserting nothing is left held on either the device or the context;
- a port that is not ACTIVE at open lands in `DEVICE_PAUSED` with everything built;
- `openDevice()` seeds the effective speed, and falls back to the encoded rate when the verb reports 0;
- five async-event cases through `Workers::applyContextEvent`: `PORT_ACTIVE` re-seeds the selector only when the speed changed and still recovers the device when its re-read fails; `DEVICE_SPEED_CHANGE` re-seeds without touching availability, keeps the EWMA at an unchanged speed, and changes nothing when the re-read fails.

Not covered: `epoll_create1` and the fcntl/epoll_ctl exits, which are syscalls the table cannot stand in for, and the `active_speed_ex` decode, which the build image's rdma-core header lacks.

title: [Store] Prefer LOCAL_DISK replica when both LOCAL_DISK and DISK types exist
body:
## Description
This PR fixes a data retrieval failure and routing bug in `RealClient` during SSD Offloading when an object simultaneously possesses both `LOCAL_DISK` and `DISK` replicas. It ensures proper data retrieval functionality when `LOCAL_DISK` and `DISK` mutually coexist after an object's memory replica has been evicted.

**The Issue:**
1. **Ignored Priority System (Blind Indexing)**: In `RealClient::batch_get_into_internal` (and identically across `batch_get_buffer_internal`), the fetch dispatcher skipped `GetPreferredReplica()` entirely and naively locked onto `query_result_values.replicas[0]`. 
2. The system was coerced to bypass the dedicated high-efficiency SSD offline proxy (`batch_get_into_offload_object_internal`) and push the `LOCAL_DISK` item into the standard `Client::BatchGet` pipeline mappings. Standard backend transfers failed to parse or resolve `LocalDiskDescriptor` schemas concurrently, resulting in broken routes and failures.

**Fix**
- **Removed Hardcoded Indexing (Blind Indexing)**: Rewrote `RealClient` fetch pipelines to strictly call `client_->GetPreferredReplica()` uniformly across all batch operations instead of blindly seizing `replicas[0]`.
- **Removed Restrictive Routing Constraints**: Completely eliminated the `replicas.size() == 1` precondition. The path dispatcher now seamlessly routes data internally based purely on whether the optimal replica evaluates to `.is_local_disk_replica()`.
- **Secured Target Fetch Accuracy (Key Operations)**: Updated `KeyOp` properties to meticulously cache and utilize the specifically chosen `preferred_replica`. This guarantees that configurations with `[LOCAL_DISK, DISK]` naturally and safely detour into the `batch_get_into_offload_object_internal` channel, averting parsing collisions.

title: fix(s3_helper): disable flexible checksums for S3-compatible backend …
body:
## Problem

AWS C++ SDK >= 1.11.x defaults `requestChecksumCalculation` to `WHEN_SUPPORTED`, which appends CRC32 checksums via `aws-chunked` Transfer-Encoding trailer. Many S3-compatible backends (Baidu BCE, some MinIO/Ceph versions, Cloudflare R2) do not support flexible checksums and reject requests with `BadDigest` / `BadDigestSHA256` errors.

This breaks snapshot upload/restore in HA mode when using non-AWS S3 storage.

## Solution

- Set `requestChecksumCalculation` to `WHEN_REQUIRED` by default, so checksums are only sent when the API mandates them (e.g., `DeleteObjects` still gets `Content-MD5`).
- Controlled by env var `MOONCAKE_S3_DISABLE_FLEXIBLE_CHECKSUMS` (default: `true`). Users connecting to AWS S3 with strict checksum requirements can set it to `false` to restore the SDK default behavior.
- Guarded by SDK version macro (`AWS_SDK_VERSION_MAJOR >= 1 && AWS_SDK_VERSION_MINOR >= 11`) and `__has_include` to ensure backward compatibility with older SDK versions.

## Testing

- Tested in production with Baidu BCE Object Storage
- HA failover scenario: leader kill → standby promotion → snapshot restore from S3 ✅
- Snapshot upload (PutObject) ✅
- Snapshot download (GetObject) ✅

## Compatibility

| SDK Version | Behavior |
|---|---|
| < 1.11 | No change (flexible checksums API doesn't exist) |
| >= 1.11, env default | Checksums disabled (WHEN_REQUIRED) |
| >= 1.11, env=false | SDK default restored (WHEN_SUPPORTED) |

title: [Bugfix][TENT] Allow default host allocations with SHM
body:
## Description

With SHM enabled, `allocateLocalMemory(&ptr, size)` selects SHM for host memory but fails because SHM rejects the default `"*"` location. On a SHM-only engine, the `MemoryOptions` overload also fails: its unspecified-type selection never considers SHM.

Resolve the default host location in the engine before calling SHM, and add SHM as the last host allocator fallback without changing existing allocator priorities. SHM retains its CPU-only validation. The engine supplies `cpu:0` for the allocation call, then restores the caller's `"*"` location on both success and failure so subsequent registration still uses the actual memory-location probe. This does not add a NUMA placement policy or change other transports.

This is separate from #3581, which handles stale remote SHM mappings after reallocation.

## Description

title: [Store] Spread bucket offload across several disks
body:
## Description

We run SSD offload in production. It gives us a much larger cache tier than DRAM
alone and measurably lifts our KVCache hit rate. Our serving hosts, however,
have several SSDs each, and today offload can only use one of them: the rest of
the disks sit idle while the single configured disk caps both our offload
capacity and our offload bandwidth. To actually use the hardware we have, SSD
offload needs to span multiple disks.

`BucketStorageBackend` assumes a single offload root throughout: one quota, one
FIFO/LRU eviction order, one path builder. This PR lets
`MOONCAKE_OFFLOAD_FILE_STORAGE_PATH` take a comma-separated list of roots and
makes the bucket backend per-disk end to end. A single path keeps behaving
exactly as before — the single-disk case is just a list of length one.

RFC: #4230

**Configuration**

```bash
# Two offload disks, 200 GiB on each
export MOONCAKE_OFFLOAD_FILE_STORAGE_PATH=/nvme0/mooncake,/nvme1/mooncake
export MOONCAKE_OFFLOAD_BUCKET_MAX_TOTAL_SIZE_LIST=214748364800,214748364800
```

- `MOONCAKE_OFFLOAD_FILE_STORAGE_PATH` accepts a comma list; whitespace around
  entries is trimmed and empty entries dropped. Each root is validated on its
  own (`stat` of the raw list string would always be `ENOENT`).
- `MOONCAKE_OFFLOAD_BUCKET_MAX_TOTAL_SIZE_LIST` is a new, optional per-disk
  quota list, positionally aligned with the path list. Empty means broadcast
  the scalar `MOONCAKE_OFFLOAD_BUCKET_MAX_TOTAL_SIZE` to every disk; a shorter
  list reuses its last entry for the remaining disks. Because the alignment is
  positional, one unparsable entry cannot be skipped silently — that would
  shift every later disk onto its neighbour's quota — so the whole list is
  dropped with an error log and the scalar quota is used instead. Entries must
  be `> 0`, which is deliberately stricter than the scalar (where `<= 0` means
  "derive a default").
- **Limitation:** only `bucket_storage_backend` understands the list.
  `file_per_key_storage_backend` and `offset_allocator_storage_backend` use
  `storage_filepath` as a single directory, so they must stay on one path.

**Design points**

- **Per-disk accounting.** New `DiskState` holds `max_total_size`,
  `total_size`, `pending_write_size`, `pending_eviction_size`, its own
  FIFO/LRU eviction indices and its own `ActualDiskBytesUsed` scan cache.
  Quotas must not be global: a write reserved on one disk counted against
  another would make that disk evict to make room for bytes it never receives.
- **Disk selection is round-robin**, not most-free-wins. Free-space-greedy
  selection collapses onto one disk once the disks equalize, undoing the point
  of spreading writes.
- **Selection, reservation and eviction happen in one critical section**, so a
  concurrent writer cannot pick the same disk on stale free-space numbers. The
  chosen disk travels in `PendingEviction::disk_index` and every
  restore/commit/release step credits that same disk.
- **`BucketMetadata::disk_index`** routes path construction. It is not
  serialized: `Init()` re-derives it from the disk whose root the `.meta` file
  was found under, so existing on-disk data is readable without migration.
- **Watermark eviction is per-disk**, driven one disk at a time rather than off
  a single global watermark. `MOONCAKE_OFFLOAD_BUCKET_MAX_PHYSICAL_BYTES`
  likewise becomes a per-disk cap, since the `du`-equivalent scan runs per root.
- **Overlapping roots are rejected at `Init()`**, compared by path component so
  `/data/d1` is not mistaken for a child of `/data/d`.

Split into three reviewable commits:

1. `[Store] Parse multi-disk offload configuration` — config/env parsing,
   `SplitCommaList`, `ResolveOffloadDiskPaths`, validation. Compiles and passes
   tests on its own.
2. `[Store] Spread bucket offload across several disks` — the backend
   conversion.
3. `[Doc] Document multi-disk SSD offload configuration` — deployment docs for
   the new path form and quota list.

title: [CI] Stabilize HP TCP lane-distribution flake
body:
Fixes #4080.

`InterleavedPeersUseEveryConfiguredLane/1` (sliced read) flakes on contended CI: not every configured lane is woken for a 4 MiB transfer, and a recycled RPC port can hit a stale pooled connection.

- retry `getRemoteCached` once on `RpcServiceError` after `openRemote`
- print submit status on failure
- sliced-read: require `1..connections_per_peer` active sessions; WRITE path still expects full fan-out

Test-only.

title: [Store] Measure utilization and reuse in allocation_strategy_bench
body:
## Description

Follow-up to the discussion on #3787 and #4000: before deciding whether the allocator needs a new placement strategy for RL data-plane offload, we need a benchmark that says how much of the pool the current strategies actually keep
useful, and how much of that #3787 (`MANTISSA_BITS` 3 → 4) recovers on its own. This PR only adds that measurement to the existing `size_class_churn` workload of `allocation_strategy_bench`; it changes no allocator or master code.

### What is added

Four columns that split "utilization" into the parts different fixes can move:

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Useful%` | Live *requested* bytes / cluster capacity. The share of the pool doing work. |
| `IntFrag%` | Bytes the allocator *charged* minus bytes requested, / capacity. This is the size-class round-up, i.e. exactly what `MANTISSA_BITS` controls. Measured, not modelled: requested sizes are tracked in the live set and differenced against the allocator's own free-space report, so multiplier quantization is included. |
| `Fail@Util%` | `Useful%` at the first failed allocation. A run that fails with most of the pool free shows up here without reading the log. |
| `Survive%` | Share of objects that reached their own removal instead of being evicted to make room for another object. This is the benchmark's reuse rate: an object that is evicted before its consumer reads it is a cache miss for that consumer. |

Two size-class patterns:

- `variable`: equally weighted classes spread log-uniformly over
  `[--variable_min_kib, --variable_max_mib]`, four per octave. KV cache traffic
  is near-fixed-size, so a segment only has to have *enough* bytes free; RL
  offload hands the allocator data-dependent sizes spanning several octaves,
  and then a segment also has to have them *contiguous*. Quarter-octave steps
  keep sizes off power-of-two boundaries, which are exactly representable for
  any mantissa and would report `IntFrag% = 0` regardless of #3787.
- `trace`: size distribution read from a captured trace
  (`--size_class_trace_file`, one class per distinct requested size, weighted
  by count; accepts a sizes file or `put/remove` event lines from the master's
  `--v=1` log). Sizes are used as recorded; to make a small trace exercise a
  full pool, shrink `--segment_capacity` rather than scaling the sizes up.

The live set now records the requested byte count next to each replica vector
so the requested/charged split can be computed; the DSA path is untouched.

### What it shows

All numbers: 20000 allocations after prefill to 70%, `--size_class_evict_ratio=0.02`,fixed seed, averaged over the built-in {1, 10, 100} segments × {1, 2, 3} replicas × {uniform, skewed} matrix. "M=3" is `main` at `68ce2386`; "M=4" is
the same commit with #3787 merged, so the only difference between the two binaries is the allocator's bin granularity.

**Synthetic patterns, 4 GiB segments** (`variable` = 64 KiB … 1.5 GiB):

| Pattern | Strategy | Arm | AvgUtil% | IntFrag% | Fail@Util% | Survive% | Failed allocs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| kv_mixed | random | M=3 | 84.2 | 2.81 | – | 88.7 | 0 |
| kv_mixed | random | M=4 | 85.4 | 0.04 | – | 89.6 | 0 |
| kv_mixed | free_ratio_first | M=3 | 85.0 | 2.95 | – | 87.4 | 0 |
| kv_mixed | free_ratio_first | M=4 | 86.2 | 0.05 | – | 88.1 | 0 |
| variable | random | M=3 | 74.5 | 3.04 | 82.1 | 2.9 | 11433 |
| variable | random | M=4 | 73.8 | 1.34 | 83.6 | 3.1 | 11332 |
| variable | free_ratio_first | M=3 | 73.8 | 3.02 | 77.9 | 2.9 | 11250 |
| variable | free_ratio_first | M=4 | 74.5 | 1.37 | 79.7 | 3.0 | 11110 |

**Captured RL traces** (miles / Qwen3-0.6B GRPO through the Mooncake object
store, `put_parts` + explicit remove; segment size chosen so the largest object
is ~30% of a segment, the same ratio as the 1.25 GiB object in a 4 GiB segment
that motivated this work):

| Trace | Strategy | Arm | AvgUtil% | IntFrag% | Fail@Util% | Survive% | Failed allocs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| miles2 (max 11.8 MiB, 38 MB seg) | random | M=3 | 70.8 | 3.20 | 79.0 | 4.0 | 5339 |
| miles2 | random | M=4 | 66.3 | 1.43 | 79.0 | 4.5 | 5299 |
| miles2 | free_ratio_first | M=3 | 68.3 | 3.15 | 80.0 | 4.1 | 5013 |
| miles2 | free_ratio_first | M=4 | 69.1 | 1.50 | 81.7 | 4.4 | 4856 |
| miles1 (max 0.5 MiB, 2 MB seg) | random | M=3 | 68.1 | 2.30 | 71.5 | 4.8 | 4807 |
| miles1 | random | M=4 | 64.8 | 1.36 | 84.1 | 5.1 | 5162 |
| miles1 | free_ratio_first | M=3 | 70.0 | 2.47 | 73.1 | 4.7 | 4539 |
| miles1 | free_ratio_first | M=4 | 66.5 | 1.43 | 80.5 | 5.0 | 4596 |

Reading the columns:

1. **#3787 does what it says on internal fragmentation.** `IntFrag%` halves
   (3.0 → 1.35%) on every variable-size run, matching the `2^-M` bound. On
   `kv_mixed` it drops to ~0.04% because 3198 KB happens to sit 0.06% below an
   M=4 bin edge; that is a property of that one size, not a general gain.
2. **It does not move useful utilization or failures.** `AvgUtil%` changes by
   under 1 point in either direction; failed allocations change by −1% to +7%;
   `Survive%` is unchanged. Every variable-size run, synthetic or captured,
   starts failing with 15–30% of the pool still free (`Fail@Util%` 70–85%),
   identically on both arms. Recovering 1.6 points of scattered bytes does not
   produce a contiguous run.
3. **The driver is largest-object / segment-size, not size diversity.**
   `kv_mixed` has zero failures at 4 GiB segments, where its 3198 KB class is
   0.08% of a segment. Rerun with `--segment_capacity=10` so that class is 31%
   of a segment, it fails ~7000 times out of 20000 at 83–90% utilization; M=4
   drives `IntFrag%` to 0.03% there and failures drop by 2%. This is the
   incident's shape: 1.25 GiB objects in 4 GiB segments. Fixed-size KV traffic
   has never hit it because its objects are three orders of magnitude smaller
   than a segment.
4. `random` and `free_ratio_first` are indistinguishable on every column.
   Both spread load across segments, which is what keeps every segment's holes
   medium-sized.

The conclusion I draw is that the utilization gap under variable-size offload
is a placement problem, and #3787 is worth having for what it fixes but is not
a fix for this. Whether a placement change is warranted is left to a separate
PR with its own numbers from this benchmark; this one just makes the
measurement reproducible.

### Reproduce

```bash
# variable-size, 4 GiB segments, 64 KiB .. 1.5 GiB objects
./allocation_strategy_bench --workload=size_class_churn --size_class_pattern=variable \
  --segment_capacity=4096 --num_allocations=20000 --prefill_pct=70 \
  --size_class_evict_ratio=0.02 --variable_min_kib=64 --variable_max_mib=1536

# captured trace, segment sized so the largest object is ~30% of a segment
./allocation_strategy_bench --workload=size_class_churn --size_class_pattern=trace \
  --size_class_trace_file=miles2_events.txt --segment_capacity=38 \
  --num_allocations=20000 --prefill_pct=70 --size_class_evict_ratio=0.02

# fixed-size KV mix at the same object/segment ratio as the incident
./allocation_strategy_bench --workload=size_class_churn --size_class_pattern=kv_mixed \
  --segment_capacity=10 --num_allocations=20000 --prefill_pct=70
```

Build the second binary from a checkout with #3787 merged; the bench source is
identical on both.

## Module

- [x] Mooncake Store (`mooncake-store`)

## Type of Change

- [x] Other: benchmark instrumentation

## How Has This Been Tested?

**Test commands:**
```bash
cmake --build build --target allocation_strategy_bench
./build/mooncake-store/benchmarks/allocation_strategy_bench --workload=size_class_churn --size_class_pattern=all --num_allocations=500
./build/mooncake-store/benchmarks/allocation_strategy_bench --workload=size_class_churn --size_class_pattern=variable --segment_capacity=4096 --num_allocations=20000 --prefill_pct=70 --variable_max_mib=1536
./build/mooncake-store/benchmarks/allocation_strategy_bench --workload=size_class_churn --size_class_pattern=trace --size_class_trace_file=miles2_events.txt --segment_capacity=38 --num_allocations=20000 --prefill_pct=70
```

title: [Store] Bridge BatchGet completion into CUDA graph waits
body:
## Description

Add a CUDA-only completion barrier that lets a captured graph wait for a Store `TransferFuture` or a background `Client::BatchGet`. The barrier uses a mapped pinned host flag and `cuStreamWaitValue32`; it can be rearmed after each replay. `StartBatchGetWithCudaBarrier` retains the existing replica selection and read lease path. A failed read still releases the graph wait, and callers must discard graph output unless `barrier->wait()` returns `ErrorCode::OK`.

This is an incremental piece of #3610. It does not route the user's stream through Store transports, add `RealClient`/`PyClient` `*_on_stream` APIs, or cover Ascend/ADXL.

title: [TransferEngine] Cut WorkerPool submit locks with batched enqueue and rail count
body:
## Description

When several threads call `submitTransfer` at the same time, WorkerPool takes the per-worker queue mutex once per slice, and takes `rail_state_lock_` on every `isRailAvailable` check even when no rail is paused.

This PR:

1. Groups prepared slices by owner thread, then enqueues each owner's list under **one queue lock per worker per batch**.
2. Keeps an atomic `paused_rail_count_`. The healthy path of `isRailAvailable` returns immediately when the count is 0, without `rail_state_lock_`.
3. Increments the count only when a rail **first** pauses; decrements it when the pause expires. A second pause on an already-paused rail does not bump the count again.

API and completion semantics are unchanged. Slice posting, failover, and rail pause behavior are the same; only lock frequency on the submit path changes.

**Not in this PR:** CQ / `getBatchTransferStatus` (#4184), unsignaled WRs, NIC-path intern, last-hit device, or MR lookup (#4132). This is submit-path lock reduction only.

### Benefit (same tebench wait, this change only)

H20, `mlx5_bond_0` loopback, DRAM READ, 4096 B blocks, 5 s. Both sides use stock classic wait (`getTransferStatus` per task). Independent variable is WorkerPool vs `origin/main`.

Headline is **4-thread `submit_us`**. tebench `--start_num_threads=4` runs four full batches in parallel, so they contend on the same worker locks. The last row uses 4 threads × 51840, i.e. the same 207360 descriptors issued as four concurrent submits.

| threads | batch size | main submit p50 | this PR submit p50 | speedup | submit p99 |
|--------:|-----------:|----------------:|-------------------:|--------:|-----------:|
| 1 | 4096 | 2784 µs | 2638 µs | 1.06× | 2826 → 2682 µs |
| **4** | **4096** | **4025 µs** | **3190 µs** | **1.26× (−21%)** | 4170 → 3263 µs |
| 1 | 207360 | 69.7 ms | 63.9 ms | 1.09× | 70.3 → 66.7 ms |
| **4** | **51840** | **30.0 ms** | **23.1 ms** | **1.30× (−23%)** | **194 → 73 ms** |

- Single-thread submit barely moves, as expected: there is no queue-lock contention, only fewer lock/unlock pairs.
- Four threads show the lock tax: the same 4096-sized batch goes from 2.78 ms (1 thread) to 4.03 ms on main, and only to 3.19 ms with this PR. Four threads × 51840 also cuts the submit p99 from 194 ms to 73 ms (contention tail).
- Wait still walks every task, so it dominates wall time. Do not treat e2e BW as the win (4 threads × 51840 BW was 1.06 → 0.95 GB/s; wait noise). After #4184 the wait path is a separate O(1) poll; this PR does not replace that.

title: [Store] Parallelize OSS batches with independent request-scoped CURLM
body:
## Description

Performance follow-up to #3714. 

- Add synchronous `ObjectStorageAdapter::GetBatch` / `PutBatch`.
- Execute OSS requests concurrently within each batch using an independent request-scoped `CURLM`.
- Keep a bounded admission window so waiting requests retain their full HTTP timeout. 
- Receive GET data directly into caller buffers, eliminating the intermediate full-object string and subsequent copy.
- Reuse the existing iovec PUT path and support upload rewind on connection retry.

For compatibility with older system libcurl, use `curl_multi_wait` on all supported versions. Guard optional upload-buffer tuning on headers older than 7.62.0; the library default remains in effect there.

**Buffer lifetime:** synchronous batch calls return only after the batch finishes. Callers must keep download buffers, upload iovec arrays and upload payloads valid until return; upload memory must remain unchanged. This is not end-to-end zero-copy.

title: [Store]Redesign of NVMe‑oF High‑Speed Read‑Write Layer
body:
# Redesign of NVMe‑oF High‑Speed Read‑Write Layer

## Description

Redesign the Mooncake Store NVMe-oF I/O subsystem from single-qpair to multi-qpair pipeline architecture. Achieves **5.4× throughput improvement** (616 MiB/s → 3.26 GiB/s) on FORINN targets.

**Module**: Store — `mooncake-store/src/spdk/`
**Type**: New feature + bug fixes (existing `SpdkWrapper` API preserved, new methods added)

---

## Problem Statement

| Issue | Impact |
|-------|--------|
| Single I/O qpair per namespace | Write perf capped at ~1,820 MB/s (60% of target max) |
| No pipeline — sub-I/Os serialized on one qpair | Cannot exploit multi-qpair parallelism |
| `keep_alive_timeout_ms=0` (legacy `ApplyCtrlrOptsFromEnv`) | Stale connections permanently consume target queue slots after crash |

## Architecture

```
NofConfig (MC_NVME_* / MC_NOF_* env var configuration)
    │
NofConnection (multi-qpair connection factory, keep_alive > 0)
    │  └─ NofQpairPool (N qpairs, round-robin dispatch + inflight tracking)
    │
NofSegment (contiguous LBA range on one connection)
    ├─ SubmitRead/Write   (async single-request, backwards-compatible)
    ├─ PipelineRead/Write  (blocking pipeline, high-throughput — not yet wired into hot path)
    └─ PollCompletion      (poll all qpairs)
    │
SpdkWrapper (compatibility layer — existing API unchanged)
    ├─ QidPressureGauge   (sliding-window QID pressure sensing, mutex-protected)
    ├─ OpenNofSegment     (connect with backoff retry + adaptive degradation + TryGrow recovery)
    ├─ CloseNofSegment    (no-op on stale handle — prevents double-free during static destruction)
    └─ ProbeNofSegment    (heartbeat probe, independent temp connection, connect_mutex_-serialized)
```

## Files Changed

### New (5)

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `include/spdk/nof_config.h` | `NofConfig` struct + env var parsing (`FromEnv`, `ForRead`, `ForWrite`, `ForProbe`) |
| `include/spdk/nof_connection.h` | `NofQpairPool` + `NofConnection` class declarations |
| `src/spdk/nof_connection.cpp` | `Connect()` factory, qpair allocation, TryGrow recovery |
| `include/spdk/nof_segment.h` | `NofSegment` class + `PipelineCtx` |
| `src/spdk/nof_segment.cpp` | `PipelineIO` core loop, `SubmitRead`/`Write`, `PollCompletion` |

### Modified (7)

| File | Changes |
|------|---------|
| `include/spdk/spdk_wrapper.h` | `QidPressureGauge`, new segment APIs, internal state private |
| `include/transfer_task.h` | `SpdkNofTask`/`SubTask`/`Qos`, `SpdkNofWorkerPool`, `nof_cache_mutex_` |
| `src/spdk/spdk_wrapper.cpp` | Adaptive connect + backoff retry, heartbeat probe serialized, dead code removed |
| `src/transfer_task.cpp` | Worker thread with flow-control backpressure, periodic TryGrow rebalance, OOM-safe |
| `src/client_buffer.cpp` | NoF DMA buffers via unified `free_memory()` |
| `src/spdk/CMakeLists.txt` | Add new source files |
| `src/spdk/README.md` | Architecture, component reference, benchmark data, FAQ (English) |

## Core Implementation

**PipelineIO — high-throughput path** (`nof_segment.cpp`)

```
1. max_inflight = pool.Size() × max_inflight_per_qpair
2. chunk_blocks = config.chunk_blocks (default 512 = 2 MiB @ 4 KiB)
3. Guard: reject lba + total_blocks > num_blocks_
4. Guard: reject chunk_blocks == 0 || max_inflight == 0
5. while (next_block < total || inflight > 0):
   a. Submit: while (inflight < max_inflight && next_block < total):
      - chunk = min(remaining, chunk_blocks)
      - qp = pool.GetNextQpair()    // round-robin
      - spdk_nvme_ns_cmd_read/write(ns, qp, ptr, abs_lba + next_block, chunk, cb)
      - next_block += chunk, inflight++
   b. poll_rc = pool.PollAll(0)     // harvest all qpairs
   c. if (poll_rc < 0) return -1    // qpair fault → fail fast
6. return total_blocks × block_size
```

**NofConnection::Connect() — multi-qpair factory** (`nof_connection.cpp`)

```cpp
probe_cb:
    opts->num_io_queues        = config.num_io_queues;
    opts->keep_alive_timeout_ms = config.keep_alive_timeout_ms;
    // Unique hostnqn per connection (nqn.2024-08.mooncake:c<N>)

attach_cb: ctx->ctrlr = ctrlr;

// Sequential allocation — take as many as available, fail if < min_io_queues
for (i = 0; i < requested; i++) {
    qp = spdk_nvme_ctrlr_alloc_io_qpair(ctrlr, nullptr, 0);
    if (!qp) break;
    qpairs.push_back(qp);
}
```

## Key Design Decisions

| Category | Decision | Rationale |
|----------|----------|-----------|
| Correctness | LBA bounds check + `start_lba_` translation | Prevents silent cross-segment data corruption |
| Correctness | `CloseNofSegment` no-op on stale handle | Prevents double-free during static destruction |
| Correctness | OOM-safe: `set_completed(FAIL)` before discard | Prevents submitter hang on allocation failure |
| Thread safety | Double-checked locking for `nof_handle_cache_` | Cache hits brief; blocking `OpenNofSegment` outside lock |
| Thread safety | `connect_mutex_` in `ProbeNofSegment` too | `spdk_nvme_probe()` not thread-safe; heartbeat + I/O must serialize |
| Thread safety | Worker pool reset before handle close in `~TransferSubmitter` | Workers joined → no inflight tasks → handles safe to free |
| Performance | Round-robin qpair dispatch (`fetch_add`) | Uniform load distribution, lock-free |
| Performance | Adaptive inflight = `nq × inflight_per_qpair × blocks_per_chunk` | I/O count → block count conversion; shrinks on degradation |
| Robustness | Exponential backoff capped at 30 s | Prevents multi-hour hangs with extreme config |
| Robustness | `errno` reset before `strtoull`, `#include <cerrno>` | Self-contained parser, no stale-errno false failures |
| Transport | Trtype passed through, not hard-coded RDMA | `MC_NOF_TRTYPE=TCP` works end-to-end |
| API | Pipeline API implemented, not yet wired | `PipelineRead`/`Write` available for future hot-path integration |

## Benchmark Results

Test: FORINN HWE62P447T6L00LN target, single SSD, 8 MiB random read, `MC_NVME_MAX_INFLIGHT_PER_QPAIR=4`.

```bash
for qp in 1 2 4 8 16 32 64; do
    MC_NVME_NUM_IO_QUEUES=$qp MC_NVME_MAX_INFLIGHT_PER_QPAIR=4 \
    ./nof_worker_pool_bench \
        --endpoints "traddr:10.10.10.100 trsvcid:4420 subnqn:... trtype:RDMA adrfam:IPv4 ns:1" \
        --rw randread --io_size 8388608 --iodepth 64 --duration_sec 20 --warmup_sec 5
    sleep 5
done
```

| Req qp | Actual qp | Per-qp inflight | Total inflight | BW | vs qp=1 | Efficiency |
|--------|-----------|-----------------|----------------|-----|---------|------------|
| 1 | 1 | 4 | 4 | 616 MiB/s | 1.00× | — |
| 2 | 2 | 4 | 8 | 1.15 GiB/s | 1.91× | 96% |
| 4 | 4 | 4 | 16 | 2.11 GiB/s | 3.50× | 88% |
| 8 | 8 | 4 | 32 | **3.25 GiB/s** | **5.40×** | 68% |
| 16 | 8¹ | 4 | 32¹ | 3.28 GiB/s | 5.45× | — |
| 32 | 8¹ | 4 | 32¹ | 3.26 GiB/s | 5.43× | — |
| 64 | 8¹ | 4 | 32¹ | 3.26 GiB/s | 5.43× | — |

> ¹ Target per-controller I/O Queue cap (`nn`) limits allocation to ~8 qpairs. Throughput flatlines from qp=8 through qp=64 — the target, not client code, is the bottleneck.

- Multi-qpair scaling is near-linear up to the target's nn cap
- Low per-qpair inflight (=4) avoids target-side completion congestion
- Recommended config: `MC_NVME_NUM_IO_QUEUES=8`, `MC_NVME_MAX_INFLIGHT_PER_QPAIR=4`

title: [Store] Add WeightRevision metadata registry (RFC #4017 )
body:
## Description

Partial implementation of RFC #4017 (revision-level Weight Management), **slice PR1**.

Adds an in-memory `WeightMetadataStore` and Master/client/RPC APIs so a weight revision can be:

1. registered via `BeginWeightImport` (`IMPORTING`, invisible to Get/List)
2. published via `CommitWeightImport` as **READY + HOT** after payload/manifest keys exist
3. discovered via `GetWeightMetadata` / `ListWeightRevisions`
4. policy-updated with generation fencing via `UpdateWeightPolicy`

Related: #4017

### Out of scope for this PR

Python `weight_*` API convergence, HA OpLog/snapshot, residency migration, and revision leases.

### Follow-up plan (3+1)

**PR2 - safe read path + protect managed groups**
1. Revision lease for `weight_get` (TTL; blocks delete / release of existing readable replicas while held; allows creating new replicas)
2. Master + client wiring for lease acquire/release on the get path
3. Managed-group guard so generic `BatchEvict` / single-key `Remove` / cleanup **skip** members of a published weight group (with a skip metric)
4. Tests: get-with-lease vs remove returns BUSY; eviction cannot partially dismantle a READY revision

**PR3 - residency migration**
1. Explicit `weight_migrate` (HOT / COLD / MIXED) with operation records + batched progress
2. AUTO reconciliation under memory pressure (bounded per round, cooldown)

**PR4 (optional / later) - HA + API convergence**
1. Persist weight metadata / leases / operations via OpLog + master snapshot
2. `weight_management_oplog_capability_confirmed` rolling-upgrade gate
3. Converge public API to the RFC `weight_*` surface (remove unmanaged entry points last)

Happy to adjust these boundaries based on maintainer feedback.

title: [TransferEngine] Drain CUDA TCP prefetch before publishing failure
body:
**Closed:** the follow-up fix is now supplied directly in [the review thread on #4233](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/4233#discussion_r4059681599) as [commit 691a0055](https://github.com/jacklin78911-collab/Mooncake/commit/691a00557caeeabe8dec3658bd1d4aee3de0a7a9), for incorporation into that PR. This avoids maintaining a separate upstream PR that also includes #4233's changes. The fix has not yet been incorporated into #4233.

---

## Description

A failed multi-chunk CUDA TCP WRITE can publish `FAILED` while the next D2H prefetch still reads the caller's source buffer. The Asio completion handler retains the session through the terminal callback, so synchronizing only in the pipeline destructor is too late: callers may recycle the source as soon as the transfer becomes terminal.

Drain the send pipeline before the failure callback and during explicit cancellation, including shutdown paths that publish failure after stopping the IO pool. Successful transfers keep their existing synchronization and overlap. Add gated CUDA regression cases for pooled and unpooled transfers.

**Dependency:** this is a follow-up to #4233, which is still open, and addresses [the source-lifetime review comment](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/4233#discussion_r4056015195). The branch contains that PR's commit `c5c39093` followed by this fix. The incremental change is [commit 691a0055](https://github.com/jacklin78911-collab/Mooncake/commit/691a00557caeeabe8dec3658bd1d4aee3de0a7a9). This draft should follow #4233, or the fix can be incorporated into that PR.

title: [TransferEngine] Pipeline CUDA TCP staging with pinned buffers
body:
## Description

Use CUDA pinned host buffers for TCP staging and prefetch the next device-to-host chunk while the socket sends the current chunk. The two buffers are reused within a session; non-CUDA device backends retain their existing staging path. This is a focused part of the TCP fallback work in #3446.

On one RTX 5090 using same-host TCP loopback, 16 MiB transfers with 64 KiB chunks (30 iterations per run, three runs) had median WRITE throughput of 2536.88 to 3771.82 MiB/s (+48.7%) and READ throughput of 2538.43 to 3808.08 MiB/s (+50.0%). Cross-host performance has not been measured.

title: [Store] Serve Ping on a separate RPC server that clients discover on Connect
body:
## Description

**`Ping` can be served by a separate RPC server whose only thread never runs a data-plane handler, and clients find it by themselves.** This is the thread half of RFC #4181. The lock half is #4180, which removes `client_mutex_` and the guards from the `Ping` path but does not touch RPC threading. Production code: +114/−4 in six files. Default off.

**Depends on #4180.** With a single heartbeat thread, any lock wait inside `Ping` stalls every heartbeat at once. Without the lock half, one healthy client went `OFFLINE` in the RFC's join-storm run. Do not enable `--heartbeat_rpc_port` on a master without #4180.

### Why

coro_rpc gives each io thread its own `io_context`, binds an accepted connection to one of them for its lifetime, and runs non-coroutine handlers inline on the thread that read the request. A `Ping` is therefore read only by the io thread that owns its connection. If that one thread is inside a long handler, the `Ping` waits for it, even when every other io thread is idle, so raising `rpc_thread_num` does not remove the wait, and removing locks from `Ping` cannot help because nothing is waiting on a lock.

On `main`, `UnmountSegment` runs its O(keys) `ClearInvalidHandles` sweep inline when HA, snapshot or CXL is enabled. On a non-HA rig with `--enable_snapshot`, 18M keys and 12 concurrent unmounts, healthy clients' heartbeats stopped for 19.8 s on `main` and the master marked 6 of them `SUSPECTED`. Every `Ping` that took longer than 2 s completed within 8 ms of an `UnmountSegment` returning. With this PR the worst gap was 1.0 s and nothing was suspected. A run with only the lock half (#4182, now closed in favour of #4180) showed 29.1 s; the lock half does not act here, and the spread most likely comes from which io thread a heartbeat's connection happened to share with the deepest unmount queue. Each figure is a single run (RFC #4181 §4).

### What changes

- **Master.** `--heartbeat_rpc_port` (default 0; non-HA mode) starts a second `coro_rpc_server` with one io thread that serves only `Ping` and `ServiceReady`. Each `coro_rpc_server` owns its own `io_context_pool`, so the two servers share no io thread. A new `GetHeartbeatRpcPort` RPC on the main server returns the port (0 when disabled). In HA mode the flag logs a warning and is ignored.
- **Client.** `MasterClient::Connect` asks for the port, probes `ServiceReady` on it, and then sends `Ping` there. The heartbeat address gets its own connection pool, so a `Ping` also no longer shares connections with the client's own data-plane RPCs. Other RPCs are unchanged.

### Scope

- Non-HA only. In HA the remount after a promotion walks every metadata shard under exclusive `snapshot_mutex_`, which is where a heartbeat server would matter most; HA support (the supervisor's server lifecycle) is the follow-up listed in the RFC.
- RFC #4181 §7 asks the maintainers whether they would rather run every non-`Ping` handler on a worker pool instead; this PR will follow that answer.

### Rollout needs no coordination

The main server keeps serving `Ping`. A client that predates this change, a master that does not advertise a port, and an advertised server that does not answer all leave `Ping` on the main server. This is the design of #3541 on the P2P branch applied to `main`'s `Ping`, with the port discovered from the master instead of configured on every client, which removes the client/master mismatch cases #3541 had to add error codes for. (A new client connecting to an older master logs one `RPC call failed` line per `Connect` for the unknown RPC, then behaves as before.) A deployment that remaps ports between the client and the master (for example a Kubernetes Service whose `port` differs from its `targetPort`) must expose the heartbeat port under the same number; otherwise clients stay on the main server.

## Module

- [x] Mooncake Store (`mooncake-store`)

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix
- [x] New feature

## How Has This Been Tested?

**Integration test (new) `heartbeat_rpc_server_test`**, with real servers and a real `MasterClient`:
- `PingIsServedWhileTheMainIoThreadIsBusy`: with the heartbeat server, `Ping` returns within 2 s while the main server's only io thread is held by a blocking handler.
- `PingWaitsForTheMainIoThreadWithoutTheServer`: the control. Without it, `Ping` does **not** return within 2 s.
- `PingFallsBackToTheMainServerWhenUnreachable`: an advertised port nobody listens on leaves `Ping` on the main server.
- `PingWaitsForABusyIoThreadEvenWhenAnotherIsIdle`: the main server has two io threads and one of them is held. Of two connections opened before the hold, the `Ping` on the one that shares the held thread does not return within 2 s, while the other does. Raising `rpc_thread_num` leaves the wait in place for the connections on a busy thread.

**Results:** the three original tests 3/3, repeated 5× with no flake; `master_service_test` 58/58 (Release, GCC 13, Ubuntu 24.04). The new test: a standalone copy with the same fixture and the pinned yalantinglibs passes 50/50, and the same assertion fails with one or three io threads, so it does check the placement. On the real target it passes in this PR's CI (`CTest unit tests`).

**Rig.** Measurements for both dimensions, alone and together, are in RFC #4181 §4.

title: [Store] Defer a client mass expiry the master cannot rule out as its own stall
body:
## Description

## The failure mode

`ClientMonitorFunc` expires a client whose heartbeat deadline has passed, and expiry
is irreversible: the client's segments are unmounted and every key they held is
erased from the index. The monitor decides this from the **absence** of heartbeats,
which looks exactly the same whether the clients died or the master stopped serving
`Ping`.

So any stall in the master longer than `client_ttl` (default 10 s) makes it expire
**every client at once** and destroy the whole cluster's cache index. A transient
control-plane stall becomes permanent, cluster-wide data loss.

We hit this in production and reproduced all of it. `Ping`'s body is a shared-lock
read of `ok_client_` plus a push onto a lock-free queue, so an exclusive
`client_mutex_` holder is the one thing that can stop the handler running at all —
and because coro_rpc runs a non-coroutine handler inline on the io thread, io
threads blocked on that lock stop reading pings off their connections entirely. We
measured `master_ping_requests_total` completely flat for nine consecutive seconds
while one such hold ran.

## Why this is an operational problem, not just a rare edge case

**The trigger sits on the rollout path.** `ReMountSegment` is the only way into
`ok_client_`, so *every* store client start goes through it — a deploy, a rolling
update, a scale-out, an eviction, a node reboot, a DaemonSet update. The operations
run most often are the ones that can wipe the cluster's cache.

**And the penalty is charged in exactly the currency operators are trying to save.**
The loss is the cache, and re-warming a cache is far more expensive than the pod
boot that preceded it, so a fleet roll turns into a roll followed by a long cold
period. The joining node's own cache also comes online late, because its segments
are not usable until its remount returns. The rational response is to avoid
restarting store pods at all — which is the opposite of fast, frequent, safe
deploys, and it blocks the ordinary capacity work of scaling a cell out and back in.

For scale: on our rig, the metadata scan in `ReMountSegment` took 0.72 s at 1M
keys, 9.76 s at 14M and 13.2 s at 18M, against a 10 s `client_ttl` — a threshold at
roughly 14.2M keys. One of our production deployments holds 14.6M, so it sits above
the threshold in steady state; a single store pod restart there expires all of its
clients.

#3533 removed the largest scan on that path, and it helped. But the exposure is
structural rather than tied to that one scan: **any** exclusive `client_mutex_` hold
that outlasts `client_ttl` reproduces the same irreversible outcome. There is also
an inconsistency between the two defaults — `client_ttl` is 10 s while the client's
own RPC wait is coro_rpc's 30 s default, so the master gives up on a client well
before that client gives up on the master.

What this PR adds is the property that makes the join path safe to keep optimizing:
a regression there becomes a bounded deferral instead of a cluster-wide cache loss.

## What the change does

A circuit breaker in `ClientMonitorFunc`. When a tick's expiry candidates cannot be
distinguished from the master's own stall, it holds them back — a true no-op, with
no unmount prepared and no sweep started — bounded by
`client_mass_expiry_grace_sec`. Recovery needs no machinery: the next queue drain
refreshes the deadlines and the episode closes itself.

The judgement is a pure function, `EvaluateClientMassExpiry`, over one tick's
readings, which is what lets its boundary cases be a table-driven test with no
sleeping.

**It judges the cause, not the symptom.** The primary condition is that an exclusive
`client_mutex_` hold overlapped `[last_ping_batch_at, now]`, the stretch over which
this master has no heartbeat of its own to show. Every site taking that lock
exclusively records its hold window into relaxed atomics; the monitor's own expiry
branch deliberately does not, so a previous tick's expiry cannot come back as
evidence that the master was stalling.

Two things about that window are load-bearing:

- A completed hold counts **only while no heartbeat has been popped since it
  released**. Once one has, the master is demonstrably serving `Ping` again, that
  hold is refuted as an explanation, and a candidate still overdue is genuinely
  gone — so an ordinary single-client death is not deferred.
- The edge follows the heartbeat stream and **not the wall clock**. After a hold
  releases, the master can stay starved for many more ticks; through that no
  heartbeat is popped, so the released hold stays evidence. A window of "holds
  within the last tick or two" would age out mid-stall and erase the cache.

A secondary condition covers a total stall with no hold recorded: the master's own
silence, gated on there being at least two tracked clients — with exactly one
client, hearing nothing says only that that client stopped, which is the client's
own problem and must be acted on at once.

We tried symptom-based rules first — "too many clients expired in one tick" — and
they were defeated twice by the same thing: a deadline is stamped by the tick that
popped that client's heartbeat, so a stall's expiries spread across consecutive
ticks and each tick's share falls under any threshold. That is why the rule is
cause-based, and it is worth not simplifying back.

## The behaviour change a reviewer should weigh

A genuine simultaneous death of every client is deferred up to the grace bound
before being expired. This is inherent, not an oversight: a fleet that has vanished
and a master that has totally stalled produce identical heartbeat streams — none —
so no rule can separate them. The cost is bounded and observable
(`master_client_expiry_deferred_total`, and a `LOG(ERROR)` when the grace is
exceeded), and it buys the difference between a bounded delay and an unrecoverable
cache wipe.

Two gaps stay open and are stated in the code:

1. A single-client deployment starved by something other than a `client_mutex_`
   hold — all io threads busy on shard locks, say — records no hold, and one tracked
   client is not silence evidence, so that deployment's keys still go. Closing it
   needs a liveness signal off the data path.
2. The whole-fleet case above.

The guard is on by default and `client_mass_expiry_guard=false` restores the
previous behaviour exactly.

## Verification

Reproduced and gated on a 13-client deployment with the master under the same 8-CPU
and 60 GiB limits it runs with in production.

- **The stall, at 18M keys.** A joining client's remount held the lock for 13.8 s
  against a 10 s TTL. With the breaker: **zero** expiries, key count held at
  18,000,000, active clients never fell below the 12 long-lived ones, and the
  episode closed itself three ticks later when the hold released. Without it, all
  13 expire in one tick and the sweep erases the keys.
- **No false positive on an ordinary death.** One client killed while the others
  keep pinging expires after one TTL (10.66 s), with zero deferral ticks. Under a
  pinned window instead of `last_ping_batch_at`, the same case was deferred for the
  full 60 s grace — which is what motivated that edge.
- **Single-client deployment, both directions.** A lone death expires 1.4 s after
  `SIGKILL`; a genuine stall defers on hold evidence alone and preserves its keys.

Unit tests on this branch, built and run against `8715bb7c`: `master_service_test`
**80/80**, `master_service_config_test` **9/9**, the breaker's own 11 cases
(7 wall-clock, 4 pure) **11/11**, and `master_service_group_test` **13/13**, which
is the other consumer of the fixture header these tests extend. The tests were also
checked for discriminating power rather than just for passing — deleting the primary
condition fails only the stall and tick-split cases, and pinning the window's left
edge fails only the ordinary-death case.

title: [Store] Let Ping record a heartbeat without waiting for client_mutex_ or its own liveness record
body:
## Description

**`Ping` no longer waits for `client_mutex_` or for its own client's liveness-record mutex.** This is the lock half of RFC #4181; the thread half is #PRB. Neither is sufficient alone — measured in the RFC — and each is reviewable on its own. Production code: +85/−8 in three files.

### Why

`Ping` read the caller's liveness record and `ok_client_` under `client_mutex_` (shared), and recorded the heartbeat through `ClientLivenessRecord::transition_mutex_`. Both are held for data-dependent time by data-plane work:
- `client_mutex_` is exclusive in `MountSegment`, `ReMountSegment` (including the 1024-shard walk after an HA promotion), `MountLocalDiskSegment`, `RestoreFromStandbyState`, client offboarding and the monitor's retirement.
- `transition_mutex_` is held for the lifetime of every `ServingGuard`/`RetainingGuard`, and `ReMountSegment` holds the remounting client's guard for the whole remount.

While either is held, a live client's heartbeat is not recorded and the RPC thread carrying it is parked, so the monitor moves healthy clients to `SUSPECTED` and eventually `OFFLINE`.

### What changes

1. **Immutable client view.** Every exclusive `client_mutex_` section that changes `client_liveness_records_` or `ok_client_` publishes a `ClientView` copy of the two on scope exit, through an RAII helper declared right after the lock (so it runs before unlock on every return path). `Ping` reads the view with `std::atomic_load_explicit`, as `replica.h` and `allocator.h` already do for liveness records. Writers are unchanged.
2. **`ClientLivenessRecord::ObserveHeartbeat`.** Publishes the heartbeat time atomically and only *try*-locks `transition_mutex_`. If a guard holds it, `Evaluate` still counts the heartbeat — an `ACTIVE` client is not suspected and a `SUSPECTED` client does not go `OFFLINE` — and the next heartbeat that gets the mutex recovers the state exactly as `Observe` does. Only `Ping` uses it.

### Why semantics are preserved

- The status `Ping` returns was already stale by the time it reached the client; `view_version_` in the same response is read without the lock today.
- The view is published before `MountSegment`/`ReMountSegment` return. A `Ping` that raced one of them gets `NEED_REMOUNT` once and the client calls the idempotent `ReMountSegment` it already retries on every ping.
- A heartbeat that lands on a record the view no longer contains is lost; the next ping (1 s later) repairs it. An `OFFLINE` record still rejects heartbeats.
- `ObserveHeartbeat` changes state only under `transition_mutex_` and only from `SUSPECTED` to `ACTIVE`, so no guard invariant changes.

## Module

- [x] Mooncake Store (`mooncake-store`)

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix

## How Has This Been Tested?

**Unit tests (new).**
- `MasterServiceTest.PingRecordsLivenessWhileClientMutexIsHeldExclusively` — a thread holds `client_mutex_` exclusively; `Ping` must return within 2 s and the record must already be `ACTIVE`.
- `MasterServiceTest.PingReturnsWhileTheClientsOwnRecordIsGuarded` — a `RetainingGuard` is held; `Ping` must return within 2 s.
- `MasterServiceTest.PingSeesReMountedClientAsSoonAsReMountReturns`, `PingSeesUnknownClientAsNeedRemount`, `PingReportsNeedRemountOnceClientGoesOffline` — the view is published on the paths that matter.
- `ClientLivenessRecordTest.HeartbeatDoesNotWaitForAGuardHolder`, `HeartbeatDuringSuspicionPreventsOffline`, `HeartbeatIsRejectedOnceOffline`.

The first two **fail on current `main`** (`Ping` does not return in 2 s) and pass with this PR.

**Results:** `master_service_test` 63/63, `client_liveness_test` 8/8; the eight new tests repeated 5× with no flake (Release, GCC 13, Ubuntu 24.04).

**Integration.** Rig measurements for both PRs, alone and together, are in RFC #4181 §4.

title: [Bugfix][Store] Make local MEMORY preference independent of replica order
body:
## Description

`SelectBestReplica` documents the priority `local MEMORY > local NOF_SSD > remote MEMORY > remote NOF_SSD`, but it previously returned the first complete local MEMORY or NOF replica encountered. As a result, `[local NOF, local MEMORY]` selected NOF while the reverse ordering selected MEMORY.

This PR makes the documented priority independent of the order returned by the master.

## Change

The selector scans all complete MEMORY and NOF candidates before deciding, records local and remote candidates separately, and then applies the existing priority. Other replica tiers and remote-replica scoring behavior remain unchanged.

## Regression coverage

- `LocalMemoryBeatsLocalNoFInBothOrders`: local MEMORY wins in both permutations.
- `IncompleteLocalMemoryFallsBackToLocalNoF`: an unreadable local MEMORY candidate does not hide a usable local NOF replica.
- `LocalNoFPrecedesRemoteMemory`: locality still outranks a remote MEMORY candidate.

The final two guard cases were adapted from `2sumtech/Mooncake@67bfff5d`, as coordinated in #3742.

## Scope coordination

- #3903 has merged MEMORY/DFS ranged-session support. This PR no longer changes `batch_get_session_start`, session replica selection, or ranged-session execution.
- Maintainer guidance in #3742 selected #3662 as the canonical implementation of the ordering fix and requested moving #3742's guard coverage here.
- #3658 remains open for file-backed/SSD session behavior; this PR does not claim to fix it.

title: [Store] Add exist_key_grant_lease flag to opt out of leasing on existence probes
body:
## Description

`ExistKey` / `BatchExistKey` currently grant a read lease on **every hit** (`master_service.cpp:2780` and `:2851`). A read lease pins the object so it cannot be evicted until the lease TTL expires (default 10s), and `BatchEvict` skips any leased object outright:

```cpp
// master_service.cpp:10250
if (!it->second.IsLeaseExpired(now) || !has_evictable) continue;
```

This is fine when existence checks track actual reads one-to-one. **But for read-heavy workloads the probe rate and coverage vastly exceed the read rate, and leasing on probes starves eviction.** The concrete trigger is vLLM's KV-cache-offload connector (`MooncakeStoreConnector`, in the vLLM tree at `vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/mooncake/store/`):

- On every request, the scheduler calls `client.lookup(...)` (`connector.py` → `scheduler.py`) to decide how much prefix it can reuse.
- `lookup` expands **all** prefix-candidate block hashes — further multiplied across each rank namespace — into one big `candidate_keys` list and issues a single `store.batch_is_exist(candidate_keys)` (`worker.py:1944`), which lands as `BatchExistKey` on the master.
- It then reads back **only the longest matching prefix** (`worker.py:1964-1990`). Every other hit — probed but not read this request — still got a fresh 10s lease.

With a small memory tier under steady-state eviction, the same hot blocks are re-probed faster than TTL/2, so their leases never expire. Nearly the entire working set stays pinned, `BatchEvict` finds no evictable candidates, and new `Put`s fail with `NO_AVAILABLE_HANDLE`. This was observed in production as **Eviction Success/Attempts = 39/1123** with puts rejected (`-200`).

**Fix:** add a master config flag `exist_key_grant_lease` (default `true`, i.e. upstream behavior unchanged), wired through the existing gflag/config path exactly like `promotion_on_hit`. When set to `false`, `ExistKey`/`BatchExistKey` no longer grant leases — intended for read-heavy + frequent-eviction deployments (e.g. vLLM KV offload on a small memory tier).

**Why this is safe:** actual reads are unaffected — `GetReplicaList` grants its own lease (`master_service.cpp:3678` / `3865`) to protect the read-in-flight window. The only behavioral change when disabled is that a probe→read race may evict an entry in between, which for the offload connector is just a normal cache miss (the tokens are recomputed locally). Correctness is preserved either way. This is an opt-in, backward-compatible flag with no `USE_PHOENIX` dependency.

## Module

- [x] Mooncake Store (`mooncake-store`)

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix
- [x] Performance improvement

## How Has This Been Tested?

Added three unit tests in `mooncake-store/tests/master_service_test.cpp`:

- `ExistKeyGrantsLeaseByDefaultBlockingEviction` — default (`true`): an `ExistKey` hit leases the object, so it survives `RunBatchEvictForTesting(1.0, 1.0)`.
- `ExistKeyDoesNotGrantLeaseWhenDisabled` — `false`: the probed object is evicted under full pressure; a subsequently re-put object read via `GetReplicaList` still survives (confirming real reads remain protected).
- `BatchExistKeyDoesNotGrantLeaseWhenDisabled` — `false`: same for the batch path.

title: [Store] Add ProbeKey/BatchProbeKey RPCs for lease-free existence probes
body:
## Description

Implements Option A of #3769: add `ProbeKey` / `BatchProbeKey`, lease-free twins of `ExistKey` / `BatchExistKey`, for point-in-time existence checks.

Unlike `ExistKey`, a successful probe grants no read lease, so speculative scans (e.g. probing candidate keys for KV-cache prefix reuse) can no longer pin the working set against eviction and block the demotion path to SSD. A `true` result only means the object existed at the time of the call; callers must treat a following miss as normal. Reads remain protected since `GetReplicaList` grants its own lease.

The new RPCs share the same lookup path as `ExistKey` (refactored into a `grant_lease`-parameterized impl) and cross all client layers: `WrappedMasterService` (coro_rpc), `MasterClient`, `Client`, `RealClient` / `DummyClient` (`PyClient`), and the Python binding (`probe_key` / `batch_probe_key`), plus the Python API docs. `store_c.h` and the generated Rust bindings are intentionally untouched, per the RFC. Purely additive: existing clients are unaffected and rolling upgrades are safe in both directions.

## Module

- [x] Mooncake Store (`mooncake-store`)
- [x] Integration (`mooncake-integration`)
- [x] Docs

## Type of Change

- [x] New feature

## How Has This Been Tested?

**Test commands:**
```bash
./build/mooncake-store/tests/master_service_test --gtest_filter='*ProbeKey*:*ExistKeyLeasesPinSegment*'
./build/mooncake-store/tests/master_service_test
./build/mooncake-store/tests/pybind_client_test
```

**Test results:**
- [x] Unit tests pass

title: [Bugfix][Conductor] Clamp query match to the queried token count
body:
# Issue #4153 — incorrect external prefix-cache reuse from partial hash hits

## 1. Root cause

`PrefixCacheTable::Query` converts a matched *block* count into a *token* count
with `TokensForBlocks(cursor, context.block_size)`, i.e. it assumes every block
in the query's hash chain covers exactly `block_size` tokens.

That assumption holds for the vLLM chain, whose `BlockCount()` is
`token_ids.size() / block_size` (complete blocks only). It does **not** hold for
the SGLang chains: `SglangHashChain` deliberately mirrors the engine and ends
its chain with a *partial* block —

```
block_count_ = token_ids.size() / block_size_ + (token_ids.size() % block_size_ != 0)
```

(see `SglangHashChain` in `mooncake-conductor/src/prefixindex/hash_strategy.cpp`
and the existing `SglangHashChain.IncludesPartialFinalBlock` test).

So whenever a query's prompt length is not a multiple of `block_size` **and**
the trailing partial block is present in the index, `Query` reported

    ceil(n / block_size) * block_size  tokens

for a prompt of only `n` tokens. Concretely, with `block_size = 16` and a
40-token prompt the conductor answered `longest_match_tokens = 48` — 8 tokens
that no indexed block ever covered, and that lie past the end of the prompt
altogether.

This is the mechanism described in the issue: the hit is real at the *hash*
granularity, but the reported reusable length runs past the region the hash
actually pinned down. A router or scheduler that trusts that length skips
recomputing KV slots whose contents belong to whatever request wrote them,
which surfaces as out-of-order / off-topic generation. The over-report grows
with `block_size`, which is why it only became visible on a deployment where
hash blocks and attention blocks were not aligned, and why forcing the two to
be equal (so no partial tail is ever hit) made it disappear.

The three tiers are all affected, because `gpu`, `cpu` and `disk` share one
cumulative cursor and all three go through the same conversion.

## 2. The fix and why

`mooncake-conductor/src/prefixindex/prefix_indexer.cpp`

Added a small `MatchedTokens(block_count, block_size, queried_tokens)` helper
next to `TokensForBlocks`, and used it for the `gpu` / `cpu` / `disk` numbers.
It is `TokensForBlocks` clamped to the number of tokens the query actually
carries.

Why a clamp is exactly right rather than merely safe:

- **vLLM chain** — `block_count * block_size <= n` by construction, so the
  clamp never fires. Behaviour is bit-for-bit unchanged.
- **SGLang chain** — blocks `[0, c)` cover `min(c * block_size, n)` tokens, so
  the clamp reproduces the true covered length, including the full-match case
  where the answer should be the whole prompt.
- **SGLang bigram chain** — the chain covers `n - 1` bigram positions. Matching
  all of them pins every one of the `n` tokens, so clamping to `n` is correct;
  a partial run still reports `c * block_size`, which is one token short of
  what the bigram overlap strictly proves and therefore conservative.

Under-reporting is a missed cache hit; over-reporting is silent corruption, so
where the two chains disagree the code now rounds toward the safe side.

The alternative — dropping the partial block from the SGLang chain entirely —
was rejected: including it is a deliberate, tested property that mirrors what
the engine publishes, and removing it would throw away genuine hits. The bug is
in the accounting, not in the hashing.

The design doc claimed `/query` "ignores trailing partial blocks", which was
already untrue for the SGLang strategies before this change. That sentence now
states the per-strategy behaviour and the token-count rule.

## 3. Files changed

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `mooncake-conductor/src/prefixindex/prefix_indexer.cpp` | New `MatchedTokens` helper; `Query` uses it for the gpu/cpu/disk token counts. |
| `mooncake-conductor/tests/prefix_indexer_test.cpp` | `SglangProfile()` / `SglangHashes()` helpers plus two regression tests. |
| `docs/source/design/conductor/conductor-architecture-design.md` | Corrected the one-sentence description of partial-block handling in `/query`. |

## 4. Risk / uncertainty

- **Low blast radius.** The only behaviour change is a `std::min`, and it can
  only lower a reported number. For the vLLM strategy it is provably a no-op
  (`block_count = floor(n / block_size)`), so existing vLLM deployments and all
  31 pre-existing conductor unit tests are unaffected.
- **Routing shifts slightly for SGLang.** Instances whose match previously
  rounded up to a block boundary now report the real prompt length. That can
  change which instance a cache-aware router picks when two candidates are
  within one block of each other. This is the intended correction.
- **Bigram partial runs stay conservative** (`c * block_size` rather than
  `c * block_size + 1`). Deliberate: it can only cost a single token of reuse,
  never invent one. Worth a maintainer's confirmation if bigram partial-run
  precision matters to them.
- **Not addressed here (out of scope for this issue):** `ValidateLayout` still
  requires `effective_block_size == context.block_size`, so a publisher whose
  attention block differs from its hash block is rejected at registration
  rather than handled. If the conductor ever needs to index a engine whose
  page size exceeds the hash unit, the match would additionally need rounding
  down to the page boundary. Nothing in the current tree exercises that path.
- The issue text also mentions eviction failures and a near-full store. Those
  are separate symptoms; this change does not touch them.

## 5. How it was verified

The container has no glog/gtest/OpenSSL dev packages, so the full CMake build
could not run. The affected translation units were instead compiled and
executed directly, against the **real** OpenSSL (`libcrypto.so.3`, EVP path) so
the hash chain is genuine, with a stub header only for glog's two logging
macros:

```
g++ -std=c++20 -DCONDUCTOR_HAS_LOWLEVEL_SHA256=0 \
    -I mooncake-conductor/include -I mooncake-common/include -I <glog-stub> \
    mooncake-conductor/src/prefixindex/{hash_strategy,prefix_indexer}.cpp
```

1. **Reproduced the bug.** A driver registering an `sglang` profile with
   `block_size = 16`, storing all 3 chain hashes of a 40-token prompt, then
   querying it. Against `HEAD`'s `prefix_indexer.cpp`:

   ```
   block count: 3
   full-match  gpu=48 cpu=48 disk=48 longest=48 (prompt=40)
   ```

   48 reported tokens for a 40-token prompt — 8 phantom tokens.

2. **Confirmed the fix.** Same driver against the patched file:

   ```
   full-match  gpu=40 cpu=40 disk=40 longest=40 (prompt=40)
   whole-only  gpu=0 cpu=0 disk=32 longest=32
   ```

3. **Ran the real unit-test file.** `prefix_indexer_test.cpp` was linked against
   a fused gtest and run:
   - patched build: **32/32 pass**, including the two new tests;
   - `HEAD` build with the new tests applied: **31 pass, 1 fail** —
     `Query.TrailingPartialBlockNeverReportsMoreThanPromptTokens`.

   So the new test is a genuine regression guard, and no pre-existing conductor
   test changed behaviour.

4. **Formatting.** `pre-commit` is not installed here; `clang-format` (the
   `mooncake-code-format` hook's tool) was run over both changed C++ files and
   produced no further edits. Trailing whitespace and end-of-file newlines were
   checked by hand on all three files. `make html` was not run for the
   docs/ change — the Sphinx toolchain is not available offline; the edit is a
   prose-only sentence replacement inside an existing paragraph, with no links,
   directives, or toctree entries touched.

title: [Store] Add AgentHints retention hint and prototype soft-pin behavior
body:
## Description

Refs #2098.

Add the Store-side `agent_hints` contract for agent-aware KV cache work: an
optional `AgentHints { reuse_hint, cache_ttl_ms }` carried on
`ReplicateConfig`, validated and translated into the existing soft-pin
retention when a write resolves its soft-pin request.

The v1 hint surface is intentionally minimal. Only `reuse_hint="keep"` and
`cache_ttl_ms` drive behavior (soft-pin retention bounded by the master's
max soft-pin TTL); `neutral` and `discard` add no retention, and invalid
hints are rejected with `INVALID_PARAMS`. Hints are never stored as object
metadata and the snapshot format is unchanged: the materialized soft-pin
deadline is the only retained state, and soft pin remains runtime-only per
the existing design. Fields with no store-side consumer are deliberately
not carried; they can be added when a consumer exists.

This revision is a refactor of the earlier draft: the twelve-field
speculative schema, its size-limit validation machinery, the agent-hints
snapshot encoding (v5/v6 formats and the standby-provider tail heuristic),

title: [TENT]: Rate-limit TENT failure-storm logs & fix rail-cooldown defects
body:
## Description

When a peer store is killed or restarted, the TENT produces tens of thousands of noise lines per second (1.1GB observed in one incident), and the rail cooldown has two defects that amplify the outage window.
Two parts: **(1) log rate-limiting**; **(2) rail-cooldown semantic fixes (defects A/B)**.

## Problem

After a store kill/restart, RDMA completion errors trigger `RailMonitor::markFailed`, which pauses the rail.
While paused, these logs flood per slice/task (observed counts):

| Log | Source | Count |
|---|---|---|
| `Failed to generate post path ... DeviceNotFound` | `workers.cpp` `generatePostPath` | 3.2M |
| `Transport failover: rdma -> tcp` | `transfer_engine_impl.cpp` `resubmitTransferTask` | 3.2M |
| `TCP transfer retry/failed` | `tcp_transport.cpp` retry loop | ~1800 |
| `SubscribeSegmentUpdate RPC failed` | `control_plane.cpp` | ~430 |
| `Optimal device pair not available` / `fallback device selection` | `workers.cpp` `selectOptimalDevice` | 10k+ |

This fills the disk (1.1GB), slows the hot path (glog lock + formatting), and drowns `Detected error WQE` / `Endpoint marked for destruction`, the triage-critical logs (only 8 in a single failure).

Before the fix (09-07 12:58 incident): 8 error WQEs → cooldown escalated to 300s → 5-minute flood (3.2M lines / 1.1GB).

After the fix (09-08 02:06 incident, three-side logs aligned):

| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| 02:06:27 | store killed; rail paused (cooldown=30s, no longer 300s ✓) |
| 02:06:35 | new store registers new segment |
| 02:06:57 | rail cooldown 30s expires, but sglang **does not recover** |
| 02:07:18 | master `unmount_expired_mem_segment` clears old segment (**bottleneck**, 51s after kill) |
| 02:07:20 | sglang `Opened segment` → switches to new port → recovers |

**The real bottleneck is master-side old-segment cleanup latency (45s)**, not rail cooldown (30s, expired 02:06:57), not store process recovery (02:06:35).
Root cause: a store restart picks a new random port → segment name changes → old replicas point at the old name → sglang keeps hitting the dead old port until master clears the old segment, after which `GetReplicaList` returns new-segment replicas.
The probe probed the dead old port and failed throughout.

> Shortening the store-kill window requires faster master-side `unmount_expired_mem_segment`, or stable segment names across restarts — both are follow-up RFC scope.

## Changes (1): log rate-limiting

All per-slice/per-task/per-attempt logs drop to `VLOG(1)` + `LOG_EVERY_N(., N)` sampling; steady-state outages no longer flood; `-v=1` enables full trace.
Triage-critical logs (`Detected error WQE` / `Endpoint marked for destruction`) are unaffected.

| File | Log | Change |
|---|---|---|
| `rail_monitor.cpp` | `Rail paused` | log only at the non-paused→paused transition (recovery already logs `Rail recovered`) |
| `workers.cpp` | `Optimal device pair` / `fallback device selection` | `LOG_EVERY_N(INFO,100)` → `VLOG(1)` + `LOG_EVERY_N(WARNING,10000)` |
| `workers.cpp` | `Failed to generate post path` | `LOG(ERROR)` → `VLOG(1)` + `LOG_EVERY_N(ERROR,10000)` |
| `workers.cpp` | `Slice failed: retry count exceeded` | `LOG(WARNING)` → `VLOG(1)` + `LOG_EVERY_N(WARNING,100)` |
| `transfer_engine_impl.cpp` | `Transport failover` | `LOG(INFO)` → `VLOG(1)` + `LOG_EVERY_N(INFO,1000)` |
| `transfer_engine_impl.cpp` | `No more transports available` | `LOG(WARNING)` → `VLOG(1)` + `LOG_EVERY_N(WARNING,100)` |
| `tcp_transport.cpp` | `retry attempt` / `failed after N retries` | `LOG(INFO/WARNING)` → `VLOG(1)` + `LOG_EVERY_N(.,100)` |
| `tcp_transport.cpp` | `attempt N failed` | `LOG(WARNING)` → `VLOG(1)` + `LOG_EVERY_N(WARNING,1000)` |
| `control_plane.cpp` | `SubscribeSegmentUpdate RPC failed` | `LOG(ERROR)` → `VLOG(1)` + `LOG_EVERY_N(ERROR,100)` |

## Changes (2): rail-cooldown semantic fixes

State machine: **Closed** (healthy) → **Open** (cooling down, probing) → **Half-Open** (one trial on expiry) → Closed/Open.

### Defect A: per-error cooldown doubling within a burst

`markFailed` ran `cooldown *= 2` (cap `kMaxCooldown=300s`) on **every call**, regardless of whether the rail was already paused.
A burst of 8 error WQEs from one store restart (one 10s window) pushed cooldown 30s→60→120→240→300, arming `resume_time = now+300s` → a 5-minute flood.

Exponential backoff is meant to escalate across failure *cycles* (recover→fail), but the implementation treated every error in one burst as a new cycle.

**Fix** (`markFailed`): set/escalate cooldown **only when a fresh pause arms** (`was_paused == false` and not Half-Open); errors while already paused (Open) do not escalate or re-arm.
`cooldown==0` (reset by `markRecovered`, proven healthy) → initial value.

### Defect B: expiry fully reopens + no early recovery while paused

Two sub-problems:

1. **Expiry fully reopens**: when the cooldown timer fired, `available` cleared `resume_time` and admitted **all** slices. If the peer was still dead, every slice RDMA-failed at once → `markFailed` re-armed and escalated — exactly the storm the breaker exists to prevent, now recurring at 30s / 60s / 120s intervals. Elapsed time does not prove the path is healthy.
2. **No early recovery**: `markRecovered` fires only on a successful RDMA transfer, but while paused no RDMA posts are issued → no successes → forced to wait out the full cooldown.

Not covered (follow-up PR)



## Verification

- **Logs**: single incident drops from 1.1GB (3.2M lines) to <1MB; `Rail paused` / `Rail recovered` / `Rail half-open` print once each.
- **Unit tests** (`tent/tests/rail_monitor_test.cpp`):
  - `BurstFailuresDoNotEscalateCooldown`: 8 consecutive markFailed do not escalate a 1s cooldown (expires at 1.5s, not 256s).
  - `ExpiryRetainsCooldownForNextCycle`: after expiry, a re-failure escalates 1→2s.


## Configuration

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `transports/rdma/rail_error_threshold` | 3 | error count threshold in the window |
| `transports/rdma/rail_error_window_secs` | 10 | error-count window |
| `transports/rdma/rail_cooldown_secs` | 30 | initial cooldown (seconds) |
