title: Feat/support mooncake-store with local shmem copy
body:
## Description
Enable Mooncake Store to allocate the host DRAM global segment as a Transfer Engine shared-memory object so same-host, cross-process clients can copy via classic `ShmTransport` instead of intra-node RDMA.
Depends on the existing TE `allocateSharedMemory` / `SharedMemoryOptions` (hugetlbfs) support.
**Behavior (opt-in):**
- When `MC_STORE_USE_SHM_SEGMENT` is set (or `MC_FORCE_SHM`), Store installs `ShmTransport` (classic TE only; rejected under TENT) and allocates the host segment through `allocateSharedMemory`.
- Hugepage policy follows `MC_STORE_USE_HUGEPAGE` / `MC_STORE_HUGEPAGE_SIZE` / optional `MC_HUGETLBFS_PATH`; populate is deferred so Store can `mbind` then populate.
- Optional `MC_STORE_SHM_ALLOW_TMPFS=1` falls back to POSIX shm if hugetlbfs allocation fails.
- Applies only to host-DRAM protocols (e.g. rdma/tcp/efa); device/CXL/NVLink-style protocols are unchanged.
- Prefer `ENABLE_MULTI_PROTOCOL=ON` so rdma/tcp remain available alongside shm.
Related: RFC #3912 / TE #3918 / prior TE SHM PRs (e.g. #4110).
## Module
- [ ] Transfer Engine (`mooncake-transfer-engine`)
- [x] Mooncake Store (`mooncake-store`)
- [ ] Mooncake Conductor (`mooncake-conductor`)
- [ ] Reshard (`mooncake-reshard`)
- [ ] Mooncake EP (`mooncake-ep`)
- [ ] Mooncake PG (`mooncake-pg`)
- [ ] Integration (`mooncake-integration`)
- [ ] P2P Store (`mooncake-p2p-store`)
- [ ] Python Wheel (`mooncake-wheel`)
- [x] Common (`mooncake-common`)
- [ ] Mooncake RL (`mooncake-rl`)
- [ ] CI/CD
- [x] Docs
- [ ] Other
## Type of Change
- [ ] Bug fix
- [x] New feature
- [ ] Refactor
- [ ] Breaking change
- [x] Documentation update
- [ ] Performance improvement
- [ ] Other
## How Has This Been Tested?
Added `store_shm_alloc_test` covering env flag parsing, protocol filter, SHM options, NUMA bind validation, POSIX SHM allocate/free, and optional 2MB hugetlbfs allocate (skipped when unavailable). Besides,

**Test commands:**
```bash
# Configure/build with tests (classic TE; ENABLE_MULTI_PROTOCOL recommended)
cmake --build build -j --target store_shm_alloc_test
ctest --test-dir build -R store_shm_alloc_test --output-on-failure
```

**Test results:**
- [x] Unit tests pass
- [ ] Integration tests pass (if applicable)
- [x] Manual testing done (describe below)

### Same-host functional & performance methodology

Topology (single host, rail-only NIC fabric):

1. Start one `mooncake_master`.
2. Start a **segment client** that contributes a **512 GB** host DRAM `global_segment` (RDMA protocol).
3. Start a second **HiCache-like Store client** on the same host to Put/Get against that segment.
4. Pin Transfer Engine RDMA to a **single device** `ionic_0` (rail-only; no multi-rail bonding in this run).
5. Build with classic TE and `-DENABLE_MULTI_PROTOCOL=ON` so `rdma` and `shm` coexist.

Compared SHM on vs off by toggling Store SHM env vars below; verified the active path from TE/Store logs (RDMA CQ vs `ShmTransport`  hugetlbfs allocation messages).

| Variable | Role | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MC_STORE_USE_SHM_SEGMENT` | Opt-in Store SHM global segment | `envFlagEnabled`: unset/empty/`0`/`false`/`no`/`off` = off; anything else = on. Installs `ShmTransport` and calls `allocateSharedMemory` for host-DRAM protocols. |
| `MC_FORCE_SHM` | Also enables Store SHM segment path | `store_use_shm_segment()` is true if Store flag **or** this is on (TE may install SHM first). |
| `MC_STORE_USE_HUGEPAGE` | Enable HugeTLB for Store segment | Presence-based (`HugepageConfig`): set to enable (typically `1`). |
| `MC_STORE_HUGEPAGE_SIZE` | Huge page size | `2MB` / `512MB` / `1GB` (default `2MB` when hugepage is enabled). |
| `MC_HUGETLBFS_PATH` | Optional custom hugetlbfs mount | Passed into `SharedMemoryOptions.hugetlbfs_path` only when hugepage is on. |
| `MC_STORE_SHM_ALLOW_TMPFS` | Allow POSIX shm fallback if hugetlbfs alloc fails | Off by default; when off, hugepage exhaustion fails allocation (no POSIX fallback). |

Client / TE settings used in our runs:

```bash
# Build: classic TE + multi-protocol (rdma + shm)
# cmake ... -DENABLE_MULTI_PROTOCOL=ON

# Shared by segment client + HiCache-like client
export MOONCAKE_PROTOCOL=rdma
export MOONCAKE_DEVICE=ionic_0          # or setup(..., device_name="ionic_0")
export MOONCAKE_GLOBAL_SEGMENT_SIZE=512gb   # segment client contributes 512 GB

# Baseline (intra-node same-NIC RDMA)
unset MC_STORE_USE_SHM_SEGMENT MC_FORCE_SHM
unset MC_STORE_USE_HUGEPAGE MC_STORE_HUGEPAGE_SIZE MC_HUGETLBFS_PATH
unset MC_STORE_SHM_ALLOW_TMPFS


# Hugetlbfs SHM copy (2MB)
export MC_STORE_USE_SHM_SEGMENT=1
export MC_STORE_USE_HUGEPAGE=1
export MC_STORE_HUGEPAGE_SIZE=2MB
unset MC_STORE_SHM_ALLOW_TMPFS          # no POSIX fallback when hugepages are exhausted
# optional: export MC_HUGETLBFS_PATH=/dev/hugepages
```

`MC_STORE_USE_SHM_SEGMENT` is rejected under TENT (`allocateSharedMemory` is classic-only).

### Same-host cross-instance functional tests


| Case | Observed behavior |
| --- | --- |
| SHM copy off | Intra-node transfer uses same-NIC RDMA |
| SHM copy on | Transfer uses POSIX shm copy path |
| SHM copy + 2MB hugepage | Transfer uses hugetlbfs shm copy path |
| SHM copy + 2MB hugepage, hugepages exhausted | Does **not** fall back to POSIX shm (expected when `MC_STORE_SHM_ALLOW_TMPFS` is unset/off) |

### Same-host performance (SHM vs RDMA)

Same-host Put/Get bandwidth (GiB/s), mean over 5 rounds.

**8 threads:**

| Size | SHM Put | RDMA Put | Put speedup | SHM Get | RDMA Get | Get speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 16MB | 44.1 | 22.8 | 1.9x | 33.3 | 32.0 | 1.0x |
| 32MB | 58.4 | 31.0 | 1.9x | 75.0 | 40.1 | 1.9x |
| 64MB | 69.2 | 28.1 | 2.5x | 92.3 | 32.2 | 2.9x |
| 128MB | 71.0 | 31.7 | 2.2x | 103.6 | 34.8 | 3.0x |
| 256MB | 79.6 | 28.3 | 2.8x | 112.3 | 33.1 | 3.4x |
| 512MB | 62.6 | 24.2 | 2.6x | 87.1 | 34.5 | 2.5x |
| 1GB | 64.0 | 24.9 | 2.6x | 95.6 | 27.5 | 3.5x |

**16 threads:**

| Size | SHM Put | RDMA Put | Put speedup | SHM Get | RDMA Get | Get speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 16MB | 63.9 | 25.2 | 2.5x | 59.6 | 32.0 | 1.9x |
| 32MB | 63.9 | 33.4 | 1.9x | 97.4 | 41.5 | 2.3x |
| 64MB | 105.2 | 34.2 | 3.1x | 142.1 | 38.8 | 3.7x |
| 128MB | 89.7 | 37.2 | 2.4x | 117.7 | 38.1 | 3.1x |
| 256MB | 97.1 | 36.7 | 2.6x | 130.2 | 38.5 | 3.4x |
| 512MB | 107.7 | 33.4 | 3.2x | 132.9 | 36.2 | 3.7x |
| 1GB | 75.6 | 26.1 | 2.9x | 141.2 | 26.8 | 5.3x |

SHM is typically ~2–3x Put and up to ~5x Get vs same-host RDMA in this setup.

title: [Store] Export process and allocator memory metrics, and complete the jemalloc build option
body:
## Description

Mooncake exports no process memory metrics today — nothing from `/proc/self/status`, no RSS
series, and no allocator visibility. This PR adds a process/allocator metric surface to both
the master and the client, and finishes the `STORE_USE_JEMALLOC` option added in #902 so the
allocator it selects can be observed at runtime.

RFC: #4207

**`STORE_USE_JEMALLOC` stays OFF by default.** This is not a proposal to change the default,
which is what stalled #1436 — that PR got an LGTM and then stalled on jemalloc not being
packaged on every distribution. That concern applies to flipping the default, not to this PR.
The metric half works in the default build too: with no jemalloc linked, the process series
still export and `mooncake_jemalloc_enabled` reports 0.

Motivation is #3452 (mooncake-master OOM under a long-context PD-separation workload).
Diagnosing it required a structure-level audit of the `MasterService` metadata lifecycle
because no metric could distinguish "the allocator is holding freed pages" from "Mooncake is
leaking"; the closing analysis names arenas retaining temporary allocations as the mechanism.
@ykwd suggested in that thread that jemalloc was worth trying for metadata-heavy workloads to
reduce RSS retention and fragmentation. This PR is what makes that suggestion actionable and
verifiable.

### Production evidence

We hit the same class of problem and traced it to the bottom. On a master holding ~264M keys,
two things were happening. Every client restart stepped RSS up by roughly 15 GB and it never
came back down, five times in a single day. Underneath that, RSS also grew steadily through
normal serving, with no restart involved. Neither is fixed by an HA failover. The figure
below is the one traced restart, measured end to end.

Syscall tracepoints (`mmap` / `mprotect` / `munmap` / `brk` / `madvise`, filtered to the master
pid) across one controlled client restart, with `VmRSS` sampled every 15s:

| Phase | key_count | newly committed (mprotect) | madvise / munmap | VmRSS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| erase, 4 min | 264,474,025 -> 222,467,218 (**-42.0M**) | 4 MB | **0 / 0** | +41.7 MB (flat) |
| refill, 3 min | 224,010,477 -> 263,744,892 (**+39.7M**) | **14,888 MB over 2,654,157 calls** | 58 MB / 0 | **+15.1 GiB** |
| whole window | net -0.8M (back to start) | **15.33 GiB** | 58 MB madvise | 276.15 -> **291.39 GiB (+15.23 GiB, permanent)** |

Freeing ~42M objects returned nothing (0 `madvise`, 0 `munmap`). The refill reused none of the
free lists it had just created — reuse measured at 0, not "low" — and instead filled 253
brand-new 64 MB heaps (`heaps=253 total=15.33 GiB p50=62.5MB p90=64.0MB max=64.0MB`). The
15.33 GiB of `mprotect` matches the 15.23 GiB RSS rise almost byte for byte, so nothing else
is hiding in that number. This is glibc's top-of-heap constraint: the erased metadata sat in
the middle.

After linking jemalloc into the master and client with `MALLOC_CONF=background_thread:true`:

| | glibc | jemalloc |
|---|---|---|
| key_count | 264.5M | 267.9M |
| VmRSS | 276.1 GiB | **152.7 GiB** |
| **RSS per key** | ~1.19 KiB | **~612 B** |
| anonymous mappings | 4177 mappings / 4085 64 MB heaps | **391 mappings** |
| trough under sustained churn | steps up, 58.8 -> 66.3 -> 73.4 GiB, never converging | steps down, then flat |

24h continuous sampling (2-min interval, 718 samples, zero gaps, no restarts, single
incarnation): RSS 155.09 -> 152.71 GiB, net -2.38 GiB (-1.5%), peak 155.43 GiB at 2h, trough
152.39 GiB at 21h. Over that window the resident set turned over completely (evictions +268M,
puts +272M, `allocated_bytes` swinging 3.0-4.6 TB) while `key_count` held at 267.90-268.01M —
so the decline is not keys going away.

The client was verified the same way, and that result is why this links the allocator into
`mooncake_client` rather than the master alone. The client under test had SSD offload
enabled, which puts it in the same position as the master: every offloaded object carries a
metadata entry in the client's own maps — `object_bucket_map_`, plus the LRU index and the
pending-key sets beside it — so an offload workload allocates and frees small records at the
rate objects move, and glibc holds the freed pages exactly as it does on the master. On a
client serving a 900 GB segment, resident memory under glibc grew past 1000 GB and was still
climbing when the run was cut. With jemalloc linked, the same workload settles at around
930 GB and stops growing.

Every number above came from hand-run syscall tracing and `/proc` scraping on a live leader.
None of it was visible in Mooncake's metrics, and the two hypotheses that mattered — decay
never ran, versus decay ran but fragmentation pins the pages — look identical under
cgroup-level RSS. That is what this PR's series are for.

### What is in the two commits

**`[Store] Link jemalloc into the master and client binaries`**
- Links jemalloc into `mooncake_client` as well as `mooncake_master`.
- Defines the `STORE_USE_JEMALLOC` macro, which the option never did — it linked the
  library but the definition never reached the compiler, so no source file could tell
  whether the allocator was in the process. Scoped to those two executables, so
  `libmooncake_store` stays allocator-free — it is also consumed by the Python extension,
  which must not have an allocator forced on its host process.
- Adds `LogAllocatorStatus()`: logs jemalloc version, `background_thread` state, live
  background thread count, and both decay knobs at startup. Release binaries are linked with
  `-s`, so this line is the only evidence that jemalloc actually replaced the system
  allocator. Compiles to an empty function when the option is off.
- Keeps #902's `${JEMALLOC_STATIC_LIBRARIES}` and its indirection through
  reset-on-configure variables, renamed `MASTER_EXTRA_*` -> `ALLOCATOR_*` because the
  client now uses them too, and extended with the compile definition and library
  directory. The reset is load-bearing: `pkg_check_modules` writes its `JEMALLOC_*`
  results into the CMake cache, so referencing those names directly on the targets makes
  a build directory reconfigured back to `STORE_USE_JEMALLOC=OFF` keep linking the
  allocator while the compile definition is gone. The binary then runs on jemalloc while
  `LogAllocatorStatus()` is the empty stub and no collector is installed — `ldd` shows
  `libjemalloc.so.2` while `/metrics` reports `mooncake_jemalloc_enabled 0`. Reproduced
  and then fixed by reconfiguring ON -> OFF -> ON in one build directory.

**`[Store] Export process and jemalloc memory metrics from master and client`**
- `AllocatorMetric`, held by both `MasterMetricManager` and `ClientMetric`, so both sides
  expose the same series.
- Process series from `/proc/self/status`, exported whichever allocator is linked, so they
  stay comparable across a glibc/jemalloc switch.
- jemalloc series from `mallctl`, including dirty/muzzy bytes kept apart (jemalloc 5 decays
  them on separate paths and exposes no combined counter) and cumulative purge counters.
- Per-size-class occupancy (`bin_regs` / `bin_slabs` / `bin_used_bytes`, labelled by size
  class): a slab returns to the OS only once every region in it is free, so a class at low
  occupancy is holding `slab_bytes` while using `used_bytes`.
- `AllocatorMetric` names no jemalloc type; a collector function pointer is installed at
  startup by the binaries that link the allocator.
- Collection fails as a whole rather than partially — a build without `--enable-stats` still
  answers the epoch write, so a partial snapshot would look identical on a dashboard to a
  healthy one reading zero.
- `Refresh()` rate-limits: advancing the jemalloc epoch takes a lock shared with allocating
  threads, so an unauthenticated `/metrics` endpoint must not drive that rate.
- `hybrid_metric.h` gains `basic_hybrid_gauge` next to `basic_hybrid_counter` via a delegating
  constructor, so the per-size-class series declare `# TYPE gauge` rather than telling
  Prometheus a value that can fall is monotonic.

**`[Doc] Document the process and allocator memory metrics`**
- A `Process and Allocator Memory Metrics` section under the existing Prometheus chapter of
  `docs/source/getting_started/observability.md`: the process series and their
  `/proc/self/status` sources, the jemalloc series and the `resident/allocated` ratio to
  watch, the per-size-class breakdown, what is exported when jemalloc is not linked, and how
  to build with `-DSTORE_USE_JEMALLOC=ON`.

## Module

- [x] Mooncake Store (`mooncake-store`)

## Type of Change

- [x] New feature

## How Has This Been Tested?

**Test commands:**
```bash
cmake .. -DSTORE_USE_JEMALLOC=ON
make -j 32 allocator_metric_test mooncake_master mooncake_client
./mooncake-store/tests/allocator_metric_test

# default build, allocator off
cmake .. -DSTORE_USE_JEMALLOC=OFF
make -j 32 allocator_metric_test
./mooncake-store/tests/allocator_metric_test
```

**Test results:**
- [x] Unit tests pass — `allocator_metric_test` 10/10, in both the ON and OFF builds
- [x] Manual testing done

With `STORE_USE_JEMALLOC=ON`: `ldd` shows `libjemalloc.so.2` on both binaries; startup logs
`Allocator: jemalloc 5.2.1-..., background_thread=on, background_threads=1,

title: [CI/Build] Limit ROCm wheel builds to two parallel jobs
body:
## Description

Set `MAX_JOBS=2` for the ROCm wheel build step and pass it explicitly to `cmake --build`, replacing `-j$(nproc)`. The environment variable alone does not limit a regular CMake/Ninja build. This bounds total native build parallelism to two jobs while preserving the existing Ninja pools and retry behavior.

Motivated by [the ROCm Python 3.10 CI failure](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/actions/runs/35193035638/job/105125497967?pr=3964), which ended with exit 137 and a runner shutdown signal. OOM is not confirmed; the equivalent Python 3.12 job succeeded with the same existing limits. This is a conservative resource cap, not a claim to fix a proven root cause.

Overlap: #3970 migrates release wheel packaging, including this workflow; this PR only caps the current native build step and does not migrate packaging.

title: [TENT] Keep a retiring notify QP published until its completions are drained
body:
## Description

A notification that has already landed can still be sitting unpolled in the notify CQ: the notify worker drains sixteen completions per pass, and a sender keeps up to its 256-slot window in flight. `beginDestroyNoLock()` removed the notify QP from the transport's QP-number table before moving the QPs to ERR, and `disableNotification()` did the same after a local fault, so those pending completions came back as "unknown QP" in `processNotifyCompletions()` and were dropped. The sender's HCA had been acknowledged, so the sender saw a successful completion and had no reason to resend: the notification was lost with nothing anywhere able to recover it.

This only happens when the retirement is triggered by a thread other than the notify worker - a data-path worker after slice retries, the RPC thread when a peer re-bootstraps, the endpoint store evicting. The worker's own retirement drains the CQ in order and loses nothing.

Change:

- The notify QP stays in the table until `deconstructUnlocked()`, which already unpublishes it under `notify_resource_mutex_` before destroying the QP and freeing the buffers. `handleNotifyRecv()` takes the same mutex before it reads a slot, so handing out a completion while the endpoint retires is safe.
- Flushes stay as quiet as before: the worker now treats a retiring or disabled notify QP as not ready, and `classifyNotifyCompletion()` already skips `IBV_WC_WR_FLUSH_ERR` on a QP that is not ready. A notification still delivered after that point is handed out but its slot is not re-armed, so it costs no work on a QP that can no longer receive.
- `finishDestroy()` waits for the notify QP the way it already waited for the data QPs. Destroying a QP takes its unpolled completions with it, so every posted notification WR is counted and the count has to reach zero first, with the existing 30 s timeout as the backstop. The count is released only once a completion has been consumed - the payload copied out of its slot, or the send and error paths finished - so reaching zero means nothing is left in the worker's hand.
- A consumed RECV slot is re-armed only while the endpoint is ready and its notify QP connected. Both retirement and the local completion error that disables notifications leave the RC QP in ERR, where a replacement work request is wasted: this provider accepts it and flushes it straight back, one that checks the state rejects it and logs. The initial posting in `connect()` and `accept()` is unchanged.
- The QP is published before its first RECV is posted, so a peer that sends the moment its handshake returns cannot land on a QP number the table does not know yet.
- `deconstructUnlocked()` no longer clears `peer_server_name_` / `peer_nic_name_`: the worker reads them off a retiring endpoint without holding `lock_`, and `EP_DESTROYED` already says the endpoint is gone.

One reachability change follows: after `disableNotification()`, a later completion error on that QP now reaches the classifier with the endpoint alive but not ready, where the unpublished QP previously made it `ReportOnly`. A path fault (`IBV_WC_RETRY_EXC_ERR`) therefore retires the endpoint as on any live one and a local fault (`IBV_WC_LOC_LEN_ERR`) disables notifications that are already off; only flushes are skipped. The classifier itself is unchanged.

6 files, 191 insertions, 35 deletions, 71 of the insertions in tests. No configuration, wire or default change.

This is the first of seven PRs on notification fault tolerance, described in the series RFC (#4061); it depends on none of them and closes the one loss the resend PR later in the series cannot cover, because the sender never learns of it.

## Module

- [ ] Mooncake Store (`mooncake-store`)
- [ ] Mooncake Conductor (`mooncake-conductor`)
- [ ] Reshard (`mooncake-reshard`)

- [ ] Mooncake PG (`mooncake-pg`)

- [ ] P2P Store (`mooncake-p2p-store`)

- [ ] Common (`mooncake-common`)

- [ ] Other

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] New feature
- [ ] Refactor
- [ ] Breaking change
- [ ] Documentation update
- [ ] Performance improvement
- [ ] Other

## How Has This Been Tested?

Two new unit tests and two new assertions come with the change. `EndpointLifecycleTest.FinishDestroyWaitsForNotifyCompletions` is new: with notification WRs still outstanding, `finishDestroy()` returns false and the endpoint stays `EP_DESTROYING` until the count drains, and an extra completion does not take it below zero. `EndpointLifecycleTest.NotifyRecvIsRearmedOnlyWhileReady` is new as well and pins the re-arm decision, including the states an endpoint really passes through: ready and connected re-arms, a disabled endpoint that is still `EP_READY` does not, and a retiring one does not. `RdmaNotifyFaultTriageTest.TeardownFlushesStayQuiet` gains two assertions for the reachability change above. Negative controls: dropping the drain gate fails the first case and only that one; forcing the re-arm decision open fails the second and only that one. The lifecycle binary goes from 20 cases to 22.

`ctest` over `mooncake-transfer-engine/tent/tests` with this change alone on current `main`: 63 of 63, the same count as unpatched `main`, since the new cases run inside an existing test binary.

Whether the table entry survives retirement is only observable with a real QP, so it was measured with a two-process probe on one host with two BlueField-3 integrated ConnectX-7 VFs over RoCE v2, 4000 notifications per run, the retirement injected from a detached thread while the notify worker polls. Both arms are `main` plus the same test-only injection hooks, which are not part of this PR:

| | delivered | dropped as unknown QP |
| --- | --- | --- |
| without this change (2 runs) | 3536, 3498 of 4000 | 208, 246 |
| with this change (2 runs) | 3744, 3744 of 4000 | 0, 0 |

The remaining gap to 4000 is sender-side loss, which the resend PR later in the series covers; the two fixes are independent and complementary. Stalling the notify worker for 2 ms and 20 ms after the retirement does not change either arm.

The same rig also counts what the re-arm decision does. Over three runs with the retirement injected, 197 to 251 consumed slots were handed out without a replacement work request, and no post reached the posting path while the QP could no longer receive; with the decision forced open, 198 such posts show up and none are skipped. Delivery, the drain time before the endpoint is destroyed (tens of milliseconds, far from the 30 s backstop) and the absence of dropped or unknown-QP completions are the same either way, so the gate removes work rather than changing behaviour. A run without any fault delivers 4000 of 4000 with no duplicates.

```bash
      -DUSE_CUDA=OFF -DWITH_STORE=OFF -DWITH_STORE_RUST=OFF -DYLT_ENABLE_IBV=ON

```

title: [TransferEngine] Wait classic tebench batches with getBatchTransferStatus
body:
## Description

Classic tebench waited by looping `getTransferStatus(batch, i)` on every task. That is the wrong wait for “submit a batch, then wait for the batch”:

1. It diverges from TENT, which already waits at batch granularity.
2. `TIMEOUT`, `CANCELED`, and `INVALID` were ignored, so the loop could spin forever (noted on #4184).

This PR polls `getBatchTransferStatus` until the batch completes, fails, or the initiator is stopped. Engine completion logic is unchanged. On current `main`, `getBatchTransferStatus` still walks every task internally, so this is not an O(1) in-flight shortcut.

On shutdown (`g_te_running == false`) `freeBatchID` is best-effort: it refuses in-flight batches, so an aborted run can still leak that batch. That path is not the timed measurement loop.

Split out of #4184 so the benchmark wait can land and re-baseline `main` before any engine change to in-flight `getBatchTransferStatus`.

### Measurement (same engine, this wait only)

H20, `mlx5_bond_0` loopback, DRAM READ, 4096 B blocks, 1 thread, 5 s. Independent variable is classic tebench wait: per-task `getTransferStatus` vs this PR’s `getBatchTransferStatus`. Skip first 2 iterations for submit/wait p50.

Submit is the control: the engine is unchanged, so it should stay flat.

| threads | batch size | wait API | submit p50 | wait p50 | BW (GB/s) |
|--------:|-----------:|----------|-----------:|---------:|----------:|
| 1 | 4096 | per-task `getTransferStatus` | 2665 µs | 2503 µs | 2.59 |
| 1 | 4096 | this PR | 2673 µs | 2385 µs | 2.64 |
| 1 | 207360 | per-task `getTransferStatus` | 65.3 ms | 754 ms | 1.03 |
| 1 | 207360 | this PR | 65.9 ms | 785 ms | 1.00 |

- Submit p50 is unchanged within noise (4096: +0.3%; 207360: +0.9%).
- 4096 wait is slightly cheaper (−5%), consistent with one batch status call instead of 4096 per-task calls; the engine still walks the tasks inside `getBatchTransferStatus`.
- 207360 wait/BW moved the other way with only 6 samples after warmup. Treat that as noise, not a regression from this wait change.
- Do not treat a change in classic tebench BW after this PR as an engine speedup.

title: [Store] Add SSD offload task lifecycle metrics
body:
## Description

Adds five per-`client_id` counters to `MasterMetricManager` so the SSD offload pipeline — previously unobservable at the task level — can be monitored for system health:

| Metric | Meaning | Increment point |
|---|---|---|
| `master_offload_enqueued_total` | Tasks successfully enqueued (passed the queue cap) | `PushOffloadingQueue` overall success |
| `master_offload_completed_total` | Tasks written to disk (worker reported OK, new LOCAL_DISK replica registered) | `NotifyOffloadSuccess` success branch, after `AddReplica` |
| `master_offload_failed_total` | Tasks that failed to write (worker NACK) | `NotifyOffloadSuccess` NACK branch (`data_size < 0`) |
| `master_offload_cancelled_total` | Tasks preempted before write (e.g. by `UpsertStart`) | `CancelQueuedOffloadTask`, before `erase` |
| `master_offload_enqueue_rejected_total` | Tasks rejected at enqueue (queue full, `KEYS_ULTRA_LIMIT`) | `PushOffloadingQueue` on `KEYS_ULTRA_LIMIT` |

All counters are labeled by `client_id` (segment owner UUID) so throughput / success rate can be broken down per store worker. They are exposed via the existing master `/metrics` endpoint alongside the other `MasterMetricManager` counters, following the `tenant_evict_bytes_total` (`dynamic_counter_1t`) pattern.

**Reconciliation:** `enqueued = completed + failed + cancelled + in_flight`. `enqueue_rejected` is outside the pipeline. Other enqueue errors (`UNABLE_OFFLOADING`, `SEGMENT_NOT_FOUND`, etc.) are neither enqueued nor rejected — they remain on the existing `LOG(WARNING)` path (failure-cause diagnosis stays in logs, by design).

Scope is intentionally minimal: master-side only, no worker-side (`file_storage.cpp` / `SsdMetric`) changes — the existing per-worker `ssd_write_ops` continues to serve as the raw I/O view and does not conflict.

title: [Store] Persist NoF registrations across HA failover
body:
## Description

Fixes #4037.

NoF storage pool registrations currently need to be recreated after HA recovery. This PR persists these registrations so that a new master can restore the segment ID, owner, name, endpoint, base offset, and capacity without rerunning the registration tool.

- Record successful NoF mounts, remounts, explicit unmounts, and heartbeat-triggered unmounts in OpLog. Preserve logs for successful items when a later remount item fails, and avoid extra logs for duplicate mounts.
- Maintain the NoF registration list while the standby replays OpLog, and restore it when the standby becomes the new master.
- Save NoF registrations in a separate `nof_segments.bin` file in batch OpLog snapshots. Load these registrations before replaying subsequent logs. Older snapshots without this information remain readable, with an empty NoF registration list.
- Include the NoF registration file in snapshot restore, log pruning, and GC validation.

This applies to HA with OpLog enabled. Registration logs remain asynchronous: a successful registration RPC does not guarantee that its log entry is durable yet.

**Scope:** Rebuilding the allocator's occupied ranges is outside this PR. The existing behavior where allocations after HA recovery can reuse offsets referenced by restored replicas is tracked separately in #3826; the related quarantine proposal is in #3858. This PR does not fix that issue.

title: [Store] Expose client-observed Master heartbeat status and freshness
body:
## Description

A successful Master Ping can return `NEED_REMOUNT` while the client health endpoint remains healthy. Expose that distinction and the observation's freshness on the existing client `/metrics` endpoint:

- `mooncake_client_master_heartbeat_status_ok`: 1 for `OK`, 0 for `NEED_REMOUNT`.
- `mooncake_client_master_heartbeat_observation_timestamp_seconds`: client-side Unix receive time of the same response.

Both samples share existing client labels and are serialized together using YLT gauges. Failed/unsupported observations and reconnects make them absent. Connection generations reject stale responses, including late failures that would otherwise clear a newer observation. Existing health, reconnect and remount behavior is preserved.

Document missing samples, the zero-storage-client boundary, freshness queries, and the distinction from per-segment registration completeness and data-plane health. Add focused metric tests and HTTP recovery coverage.

title: [Bugfix][TENT] Keep a slice alive until the completion its post owes is handled
body:
## Description

A freed batch can return a slice to the slab while a completion for its work request is still owed, or while the handler for that completion is still reading it.

Two ways in. The software timeout resolves a slice without waiting for its completion, so the batch reads terminal and the caller may free it while the work request is live — `resetConnection()` only marks the endpoint for destruction; the queue pair goes away later, on the monitor's reclaim sweep. And on the ordinary success path, `handleCompletion()` calls `acknowledge()` mid-way, which is what publishes the terminal status the caller is waiting for; the caller frees the batch while the handler is still reading the slice for GDR feedback, rail recovery and latency stats (the failure branch does the same through `disableEndpoint()`). `freeSubBatch()` handed every slice back to the slab unconditionally. The slab's thread-local ring is 128 deep and a freed slice goes to its back, so the address comes back to a new transfer within a ring's worth of allocations. The stale completion then runs `handleCompletion()` against a live slice belonging to someone else: it drops that slice from another lane's supervision set, acknowledges on the wrong endpoint, releases its charge early, and can mark a live task COMPLETED with a length whose bytes never moved.

`RdmaSlice` now carries `completions_owed`: every work request is signalled, so each accepted post owes exactly one completion. `submitSlices()` counts it under the queue pair lock; `handleCompletion()` pays it back through a scope guard on its way out, so the count stays above zero for the whole handler, every early return included. The count, not the status, says whether the completion queue or a handler can still name this address — the status cannot, because the timeout sets it while the work request is live. `freeSubBatch()` hands any slice still owing a completion to the transport and frees the batch immediately, so none of this touches `lazyFreeBatch`'s retry and quarantine path. A reap frees an orphan once its count is exactly zero or its endpoint is gone; the monitor tick runs one every second, and `freeSubBatch()` runs one opportunistically (behind an atomic flag, so the common empty case never takes the mutex) so a straggler waits for the next batch free rather than a full second. Only the tick ages an orphan toward its lingering warning: one that outlives ~60 ticks means a queue pair is not being destroyed, logged once per slice, and the slice stays held — freeing on age would hand the completion queue a dangling address again. `uninstall()` drains the rest after the workers are joined. This follows `DeferredStageTeardown`, which exists because ProxyManager hit the same hazard; here only the at-risk slices are held back.

Four sites in `asyncPostSend()` resolved a slice that never reached the hardware and then wrote `counted_lane` on it. Such a slice owes nothing, so the batch can free it in between; the two calls are order-independent and are now count-first, matching `dropUnpostableSlice()`.

Two things stated rather than left implied. The endpoint-gone half of the reap condition rests on the provider clearing a queue pair's completions when it is destroyed (mlx5 and mlx4 do). And `finishDestroy()` decides a queue pair has drained by reading `wr_depth_list_`, which `acknowledge()` zeroes, so it can destroy one while the hardware still holds work requests — the data-QP half of what #4062 fixes for the notify QP, not addressed here.

An earlier revision also guarded `handleCompletion()` against a slice a neighbour's retry had popped with PENDING. Withdrawn: `convertConfToRdmaParams` forces worker, QP and CQ counts to match, so every queue pair has one poller and completions are handled in post order.

## Module

- [x] Transfer Engine (`mooncake-transfer-engine`)

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix

## How Has This Been Tested?

Eight cases in a new `RdmaSliceOrphanTest` fixture, borrowing `RdmaWorkersSharedQpTest`'s verbs stand-ins and driving the real `handleCompletion()`, `submitSlices()`, `freeSubBatch()` and `reapOrphanSlices()`: a slice still owed a completion is held back and released when it lands; a settled slice goes straight back; an orphan is reaped once its endpoint is gone; a lingering orphan is reported once and still held; a slice is held while its completion is being handled (the handler is stalled inside `acknowledge()` by holding the queue pair lock, the rendezvous read off the lock's ticket counter, and the batch is freed and the reaper run from the test thread meanwhile); a held slice is never handed to the next transfer (the slab's ring is drained and the address must not come back, then the stale completion is delivered and resolves the held slice); an opportunistic reap does not age an orphan; an unsettled orphan survives repeated reaps exactly once. `pretendPosted` counts the completion a post owes so it does not drift from `submitSlices`. Each case red-checked against the line it guards: entry-time payment fails the concurrent case; unconditional `deallocate` fails the hold and the reuse cases (the address comes back exactly once); `on_tick=true` from `freeSubBatch()` fails the aging case; dropping the put-back loses the unsettled orphan.

```bash

./tent_rdma_transport_test
pre-commit run --files <files changed in this PR>
```

title: [Store] Reject NoF endpoint reuse during unmount
body:
## Description

Fixes #4211

`ScopedNoFSegmentAccess::MountSegment` only rejected duplicate transport endpoints for segments in `OK` state. During NoF unmount, Prepare marks the old segment `UNMOUNTING`, and MasterService releases the manager lock while cleaning up object metadata before Commit.

A new UUID could then register the same endpoint. If it reused the segment name, `CommitUnmountSegment` could erase the new registration's `client_by_name_` entry and per-segment metrics.

Return `UNAVAILABLE_IN_CURRENT_STATUS` when a matching endpoint belongs to a non-OK segment, allowing callers to retry. Preserve `SEGMENT_ALREADY_EXISTS` for `OK` segments, since callers treat that result as a successful registration.

title: [Bugfix][Store] Support DFS replicas in ranged get sessions
body:
## Description

Related to [#3658](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/issues/3658).

This PR extends the existing ranged get session APIs to support DFS-backed replicas, while preserving the existing MEMORY fast path.

The MEMORY replica path remains unchanged and is still preferred when available. `LOCAL_DISK`, `DISK`, and `NOF` replicas remain unsupported by ranged get sessions.

`batch_get_session_start` performs a single Master `BatchQuery`, selects one complete MEMORY or DFS replica, and caches the filtered `QueryResult` together with its lease. Subsequent `batch_get_into_multi_buffer_ranges` calls reuse the cached metadata and do not query the Master again.

For DFS replicas:

- Requests use a request-scoped staging arena backed by the existing `PinnedBufferPool`.
- Pinned host memory is used when available. If it is unavailable, the synchronous path falls back to pageable host memory.
- DFS objects are read through batched `Client::BatchGet`.
- Requested ranges are scattered from staging into registered host or device destination buffers.
- Duplicate keys in one request are read once and scattered to each requested destination.
- Staging is released after the synchronous read and scatter operation completes.
- No session object cache or persistent asynchronous H2D stream is introduced.

The Python API documentation has been updated to describe MEMORY/DFS replica selection, staging lifetime, and pageable-memory fallback behavior.

title: feat(store): full RequestContext propagation via coro_rpc attachment (dummy→real→master)
body:
## Description

Enables end-to-end propagation of RequestContext (request_id, trace_id, span_id, parent_span_id) from
  MooncakeDistributedStore (Python) through DummyClient → RealClient → Master, using coro_rpc's out-of-band request attachment mechanism.

  ### Architecture
```
  Python: store.set_request_context(request_id="abc", trace_id="t1", ...)
    │  writes thread_local g_current_ctx
    ▼
  DummyClient.invoke_rpc / MasterClient.invoke_rpc_async_with_pool
    │  current_request_context_attachment() → struct_pack::serialize(RequestContext)
    │  send_request_with_attachment(bytes, args...)          ← hop A / hop B
    ▼
  RealClient V3 handler (hop A bridge)
    │  release_request_attachment() → struct_pack::deserialize → RequestContext
    │  CurrentCtxScope(rc) → g_current_ctx restored
    │  → client_service_ → master_client_ (syncAwait, same thread)
    │  → send_request_with_attachment(bytes, args...)        ← hop B
    ▼
  Master V3 handler
    │  release_request_attachment() → deserialize_request_context()
    │  VLOG: request_id=abc trace_id=t1
    │  → *Internal (shared value-returning body)
    │  → ctx.response_msg(result)
```

  ### Key changes by layer
```
   Layer                           Files                                                 Changes
  ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━  ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━  ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
   Infrastructure                  request_context.h (new)                               RequestContext struct, thread_local g_current_ctx,
                                                                                         CurrentCtxScope RAII,
                                                                                         current_request_context_attachment() (struct_pack
                                                                                         serialize), deserialize_request_context()
                                                                                         (struct_pack deserialize), YLT_REFL, test
                                                                                         instrumentation seam
  ──────────────────────────────  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Python binding                  store_py.cpp                                          set_request_context(request_id, trace_id, span_id,
                                                                                         parent_span_id), clear_request_context()
  ──────────────────────────────  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Client injection                dummy_client.cpp, master_client.h                     invoke_rpc / invoke_batch_rpc snapshot
                                                                                         current_request_context_attachment() at entry →
                                                                                         send_request_with_attachment (covers all hop A and
                                                                                         hop B RPCs)
  ──────────────────────────────  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Master handlers (V3)            rpc_service.h/cpp, centralized_rpc_service.h/cpp      7 handlers (GetReplicaList, BatchGetReplicaList,
                                                                                         BatchExistKey, ExistKey, Remove, PutStart,
                                                                                         BatchPutStart) converted to void +
                                                                                         coro_rpc::context<Ret> + response_msg. Base name =
                                                                                         V3 entry, value body = *Internal. Read attachment
                                                                                         via release_request_attachment() (consumes buffer,
                                                                                         prevents cross-request leak on connection reuse)
  ──────────────────────────────  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   RealClient hop A bridge (V3)    real_client.h/cpp, real_client_main.cpp               10 handlers (all *_dummy_helper + *_internal_rpc)
                                                                                         converted to V3. Read hop A attachment →
                                                                                         CurrentCtxScope → synchronous *_internal → hop B
                                                                                         inject. Non-dummy single-key handlers split into
                                                                                         *_internal (value body, real path) + *_internal_rpc
                                                                                         (V3, dummy path)
  ──────────────────────────────  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Tests                           request_id_attachment_test.cpp (new),                 6 test cases covering read, exist, remove, put-
                                   master_metrics_test.cpp                               start, batch-exist routes. In-process master
                                                                                         harness verifies attachment round-trip via
                                                                                         RecordObservedRequestId seam
```
  ### Design decisions

  - struct_pack::compatible: Existing fields are plain std::string. YLT_REFL enables field-name-based serialization. Future fields appended
    as struct_pack::compatible<std::string> are safely ignored by old binaries.

  - Gray rollout: attachment is out-of-band — non-reading handlers ignore it. Client/server can be upgraded independently.
  - Buffer leak fix: Using release_request_attachment() (move-semantics) instead of get_request_attachment() (read-only) ensures the
    attachment buffer is drained after each request, preventing cross-request leakage on yalantinglibs 0.5.7 connection reuse.

  - Re-entrancy safety: CurrentCtxScope always installed (even for empty attachment) on single-threaded io thread to override any residue
    from a concurrently-blocked predecessor.

title: [Store] Add the per-object entry, object route and group table
body:
## Description

Adds the storage primitives the tenant-first metadata model is built from:

| New header | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `mooncake-store/include/object_entry.h` | `ObjectEntry`: owns the `ObjectMetadata` envelope, adds the per-key task state, and keeps its lock private behind `WithExclusiveAccess` / `WithSharedAccess` |
| `mooncake-store/include/object_index.h` | `ObjectIndex`: one tenant's object route, a flat map from object key to a strong `ObjectEntry` handle |
| `mooncake-store/include/group_index.h` | `GroupIndex`: group id → one shared `Lease` plus the member keys that point at it |
| `mooncake-store/include/dynamic_replication_lease_table.h` | `DynamicReplicationLeaseTable`: the in-flight replica-action leases for one tenant, keyed by proposal id |

All four sit in `mooncake::` beside `ObjectMetadata`. Group membership is a property of the objects, not of tenancy, so the group table does not live under `include/tenant/`.

RFC #3670 moves metadata ownership from global shards to tenants and narrows the mutation boundary from one shard lock to one object lock. These are what that model stores: the per-object shell, the route that finds it, the group table that makes a group evict all-or-none, and the leases for the replica actions a client has in flight. Today the same state sits in parallel per-key maps on the shard, where one lock covers unrelated objects and a compound operation touches several maps under it.

**No behavior change: nothing constructs these types yet.**

### What the types promise

- **A strong handle means alive, not current.** `ObjectIndex::Get` returns the entry under the shared route lock and releases that lock before the caller takes the entry's own lock, so a caller revalidates through the identity-checked `EraseIf` or the entry's `generation()` instead of trusting its handle. `generation()` is atomic, because publication assigns it under the route lock while a holder reads it under no lock.
- **One key per object.** `Insert` routes by `entry->key()`, so the slot an entry lands in and the key every lookup, revalidation and erase uses cannot disagree.
- **Lookups take a view.** The route and the group tables use the transparent `TransparentStringHash` and take `std::string_view` on the lookup paths, so a caller that already holds a view does not build a string to find an entry.
- **One lock per object, and it stays inside the entry.** The per-key state is private, and the only way to read or mutate it is `WithExclusiveAccess` / `WithSharedAccess`, which hold the lock for the callback and hand out the envelope and the state together; the lock order is entry lock → route lock → metadata spin lock, never the reverse for any pair.
- **An in-flight action is not an object.** The replica-action leases are keyed by proposal id in their own table rather than folded into the route or into an entry. Several proposals can be in flight for one key, so the table also indexes them by object key and orders the expiry sweep with a deadline heap: an object teardown retracts the leases for its key without scanning, and the sweep does not scan either.
- **One lease per group.** A group is a membership table plus a single shared `Lease`. `AddMember` materializes the group, registers the member and returns that lease under one lock section, so a lease and its membership cannot disagree; the read path extends the lease on a member hit without touching this index, and eviction reads it to decide the whole group at once. Re-registering a member returns the same lease, and an empty group id is the ungrouped case: it registers nothing and returns no lease.

## Module

- [x] Mooncake Store (`mooncake-store`)

## Type of Change

- [x] New feature

## How Has This Been Tested?

Build and the store regression set on a 256-core Ubuntu box, Debug + Ninja, `USE_ETCD=ON`, GNU 11.

**Test commands:**
```bash
cmake --build build -j$(nproc)

cd build && LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$PWD:$PWD/mooncake-store:$PWD/mooncake-store/src:$PWD/mooncake-common:$PWD/mooncake-common/etcd \
  MC_METADATA_SERVER=http://127.0.0.1:18080/metadata DEFAULT_KV_LEASE_TTL=500 \
  ctest -R 'master_service|master_scenario|high_availability|tenant|object_entry|object_index|group_index|dynamic_replication|promotion|batch_oplog' \
  -j8 --output-on-failure
```

**Test results:**
- [x] Build clean, no new warnings
- [x] 43/43 pass. Each new type has its own suite — `object_entry_test` 2, `object_index_test` 5, `dynamic_replication_lease_table_test` 6, `group_index_test` 5, 18 in total — covering the route (publish, identity-checked erase, generations, duplicate rejection, snapshot enumeration), the entry (the envelope it owns, the state a shared reader sees), the lease table (proposal-keyed lookup, replacement, retraction by object key, the expiry sweep against removed and extended leases) and the group table (one shared lease per group, membership add/remove/repeat, the ungrouped case, the group dropped with its last member).

title: [Store] Structure NoFQosConfig environment settings
body:
## Description

Part of #3809. Move `MC_NOF_SUBMIT_CHUNK_BYTES` and `MC_NOF_INFLIGHT_BYTES_LIMIT` into a private, client-owned `NoFQosConfig` and the common environment catalog. The first QoS construction still caches both byte limits in the original read order, with defaults of 131072 and 33554432 bytes. Absent/empty inputs remain silent; invalid nonempty inputs fall back independently and keep the original raw-value warnings. Conversion to block counts remains in `SpdkNofQos` because it depends on the current block size. No public API or NoF worker/debug setting changes.

The shared typed integer parser is used for nonempty input. It intentionally accepts trailing ASCII whitespace (for example, `"2048 "`), which the previous `strtol` path rejected. The focused tests cover defaults, independent parsing and fallback, raw warnings and their order, integer boundaries, and process-first-use caching. Block-count assertions are guarded by `USE_NOF` and require an enabled build.

This is a separate configuration owner from the simultaneously proposed `NoFWorkerPoolConfig` PR. Open #3424 renames the QoS type and #3292 changes related QoS code, but neither moves these variables to an owned config. If either merges first and produces a real conflict or behavior change, integrate against the landed code before merge; a behind count alone does not call for rebase.

Implements the SSD/SPDK administration slice of Phase 2 from #3534 by moving
its tracked Python modules into the unified root Python project.

- move `mooncake_ssd_register.py`, `mooncake_ssd_unregister.py`, and
  `spdk_tgt_create.py` to `python/mooncake` as their single authoritative
  source;
- move the directly owned SPDK target tests to `python/tests/ssd`;

- redirect direct CMake installation and temporary legacy wheel staging to the

body:
## Description

Follow-up to #4100. The first label-triggered Hygon run failed at `actions/checkout@v4`: checkout now refuses fork PR code in a `pull_request_target` workflow unless explicitly opted in.

Set `allow-unsafe-pr-checkout: true` on all three PR checkout steps: wheel build, Transfer Engine test scripts, and Mooncake Store test scripts. Each still checks out the fork repository at the event's exact head SHA with `persist-credentials: false`.

This is an explicit opt-in under the existing `run-hygon-ci` authorization model. The person applying the label must review the current PR code, including build and Docker/SSH control scripts. This option removes checkout's default refusal; it does not provide isolation or make arbitrary fork code safe. It adds no new credentials or token permissions.

The fix must land in official `main` before the label-triggered workflow can use it. Updating the fork's workflow alone cannot validate this change in the same PR run.

title: [TE/TENT] Add adaptive RDMA congestion control core
body:
## Description

Add a shared adaptive congestion-control core for the Classic Transfer Engine
and TENT RDMA adapters. The core provides byte-window admission, pressure
hysteresis, failure classification, path quarantine, cooldown, bounded recovery
probing, and generation-aware feedback handling.

The implementation supports three modes:

- `off`: preserve the original behavior without accounting or admission
  decisions;
- `observe`: collect signals and update path state without rejecting work;
- `enforce`: apply window, quarantine, and probe admission decisions.

The public and internal names spell out congestion control: the build option is
`MOONCAKE_ENABLE_ADAPTIVE_CONGESTION_CONTROL`, startup settings use the
`MC_ADAPTIVE_CONGESTION_CONTROL_*` prefix, and the shared C++ namespace is
`mooncake::adaptive_congestion_control`. No abbreviated compatibility aliases
are introduced because these interfaces have not been released.

It also adds a shared RDMA completion and asynchronous-event classifier,
validated startup configuration, a compile-time disable option, focused unit
and concurrency tests, a CPU microbenchmark, and startup-parameter
documentation.

This PR intentionally does not connect the controller to the Classic TE or
TENT transfer paths. Those adapters are staged in follow-up PRs, so merging
this shared core alone does not change production transfer behavior. Building
with `MOONCAKE_ENABLE_ADAPTIVE_CONGESTION_CONTROL=OFF` omits the adaptive
targets entirely.

Related RFC: [#4162](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/issues/4162)

title: [TransferEngine] Skip in-flight task walk in getBatchTransferStatus for RDMA
body:
## Description

`getBatchTransferStatus()` currently walks every task on every in-flight poll. For large RDMA batches that is O(task) CPU on the wait path, even though CQ completions already know how many tasks have finished.

This PR:

1. Always publishes `BatchDesc::finished_task_count` from `Slice::markSuccess` / `markFailed` (no `USE_EVENT_DRIVEN_COMPLETION` required).
2. Marks a batch `counter_eligible` only when every submitted transport opts in via `supportsBatchCompletionCounter()` (RDMA does; TCP and mixed batches do not).
3. Seals each RDMA task after `submitTransferTask()` so a CQ completion that races submit cannot publish the task until its slice list is complete.
4. Lets in-flight `getBatchTransferStatus()` return `WAITING` from the counter when `counter_eligible && slice_timeout <= 0 && !has_failure && finished < task_count`.
5. Changes classic tebench to wait with `getBatchTransferStatus`, matching TENT’s batch-granularity wait. The old per-task `getTransferStatus(batch, i)` loop never hit this shortcut and is not the right wait for “submit a batch, then wait for the batch.”

On completion (or timeout / failure / mixed transport) the existing per-task walk still runs once to aggregate bytes and surface errors. `mp_submitTransfer` keeps the old poll path.

API and completion semantics are unchanged. Callers that already wait at batch granularity — Python `getBatchTransferStatus`, TENT, Ascend examples — pick this up without a new wait API.

**Not in this PR:** submit-path work, event-driven completion, unsignaled WRs, or MR lookup (#4132).

### Benefit (same wait API, this change only)

H20, `mlx5_bond_0` loopback, DRAM READ, 4096 B blocks, 1 thread, 5 s. Both sides use `getBatchTransferStatus` (the classic wait in this PR). Independent variable is the engine change vs `origin/main`.

| batch | version | wait p50 | **µs / poll p50** | submit p50 | BW (GB/s) |
|------:|---------|---------:|------------------:|-----------:|----------:|
| 4096 | main | 2485 µs | **60.9** | 2748 µs | 2.56 |
| 4096 | this PR | 1450 µs | **0.025** | 1965 µs | 4.08 |
| 207360 | main | 793 ms | **3019** | 73.0 ms | 0.995 |
| 207360 | this PR | 743 ms | **0.020** | 73.6 ms | 1.06 |

- **Headline:** in-flight `getBatchTransferStatus` goes from O(task) to O(1). Cost per poll drops from ~61 µs (4K) / ~3.0 ms (207K) to ~20 ns.
- **Wait wall time** improves when the task walk was a large fraction of wait (4K: −42%). At 207360 × 4 KB the RDMA plus ~73 ms submit already fill ~740–800 ms, so wait is only −6% and e2e BW is only +7%. Do not treat 207K BW as the win.
- Busy-wait tebench poll count rises after the change (each poll is cheap). That is expected; the metric is cost per poll, not poll count.
- After this PR, `tebench --backend=classic` exercises the shortcut. Do not compare new classic tebench BW to numbers taken with the old per-task wait.

title: [Store] Add batch snapshot and retention capacity metrics
body:
## Description

Batch snapshot maintenance currently exposes little information about why capture is skipped, whether publication succeeded independently of GC/pruning, or how much OpLog remains above the compaction floor.

Add `ha_snapshot_*` metrics for pointer ages/cursors, verified artifact sizes, capture pause, upload/bootstrap/replay latency, catch-up targets, lease contention/loss, GC outcomes, and pruning candidates/floor advances. Fixed operation/skip enums bound label cardinality. Gauges reset with a new standby runtime; process counters remain cumulative and legacy mode is explicitly disabled. Metrics reuse existing reads and do no storage I/O during scraping.

For example, when floor CAS succeeds but deletion fails, the floor gauge advances and the pruning error counter increments; publication remains successful. Rebootstrap exposes the installed applied cursor only after swapping the restored state.

Implements M02 observability under #3167 and #3808. This extends the existing snapshot/retention implementation; it does not implement the broader metrics architecture refactor proposed in #3158.

## Module

- [ ] Transfer Engine (`mooncake-transfer-engine`)

title: [Bugfix][TENT] Map TENT status codes to classic negative ERR_* in the shim
body:
## Description

The int-returning TransferEngine methods in the MC_USE_TENT compatibility shim returned (int)status.code() straight from TENT. That is wrong twice over:

1. Sign. The classic contract for these methods is 0 on success and a NEGATIVE ERR_* on failure; callers test `ret < 0`. TENT's Status::Code is non-negative, so every failure came back positive and was silently treated as success.

2. Numbering. TENT's Status::Code enum does not share numbering with the classic codes: TENT kDeviceNotFound == 4 but ERR_DEVICE_NOT_FOUND == -6, TENT kInvalidMetadataType == 6 collides with the classic kDeviceNotFound magnitude, TENT kNotImplemented == 200 collides with classic kMetadata, and so on. Even the magnitude was meaningless to classic callers. The Store client, for example, specifically tolerates ERR_ADDRESS_NOT_REGISTERED (client_service.cpp: `rc != 0 && rc != ERR_ADDRESS_NOT_REGISTERED`); with TENT returning +3 for kAddressNotRegistered that guard never matched and a benign unregister was escalated to a hard error.

Add a file-local tentStatusToErrCode() that maps each TENT code to its classic ERR_* equivalent (success stays 0), and route all int-returning shim methods through it: closeSegment, registerLocalMemory(+Batch), unregisterLocalMemory(+Batch), getNotifies, sendNotifyByID/ByName, and the internal Backend::closeSegment. Unmapped/internal failures fall back to ERR_CONTEXT, mirroring how the Status-returning shim methods already collapse unknown TENT failures to Status::Context.

Adds TransferEngineTentCompatibilityTest.IntApiReturnsClassicNegativeErrCodes: closeSegment() on a never-opened handle fails in TENT with kInvalidArgument, so the shim must return ERR_INVALID_ARGUMENT (-1). The test fails on main (returns +1) and passes after the fix.

Refs #3995 (P1-error-codes)

**Fix.**
Add a file-local tentStatusToErrCode() in the USE_TENT section of transfer_engine.cpp that maps each TENT code to its classic ERR_* equivalent (success stays 0), and route every int-returning shim method through it:

closeSegment, registerLocalMemory, unregisterLocalMemory, registerLocalMemoryBatch, unregisterLocalMemoryBatch, getNotifies, sendNotifyByID, sendNotifyByName, and the internal Backend::closeSegment.

title: [CI/Build] Unify release wheels on the root scikit-build backend
body:
## Description

Move release wheel assembly to the repository-root scikit-build-core backend used by source installs.

- Replace `scripts/build_wheel.sh` and the legacy setuptools project with a release configuration/metadata adapter plus an isolated auditwheel repair step.
- Migrate CUDA, CPU, EFA, ROCm, MUSA, NPU, nightly, and Docker callers; preserve variant names, output conventions, and configured native build profiles.
- Preserve CUDA EP/PG artifacts during repair, include allocator helpers and Store-only etcd runtime dependencies, and make root version metadata authoritative (0.3.13).
- Add packaging/workflow regression coverage and document migration of removed build commands.

Related RFC: #3534 (also related to #3425 and build roadmap #3556). This implements the release-backend cutover/legacy assembly removal portion, not the complete RFC. Existing subsystem migration PRs such as #3628 and #3623 move Python modules; this PR instead changes wheel construction and its callers. It does not add cibuildwheel, centralize publication, or complete private native-module facades.

```bash
/tmp/mooncake-review-venv/bin/python -m pytest -q -rs \
  python/tests/packaging \
  mooncake-wheel/tests/test_release_wheel_tags.py \
  mooncake-wheel/tests/test_testpypi_wheel_gate.py
bash -n scripts/repair_wheel.sh
git diff --check
# Used prek because pre-commit is unavailable; run only against changed files.
prek run --files <changed files>
```

**Test results:**
- [x] Unit tests pass: 65 passed, 1 skipped.
- [x] Local installed-wheel integration tests pass: see the CUDA/non-CUDA A/B validation below. The optional pytest smoke test in the earlier command remained skipped because `MOONCAKE_TEST_WHEEL` was not supplied.
- [x] Manual testing done: shell syntax and diff whitespace checks pass.

The scoped hook run passed after auto-fixes. Unrelated pre-existing Python/CMake formatting rewrites were subsequently reverted to keep the PR focused, so the final tree is not claimed to pass all formatting hooks. Regression tests were rerun after those reversions and still pass. Local CUDA/non-CUDA native builds and installed-wheel checks were subsequently completed as described below; the full hardware release matrix remains unvalidated.

### Local before/after wheel validation

Compared `140e1f43` (before the packaging migration) with `ce6460bc` using independently built **CUDA 12.8 and non-CUDA wheels** in the same Ubuntu 22.04 / x86_64 / CPython 3.12.13 environment. The old revision used the legacy setuptools release script; the new revision used scikit-build-core and the new repair script. CUDA builds included EP/PG for one representative Torch ABI (2.13.0).

For each variant, tested a fresh old installation, a fresh new installation, and an in-place `pip install --upgrade` from old to new. The new wheels used a test-only `0.3.14.dev0` version override to exercise pip's upgrade behavior; this does not change the proposed release version.

| Check | non-CUDA | CUDA 12.8 |
|---|---|---|
| Install, pip check, core imports, CLI checks | Pass in all three states | Pass in all three states |
| fast-copy, import, CLI and native BufferPool tests | 25/25 in each state | 25/25 in each state |
| Store two-client TCP put/get/remove (1 B, 4 KiB, 1 MiB) | Pass | Pass |
| TE registered CPU-memory TCP write/read | Pass | Pass |
| Real GPU-memory TCP write/read (1 MiB, RTX 5080) | N/A | Pass in all three states |

This is **150 pytest test executions** across six installation states, not 150 distinct tests. Store smoke tests disabled the same-host direct-copy shortcut with `MC_STORE_MEMCPY=0`.

Additional checks:
- Old/new/upgraded non-CUDA wheels passed real Store/TE smoke tests in a separate container without GPU, driver or CUDA libraries, after installing the required OS libraries. Neither non-CUDA wheel had CUDA DT_NEEDED dependencies.
- Public engine/store symbol and class-member sets, six console entry-point declarations, and effective base dependencies on Python 3.12 matched. Common ELF DT_NEEDED sets matched after normalizing ABI suffixes and auditwheel hashes; duplicate vendored libasio/libetcd_wrapper copies were eliminated.
- All four wheel RECORDs passed hash/size verification. Each CUDA wheel's EP/PG staged payloads were byte-identical to its own original build artifacts after repair. EP and PG 2.13 imports passed with Torch 2.13.0+cu130 and an explicitly supplied CUDA 12 runtime; this was not a distributed-kernel test.
- Missing OS/CUDA runtime dependencies and mixed CUDA/non-CUDA uninstall breakage reproduced on both revisions, so these are not new regressions.

**Compatibility observations:** Standard imports and the tested operations showed no regression. The switch to the root package removes the legacy `pkgutil.extend_path` behavior and changes generic native filenames: non-CUDA no longer includes `engine.so`, and neither variant includes `store.so` (ABI-tagged extensions are installed instead). Constructed split-namespace imports and hardcoded native-path loads therefore differ. No actual downstream dependency on these behaviors was identified; they are compatibility boundaries, not demonstrated failures of normal wheel usage.

**Limits:** These local wheels target manylinux_2_35, not the production manylinux_2_28 baseline. This A/B test does not cover CUDA 13, other Python versions, ARM64, RDMA/GPUDirect, multi-GPU/NVLink, distributed EP/PG kernels, the full Torch ABI matrix, or publication to PyPI. title: [WIP][CI] Enable TENT runtime in T-One e2e as a parallel job
body:
## Description

Two changes: (1) enable the TENT (Transfer Engine NEXT) runtime in the T-One e2e pipeline as the first step towards TENT productionization, **without reducing classic-engine coverage**, and (2) a source fix required to build TENT wheels on older glibc, discovered by the first `use-tent` CI build.

**1. T-One e2e dual-job enablement** — `e2e-ci.yml` now runs two T-One jobs in parallel: the existing classic job (unchanged) and a new TENT job that activates the runtime via `MC_USE_TENT=1`.

- `_build-wheel.yaml` gains a `use-tent` input (default `false`); `ci.yml`'s `build-wheel-cu13` (the artifact fed to T-One) opts in. One dual-engine wheel serves both jobs: without `MC_USE_TENT` the facade runs classic, with it TENT activates. **Release wheels are unaffected** (only the PR CI cu13 build opts in).
- The TENT job is selected via `USE_TENT=true` in `env_info` (same mechanism as `ARTIFACT_ID`) with a distinct T-One job name (`mooncake-ci-tent-<SHA>`); `e2e-gate` aggregates both.
- `tone_tests/scripts/common.sh` injects container-level `MC_USE_TENT=1` when `USE_TENT=true` and **fails fast** if the installed engine lacks TENT — preventing a silent classic fallback that would make the job pass without testing TENT.

**Explicitly noted behavior change for the classic job**: its wheel is now *compiled* with TENT enabled (previously without). Runtime behavior is unchanged — the classic facade is the default when `MC_USE_TENT` is unset — but the binary carries dormant TENT code.

**2. TENT wheel build fix for older glibc** — the first `use-tent` build on the manylinux2_28 runner (RHEL8-era glibc) failed because `mnnvl_transport.cpp` uses `SYS_pidfd_open`/`SYS_pidfd_getfd` without including `<sys/syscall.h>` or defining fallbacks. The fix adds the explicit include plus the arch-independent asm-generic syscall numbers (434/438) as fallbacks. Dev machines with newer glibc never see this — a portability bug the new CI coverage caught on its first run.

Validation performed before this PR (2×8×H20, sglang 0.5.17 PD
disaggregation, single-node and cross-node):

**GSM8K accuracy (200 questions, 5-shot completion, PD vs no-PD baseline):**

| Model | PD topology (TENT) | PD score | Baseline (no PD) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-8B | single-node, P=TP2 / D=TP1 | 0.950 | 0.950 |
| Qwen3-8B | single-node, P=TP1 / D=TP2 | 0.950 | 0.950 |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash | cross-node, TP4 / TP4 | 0.970 | 0.965 |

**Cross-node performance, classic vs TENT (Qwen3-8B, 24.5k-token transfers concurrent burst):**

| TP (P/D) | serial large, classic / TENT | burst p50/p99, classic / TENT | burst tput, classic / TENT |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1/1 | 3.91 / 3.92 s | 0.79/0.95 · 0.73/0.96 s | 5,180 / 5,410 tok/s |
| 2/2 | 2.09 / 2.12 s | 0.73/0.80 · 0.73/0.98 s | 11,958 / 10,771 tok/s |
| 4/4 | 1.14 / 1.15 s | 0.46/0.54 · 0.48/0.53 s | 18,420 / 17,983 tok/s |

DeepSeek-V4-Flash cross-node TP4/TP4: 1.96 / 2.00 s serial large, 4,330 /
4,228 tok/s burst (classic / TENT). All differences within run variance.

**Dynamic transport selection (TENT's core capability, no app-side
changes):**

| Scenario | Route chosen | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| intra-node GPU↔GPU | NVLink | 99.999% of KV bytes (12h soak) |
| cross-node | RDMA | 100% of bytes (13.85 GB benchmark window) |

**Stability**: 12h single-node soak — 172,584/172,584 requests (100.000%),
22 TB KV transferred via TENT, 0 transfer failures / 0 failovers, flat GPU
memory. TENT also builds clean on current main including the

title: [TransferEngine] Cache the last-hit MR and index the buffer list for selectDevice
body:
## Description

`selectDevice` used to walk every registered MR for every slice. NIXL-style
batches (N ≈ 2e5 descriptors, R ≈ 256 MRs) paid an N×R CPU scan on `post`.

This change:

- Tries the last-hit MR first.
- Builds a range index on the COW `SegmentDesc` when coverage is unique
  (`index.size() == buffers.size()` and `!overlaps()`).
- Falls back to the original linear first-match scan otherwise.

First-match semantics are unchanged. `selectTransport` reuse is not in this PR.

Measured on same-host H20 / `mlx5_bond_0` RDMA loopback (not GB200, not PD).
All runs logged `installTransport, type=rdma`. Headline metric is submit/`post`
CPU; poll/wave is RDMA completion and is not claimed.

| Workload | Metric | Before | This PR | Change |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| NIXL 207360 × 32256 B, R=256, READ | P50 `post` | 227.381 ms | 71.262 ms | 3.2×, −156 ms (−69%) |
| classic tebench DRAM, 65536 × 4 KiB, mr=256 | first-batch `submit_us` | 117.8 ms | 33.6 ms | 3.5×, −84 ms (−71%) |
| classic tebench DRAM, 207360 × 4 KiB, mr=256 | first-batch `submit_us` | 370.9 ms | 97.4 ms | 3.8×, −274 ms (−74%) |

After the change, R=256 sits on the R=1 floor on both harnesses.
