title: [TransferEngine] Add Intel XPU (Level Zero) support
body:
## Description

Adds Intel XPU (oneAPI Level Zero) support to the Transfer Engine, so XPU device
memory can be registered and moved over the existing RDMA (dma_buf) and TCP
transports. XPU reuses those transports through a cuda-alike shim layer rather
than adding a new transport.

Intel XPUs use Level Zero, a different stack from CUDA/HIP/MUSA. This follows the
same `gpu_vendor/` + `cuda_alike.h` seam the MUSA and MACA ports already use, so
no transport or engine code needed restructuring:

- `USE_XPU` cmake option with Level Zero auto-detection
- `gpu_vendor/xpu.h` / `xpu.cpp` — cuda-alike surface over Level Zero
  (ZeRuntime singleton, device alloc/free, H2D/D2H memcpy, pointer attributes,
  PCI bus id, allocation-base query, dma_buf export)
- `USE_XPU` added to the existing GPU-vendor guards in `cuda_alike.h`,
  `memory_location.cpp`, `topology.cpp` and the TCP staging path
- `rdma_context.cpp` — dma_buf export for XPU device memory
- `scripts/build_xpu.sh` for conda-based XPU builds

Scope note: this is the first phase of Intel XPU support — transports and memory
registration only. The MoE EP layer is a separate, stacked PR. The full phased
design is in the linked RFC issue rather than a file in the tree.

## Module

- [x] Transfer Engine (`mooncake-transfer-engine`)
- [ ] Mooncake Store (`mooncake-store`)
- [ ] Reshard (`mooncake-reshard`)
- [ ] Mooncake EP (`mooncake-ep`)
- [ ] Mooncake PG (`mooncake-pg`)
- [ ] Integration (`mooncake-integration`)
- [ ] P2P Store (`mooncake-p2p-store`)
- [x] Python Wheel (`mooncake-wheel`)
- [x] Common (`mooncake-common`)
- [ ] Mooncake RL (`mooncake-rl`)
- [x] CI/CD
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Other

## Type of Change

- [ ] Bug fix
- [x] New feature
- [ ] Refactor
- [ ] Breaking change
- [ ] Documentation update
- [ ] Performance improvement
- [ ] Other

## How Has This Been Tested?

Hardware: 8x Intel Arc Pro B60 (Battlemage), oneAPI 2026.1, Level Zero 1.26,
glibc 2.42, GCC 15. This host has no InfiniBand, so the TCP path is covered
end to end and the RDMA/dma_buf path is covered only at the export level (see
Caveats).

**Test commands:**
```bash
# Prerequisites: source /opt/intel/oneapi/setvars.sh, the Level Zero
# development package (level-zero-devel / libze-dev), and the usual Mooncake
# dependencies from dependencies.sh. No conda env is required; if one is
# active it is added to the CMake search paths. Level Zero is looked up in
# $LEVEL_ZERO_ROOT, then $CONDA_PREFIX, then /usr and /usr/local.
#
# Note: do NOT put a conda gtest on the include path — the project
# FetchContents googletest 1.17.0 (mooncake-common/FindGTest.cmake) and a
# second gtest causes an ABI mismatch at link time. yalantinglibs needs no
# action; FindYLT.cmake fetches it.
./scripts/build_xpu.sh build-xpu

# Unit tests
./build-xpu/mooncake-transfer-engine/tests/xpu_transport_test

# Wheel
BUILD_DIR=build-xpu ./scripts/build_wheel.sh 3.12 dist-xpu
pip install --no-deps mooncake-wheel/dist-xpu/mooncake_transfer_engine-*.whl

# CI gates
./scripts/code_format.sh --check --changed-lines --base origin/main
pre-commit run --files $(git diff --name-only --diff-filter=ACMR origin/main...HEAD)
```

**Test results:**
- [x] Unit tests pass — 21/21 `xpu_transport_test` cases on real hardware
      (init, set-device, device/host alloc, pointer attributes, H2D+D2H memcpy
      roundtrip, isDeviceMemory, dma_buf export, caller-owned fd, allocation
      base/offset, multi-alloc, GPU_PREFIX, plus 8 async/stream cases). All
      GTEST_SKIP cleanly on hosts with no Intel GPU.
- [x] Integration tests pass — `engine.so` initialises with
      `protocol=tcp, metadata=P2PHANDSHAKE`; `register_memory` /
      `transfer_sync_write` return 0; topology discovery reports
      "Level Zero XPU runtime initialized".
- [x] Manual testing done — end-to-end transfer of **XPU device memory**
      between two processes over TCP: a `torch.xpu` tensor is registered with
      `register_memory()`, written with `transfer_sync_write()`, and the
      receiving process reads back the expected byte pattern from its own XPU
      tensor. Also verified `pip install mooncake-transfer-engine` then
      importing and initialising from outside the build tree.

Fixes found by that first build/run, each with the failure it produced:

| Fix | Failure without it |
|---|---|
| `build_xpu.sh`: pass `-DWITH_STORE_RUST=OFF` | configure aborts — `WITH_STORE_RUST=ON requires WITH_STORE=ON` |
| `build_xpu.sh`: only apply `-isystem /usr/include` for the conda cross-compiler | `stdlib.h: No such file or directory` on GCC 15 (breaks libstdc++ `#include_next`) |
| `build_wheel.sh`: guard the `transfer_engine_bench` copy | wheel build aborts under `set -e` when `BUILD_EXAMPLES=OFF` |
| `rdma_context.cpp`: add `USE_XPU` to the `ibv_reg_dmabuf_mr` guard | exported dma_buf fd discarded; XPU device memory silently fell back to `ibv_reg_mr` |
| `rdma_context.cpp`: resolve the allocation base instead of assuming offset 0 | a tensor at a nonzero offset in a larger block registers the wrong bytes (the normal case with PyTorch's caching allocator) |
| `xpu.cpp`: return a `dup()` and call `zeMemPutIpcHandle()` | one leaked driver fd per export, and the caller's `close()` freed a descriptor the driver still owned |

### Asynchronous copies

`cudaMemcpyAsync` is a real asynchronous copy rather than a synchronous
fallback, with the minimum stream API to use it safely
(`cudaStreamCreate`/`CreateWithFlags`/`Destroy`/`Synchronize`/`Query` and
`cudaDeviceSynchronize`). A `cudaStream_t` is an in-order asynchronous Level
Zero immediate command list plus the device it was created on.

Three findings from bringing this up, each of which would have corrupted data
silently:

| Finding | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Level Zero immediate command lists are **not** in-order by default | A small copy overtakes a preceding large copy to the same address. Fixed with `ZE_COMMAND_QUEUE_FLAG_IN_ORDER`; `StreamPreservesSubmissionOrder` fails without it. |
| `zeMemFree` does no in-flight checking, unlike `cudaFree`'s implicit device sync | Freeing a buffer with a copy in flight corrupts silently once copies are truly async. `cudaFree`/`cudaFreeHost` now drain first. |
| `zeCommandListAppendMemoryCopy` must not be called concurrently on one command list | The per-device list is shared by every thread calling `cudaMemcpy`; the multi-threaded TCP transport would have hit this. Now locked. |

The ordering test is a real detector, not a smoke test: it needs a
write-after-write to one address, asymmetric sizes (large then <=4 KiB), and
pinned host sources. Weaken any of the three and it passes against the broken
implementation — measured, and recorded in a comment so it is not "simplified"
later.

`cudaEvent_t` is deliberately not implemented (needs an event pool, no consumer
in the XPU build yet) — callers get a link error, not silent misbehaviour.

## Checklist

- [x] I have performed a self-review of my own code
- [x] I have formatted my code using `./scripts/code_format.sh`
- [x] I have run pre-commit on the files changed in this PR and all hooks pass
- [x] I have updated the documentation (if applicable) — README protocol and
      accelerator lists
- [x] I have added tests to prove my changes are effective
- [ ] For changes >500 LOC: I have filed an RFC issue — **TODO before merge**

## Caveats / reviewer notes

- **The RDMA dma_buf path is not verified on hardware.** This host has no
  InfiniBand, so `exportDmabuf()` is unit-tested (a valid fd is produced,
  caller-owned, with the right base/offset) but `ibv_reg_dmabuf_mr` and an
  actual GPU-direct RDMA transfer are untested. Only the TCP path is covered
  end to end. Happy to run this on a Mellanox host if someone can point me at one.
- `exportDmaBufFd()` extracts the fd from the first `sizeof(int)` bytes of
  `ze_ipc_mem_handle_t.data`. That is how the xe/i915 driver lays it out today,
  but it is not guaranteed by the Level Zero spec — flagging it as the most
  driver-version-sensitive assumption here.
- `build-xpu/` added to `.gitignore` — the default build dir of the new
  `scripts/build_xpu.sh`.

## AI Assistance Disclosure

- [ ] No AI tools were used
- [x] AI tools were used (specify below)

Claude Code was used to bring up and debug the build on Intel hardware, to audit
the never-before-compiled Level Zero code (which is how the three dma_buf
defects above were found), and to draft this description. Every changed line has
been reviewed by the submitter, and every claim in the "How Has This Been
Tested" section corresponds to a command that was actually run on the hardware
described.

title: [Doc] Explain HP TCP multi-rail concurrency tuning
body:
## Description

Explain how HP TCP rail count, total connections per peer and worker count interact. Four rails with four lanes have one connection per rail; increasing worker count alone cannot add active lane owners once those four lanes already have distinct owners.

Add a matched Store `get_into` comparison on unchanged main `202ad9c89`: 8 MiB host-memory objects, four outstanding calls, CPU/new-memory placement fixed to NUMA 0. Three repeats per configuration cover two/four rails at 4 workers/4 lanes and 8/8, plus four-rail 8/4 and 4/8 controls. The guide includes all run ranges and CPU costs.

Four rails improved from 7.599 GB/s at 4/4 to 11.487 at 8/8. Against the best measured two-rail configuration (4/4, 10.371 GB/s), the gain was 10.8%, with higher client and server CPU consumption. Two rails regressed at 8/8. These results support workload-specific configuration, not raising defaults or adding runtime policy.

Related: #3834 provides static routing, #3861 provides large-READ slicing, #3987 provides per-peer lane rotation, and #3988 handles idle connections. This PR changes one documentation page; runtime code, ownership, wire format and defaults are unchanged.

## Module

```bash
make html
```

- Two reserved hosts completed 18 timing runs, each after a 32-object bytewise correctness check. Raw JSON, 36 endpoint configurations, CPU affinity and memory policies match the specified cases. Actual connection counts and per-rail payload totals match successful Store bytes.
- Seven frozen runtime files were hash-checked on both hosts for each phase. Both endpoint worker counts change together; results do not isolate client/server contributions or eliminate NUMA effects.
- Two separate stack-sampling runs confirmed four active receive workers and Store completion polling. They are excluded from performance results; snapshots do not establish function-time percentages.

title: [Integration] Release GIL during single memory registration
body:
# [Integration] Release GIL during single memory registration

## Description

`TransferEngine.register_memory()` and `unregister_memory()` currently keep the
Python GIL while their native `registerLocalMemory()` and
`unregisterLocalMemory()` calls execute. The batch wrappers already release the
GIL around the corresponding native calls.

This change applies the same scoped release to the single-buffer wrappers.
Python argument conversion remains before the C++ method, pybind11 reacquires
the GIL before converting the return value, and native address, length,
location, metadata, ordering, and error behavior are unchanged.

The regression test arms another Python thread before a bounded series of TCP
host-memory registration calls. It passes only when that thread can run during
both the single-register and single-unregister native spans. This is adjacent
to the GIL work in #300 and #3947 and the batch wrappers in #2191, but a current
open-PR search found no exact duplicate for these two wrappers.

## Module

`b41d8e7b1f16c803bac65b486fec65a8bdf3b9f1`.

The build and wheel commands below were run in a repository-devcontainer-derived
Linux image, with the repository mounted at `/src`:

**Test commands:**

```bash
cmake -S /src -B /build \
  -DWITH_STORE=OFF -DWITH_STORE_RUST=OFF -DWITH_TE=ON \

  mooncake-integration/transfer_engine/transfer_engine_py.cpp \

git diff --check origin/main...HEAD
```

**Test results:**

- [x] Unit tests pass

- [x] Manual testing done (exact unchanged-control/candidate comparison)

The candidate passed 10/10 isolated direct-module runs and 10/10 isolated runs
after fresh installation of its locally built non-CUDA wheel. The exact
unchanged control failed 3/3 because both wrappers retained the GIL. A separate
sealed probe observed both candidate wrappers release the GIL in 2/2 repeats
and both control wrappers retain it in 2/2 repeats; every registration call
returned zero.

The exact candidate configured, compiled, linked, built a repaired wheel,
installed into a fresh Python 3.10 environment, passed `pip check`, and had no
unresolved dynamic dependencies in the build container. PR-scoped pre-commit
passed.

No GPU or RDMA runtime was used. This PR claims only that the single-buffer
Python wrappers no longer retain the GIL during their native calls. It does not
claim lower native registration latency, RDMA throughput, GPU speedup, or
end-to-end workload improvement.

title: [PG][1/N] Initialize the new collective framework
body:
## Description Phase 1 of #3483. This PR introduces an opt-in device collective framework for Mooncake PG and implements GPU Ring AllReduce on that framework. The legacy GPU path couples collective algorithms to host workers, transfer submission, synchronization, and failure handling. The new framework gives algorithms a narrower contract: execute a rank-local plan through a device-facing transfer interface, while the Coordinator, runtime, and route providers handle group-wide decisions and shared execution rules. #3483 contains the broader design and rollout plan; this PR implements its first vertical slice. ### User-visible behavior and backend selection The new backend is opt-in. For the PyTorch backend, set the following consistently in every worker before creating the GPU communicator: ```bash export MOONCAKE_PG_PREFERRED_GPU_COLLECTIVE_BACKEND=new ``` An unset value or `legacy` requests the legacy backend. Any other value is rejected as a configuration error. The C API exposes the same preference through `mooncakePgCommConfig_t.preferredGpuCollectiveBackend`. The preference is local input to a group-wide decision, not permission for one rank to switch independently. The Coordinator selects the new backend only when all active ranks request it and advertise the required capability. Conflicting preferences or incomplete capabilities select the legacy backend for the entire group. The selected backend is published in `GroupView` during bootstrap and recomputed after membership transitions. `MooncakeCommunicator` applies the selected backend before group-ready or rank-activation waiters are released. GPU AllReduce then dispatches to `DeviceCollectiveRuntime`; the existing worker path remains the fallback and continues to serve all other collective operations. ### Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR Communicator -->|"default"| Legacy["Legacy backend"] Communicator -->|"opt-in GPU AllReduce"| Runtime["Device collective runtime"] Runtime --> Ring["Ring AllReduce"] Ring --> Transfer["Device transfer service"] Transfer -->|"direct"| P2P["CUDA P2P"] Transfer -->|"fallback"| Host["Host Proxy + Transfer Engine"] ``` ### Implementation details #### Control plane and dispatch Rank and communicator registration publish the transfer, workspace, view-epoch, and Ring endpoints required by the new backend. `CentralizedCoordinatorStateMachine::resolveGpuCollectiveBackend` validates group-wide preference and capability agreement and records one decision in the authoritative `GroupView`. The control-plane now: 1. The Agent installs peer endpoints before applying restored group state, and applies group state before notifying group-ready or rank-activation waiters. 2. Full group updates and incremental rank-state updates use separate effects, so an unrelated rank-state notification cannot replay a stale `GroupView` over a newer device plan. 3. Membership changes preserve endpoints for active members when automatic deactivation is disabled, and link reports are sized by the max world size rather `kMaxNumRanks`. #### Device transfer service `DeviceTransferService` gives device code one contract for payload transfer, notification, signal waiting, and completion. Algorithms address peers by `GlobalRank` and registered-region offset through `DeviceTransferHandle`, without depending on route-specific host objects. Each `RouteProvider` resolves the same endpoint snapshot, and the service selects the first reachable route for each peer. CUDA P2P directly addresses an imported peer mapping; Host Proxy uses mapped command slots and `HostTransferProxy` to submit work through the Transfer Engine host API. Route selection is independent of backend and algorithm selection and is recomputed from endpoint updates; this PR does not switch routes after an in-flight failure. #### Ring AllReduce `RingAllReduceProtocol` derives one flat ring from the active members in the committed `GroupView`. The plan binds the rank's position, neighbors, peer offsets, transfer handle, and protocol state. The kernel keeps a fixed launch shape while selecting the active channel count and tile layout from the current plan and request, then runs a pipelined reduce-scatter followed by all-gather. Before data movement starts, the startup leader publishes the invocation's view epoch to every required peer and waits for their epochs locally. Readiness and consumption sequences protect reused payload slots and are reset together with each plan update. #### Stream ordering and CUDA Graphs `StrongStream` gives device collective invocations one logical order while leaving each kernel on the caller's CUDA stream. Event handoffs preserve order across eager calls on different streams. During capture, graph-order streams establish dependencies within a graph, while external event nodes carry the latest collective tail between eager work and graph replays. Captured kernels retain stable runtime and protocol state addresses, and a graph user object prevents their release while a live graph refers to them. Membership-dependent topology lives in the device plan, allowing a control update to change membership without changing captured kernel arguments or requiring recapture. #### Host-to-device control update protocol A plan cannot be replaced with an asynchronous copy while a previous invocation may still read it. Recovery adds another constraint: its final CTA can remain parked in the failed kernel, so waiting for a separate `cudaMemcpyAsync` before releasing that CTA may deadlock. `ControlUpdate` instead carries a complete, idempotent batch that device code applies at a protocol-defined safe point. `ControlUpdateBuilder` orders state resets before the plan copy. Device execution fences each operation, so a Ready plan cannot become visible before the protocol state it depends on. The mapped `ControlUpdateSlot` follows the publication protocol defined by `ControlUpdateState`: ```mermaid stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Idle Idle --> Writing: host begins publication Published --> Writing: host replaces an unclaimed update Writing --> Published: ordinary GroupView update Published --> Claimed: startup leader claims Writing --> Pinned: recovery update Pinned --> Claimed: parked last CTA claims Claimed --> Idle: ordered operations complete ``` A published but unclaimed ordinary update can be replaced by a newer complete image, coalescing intermediate `GroupView` changes. The first CTA that becomes resident is elected startup leader and claims the latest update before any CTA reads protocol state. Other CTAs remain outside protocol state until startup completes, and `StrongStream` excludes a concurrent invocation. A recovery update becomes `Pinned` instead of `Published`, preventing replacement until the parked final CTA applies that exact update and leaves the failed kernel. #### Failure recovery Device code detects lack of progress through transfer and signal-wait timeouts but delegates membership reconciliation to the existing PG control plane: 1. The first timeout latches the failed in-group rank. Every channel stops accessing the current plan and protocol buffers before reporting completion. 2. The final channel CTA observes all channels quiescent, publishes the failure and a new `failure_generation` through `ControlMailbox`, and remains in the kernel. 3. `DeviceCollectiveRecoveryWorker` drains route work, records the local failure hint, emits an epoch-qualified `LinkEvent`, and invokes `syncAfterFailure` when enabled. 4. After the Agent applies the authoritative `GroupView`, the runtime publishes a `Pinned` update containing the protocol reset and replacement plan, then acknowledges the matching `ready_generation`. 5. The parked CTA applies that update and exits. The next eager launch or graph replay starts from the replacement plan. If reconciliation fails, the runtime invalidates the plan before publishing the pinned reset. ### Resource ownership and operational impact The main allocations are process-wide shared, and belong to `MooncakePGContext`, so creating another subgroup does not duplicate the payload workspace. | Backing allocation | Owner and allocation point | Default footprint and behavior | | --- | --- | --- | | Peer-accessible region | One per initialized CUDA PG context. It is allocated and registered during `MooncakePGContext::initialize` and released during context shutdown after all communicators are gone. | 40 MiB total: a 32 MiB payload workspace plus an 8 MiB reserve for remotely addressable control and protocol slices. | | Staging region | One per CUDA PG context. It is allocated and locally registered the first time an active plan selects a route that requires staging (e.g. Host Proxy), then shared by later invocations and communicators. Peers never address or receive this region in endpoint metadata. | An additional 32 MiB only when required. A context whose Ring routes only use direct CUDA P2P does not allocate it. | The 40 MiB peer-accessible backing region is sub-allocated as follows: - The first 32 MiB is the context-wide `DeviceCollectiveWorkspace` payload buffer shared by all communicators. - The remaining 8 MiB is a fixed reserve for control and protocol state. Each GPU communicator takes `8 * max_group_size` bytes for view epochs and `32 * max_group_size * (1 + 2 * 2) * 8` bytes for Ring receive-ready, payload-ready, and payload-consumed signals, for a total of `1,288 * max_group_size` bytes. At a capacity of 64, this is 80.5 KiB per communicator. These slices are returned when the communicator's device runtime is destroyed. The steady bulk CUDA footprint introduced here is therefore 40 MiB per initialized context on direct P2P routes and 72 MiB after Host Proxy staging is needed, plus smaller metadata and control allocations. Context initialization also creates one Host Proxy worker, one recovery worker, the 32 mapped Host Proxy command slots, device route metadata proportional to `max_world_size`, and the `StrongStream` ordering stream and event. Each GPU communicator adds ordinary device invocation and Ring state, a mapped host control mailbox, and a CUDA handoff event; these allocations are not remotely registered and are small relative to the bulk regions above. ### Supported scope and limitations | Area | This PR's behavior | | --- | --- | | Rollout | The legacy backend remains the default. The new backend requires a consistent group-wide opt-in and falls back to legacy when preferences or capabilities do not agree. | | Build support | Collective v2 is currently compiled only for CUDA. MUSA and MACA builds continue to use the legacy collective runtime. | | Operations | Only GPU AllReduce uses the new runtime. Other GPU collectives and all CPU collectives remain on their existing paths. | | Algorithm | One flat Ring AllReduce implementation. Group-wide algorithm selection and size/topology-based policy are follow-up work. | | Routes | Direct CUDA P2P and Host Proxy through the Transfer Engine. There is no IBGDA or NCCL GIN route and no dynamic route failover in this PR. | | CUDA Graphs | Eager execution, capture, replay, and reuse after membership updates are supported. Runtime state cannot be destroyed while retained by a live graph. | | C API compatibility | `mooncakePgCommConfig_t` appends `preferredGpuCollectiveBackend`. | See #3483 for the follow-up rollout. ### Review guide The suggested review order follows the control decision into the data path and then into recovery: | Order | Area | Entry points and review focus | | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | Backend decision and dispatch | `resolveGpuCollectiveBackend`, `AgentStateMachine::applyGroupView`, and `MooncakeCommunicator::allReduceGpu`: consensus, update ordering, and fallback. | | 2 | Device transfer | `DeviceTransferService`, `RouteProvider`, and `TransferLane`: route resolution and the common device contract. | | 3 | Collective protocol | `DeviceCollectiveRuntime` and `RingAllReduceProtocol`: plan materialization, launch policy, and Ring sequencing. | | 4 | Ordering and recovery | `StrongStream`, `ControlUpdateState`, `prepareCollectiveInvocation`, and `completeChannel`: graph order, update publication, safe points, and recovery handshake. | | 5 | Integration and test behavior | C/PyTorch configuration, Transfer Engine device primitives, and `test_pg_elastic.py`. | ## Module - [ ] Transfer Engine (`mooncake-transfer-engine`) - [ ] Mooncake Store (`mooncake-store`) - [ ] Reshard (`mooncake-reshard`) - [ ] Mooncake EP (`mooncake-ep`) - [x] Mooncake PG (`mooncake-pg`) - [ ] Integration (`mooncake-integration`) - [ ] P2P Store (`mooncake-p2p-store`) - [ ] Python Wheel (`mooncake-wheel`) - [ ] Common (`mooncake-common`) - [ ] Mooncake RL (`mooncake-rl`) - [ ] CI/CD - [ ] Docs - [ ] Other ## Type of Change - [ ] Bug fix - [x] New feature - [ ] Refactor - [ ] Breaking change - [ ] Documentation update - [ ] Performance improvement - [ ] Other ## How Has This Been Tested? For both legacy and new implementations: - All tests under `mooncake-pg/tests` passed. - E2E tests of scale-up and recovery are also passed. ## Benchmark The existing benchmark exercises Mooncake PG through the PyTorch integration layer. Its measurements therefore include Python/PyTorch dispatch overhead, which can dominate small-message latency and does not accurately isolate collective performance. For a more direct comparison, I used a minimal [nccl-tests shim for Mooncake PG](https://gist.github.com/caozhanhao/79eecebbba025c0ea9fc87ed1f94f1f2) that forwards the required NCCL AllReduce API to the Mooncake PG C API. This allows NCCL, the legacy Mooncake PG backend, and the new backend to run under the same `nccl-tests` harness and configuration. The sweep compares four execution modes on a single node of 8 x H20: - **NCCL default:** NCCL selects its algorithm, protocol, topology, and channel configuration automatically. - **NCCL Ring + Simple:** NCCL is forced to use the Ring algorithm and Simple protocol through `NCCL_ALGO=Ring` and `NCCL_PROTO=Simple`. This provides a closer algorithmic baseline, although NCCL still chooses its own topology and channel configuration. - **Mooncake PG legacy:** the shim forwards AllReduce to the existing host-worker-based GPU collective implementation. - **Mooncake PG new:** the shim forwards AllReduce to the device collective runtime and the GPU Ring AllReduce implementation introduced by this PR. All four modes use the same `nccl-tests` message-size sweep, datatype, reduction operation, warmup count, and measured iteration count.

title: Feat/support store shm copy
body:
## Description

Extend Transfer Engine `ShmTransport` to allocate **hugetlbfs-backed** shared memory for same-host DRAM copies, aligning with Mooncake Store hugepage sizes (`2MB` / `512MB` / `1GB`).
Previously `allocateSharedMemory(size)` only used POSIX `shm_open` (`/dev/shm`). This PR adds:
- `SharedMemoryOptions` and `allocateSharedMemory(size, opt)`
- When `opt.use_hugepage=true`: create a named file on a matching hugetlbfs mount, `mmap(MAP_SHARED)`, export the absolute path as `shm_name`
- Peer relocate opens filesystem paths with `open(O_RDWR)` (no `O_CREAT`); POSIX names still use `shm_open`
- `isPosixShmName` matches basename `mooncake_*` so `/dev/hugepages/mooncake_*` is recognized
- Strict failure: invalid mount / page-size mismatch / unsupported size → `nullptr`, **no tmpfs fallback**
- Default mounts when `hugetlbfs_path` is empty: `/dev/hugepages` (2MB), `/dev/hugepages-512M`, `/dev/hugepages-1G`
TE does **not** read `MC_STORE_*`; Store will pass options later via `get_hugepage_size_from_env()`.
Also includes small HIP/build fixes discovered while enabling tests:
- Copy `*.h` into the hipified test tree (e.g. `rdma_test_peers.h`)
- Build `mp_transport_test` only when `USE_CXL` is on
Related: same-host Store local-copy design / RFC #3912 / PR #3918 baseline.

title: [Bugfix][TENT] Preserve cached handles across send_probe
body:
## Description

Keep TENT segment handles valid after Python `send_probe()`.

#4081 opens a segment before probing and closes it afterward. TENT returns the
same handle when that peer is already open, so probing a peer previously used
for transfer removes the segment mapping while Python still retains the handle
in `handle_map_`. Every subsequent transfer through that cached handle fails.

Do not close the handle after probing. `openSegment()` is idempotent by peer
name, and the handle remains owned by the Transfer Engine until shutdown. This
also avoids serializing a network probe with unrelated Python operations.

Fixes a regression introduced by #4081.

## Module

- [x] Integration (`mooncake-integration`)

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix

## How Has This Been Tested?

The Python integration test now covers both handle ownership cases:

1. Probe before a peer is cached, then transfer successfully.
2. Probe after a successful transfer has cached the peer, then transfer again
   and verify the new payload.

On unmodified main, the second transfer returns `-1` and the destination keeps
the previous payload. With this change:

- the TENT integration test passed three consecutive runs;
- the same test passed through the unchanged Classic backend;
- the patch applies cleanly alongside open PR #4109;
- clang-format 20.1.8, Ruff 0.6.9, codespell 2.2.6, and `git diff --check`
  pass.

title: [Store] Add Chaos Tests and Fix Bugs
body:
## Main content of this PR
- Add some chaos tests to verify the system's failover ability, including chaos_test, chaos_rand_test, e2e_rand_test.
- Add chaosctl to do a manual and configurable chaos test.
- Fix bugs found in the tests.

## Bug list

- [Fixed] Once connected to address A, the coro_rpc_client does not support connect to a new address B. So we need to create a new coro_rpc_client for each connection. I reported this to yalantinglibs (https://github.com/alibaba/yalantinglibs/issues/995), they identified this as a bug and said they will fix it. Nonetheless, I still fix it in master_client by creating a new coro_rpc_server each time the leader address changes.
- [Fixed] YLT_REFL(PingResponse, view_version, error_code) -> YLT_REFL(PingResponse, view_version, client_status, error_code). The missing client_status in YLT_REFL will cause the serialization/deserialization ignore the client_status.
- [Fixed] ReMountSegment is not registered in RegisterRpcService. This will cause the ReMountSegment rpc  call fail. And moreover, once the ReMountSegment is called, all the subsequent rpc calls will also fail, until a new coro_rpc_client is created. 
- [Not Fix] If the protocol is tcp, and get a kv right after put it, there is a small chance the data read is not correct because the engine's write returns without waiting the write to truly complete.

## Limitations

This pr only covers a few cases that can be easily performed on a single server without extra dependencies. We need to add more tests and import chaos test tools, such as chaosmesh, in the future.

## P.S.

When there are too many building targets, "make -j" may consume too many resources and hang forever (see https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/actions/runs/15963074477/job/45018610213). Therefore, I changed it to "make -j$(nproc)" in the Dockerfile. After this change, it is less likely to hang, but may take longer to compile.

title: [Store] Fix CI bugs & Improve log output & Refactor TE Initialization
body:
This pr solves the following issues:

1. In pybind_client_test, there is a test case where the zero copy method is used, but the memory is not registered before, which will fail in rdma env.
2. In pybind_client_test, there are two test cases that will output 30k+ lines of error log, which greatly hinders reading the ci log.
3. In client.cpp, InitTransferSubmitter is put in the same function as InitTransferEngine. Previously, both the init of TE and submitter will be executed. But now the init of TE will be skipped if the TE is passed as a parameter. Now the skipping check is controlled by a private member of client, and this member is only used in this place.

title: [Docs] [6/N] Refactor Readme: Streamline README and move setup/trace details to other places
body:
## Summary

This PR streamlines the root `README.md` and moves detailed setup and trace content into the documentation site and `FAST25-release/`, so the README stays a concise entry point while full guides remain easy to find.

## Motivation

The root README had grown long, with setup details duplicated between the README and the docs. This change:
1. Makes the README easier to scan for new visitors.
2. Keeps detailed instructions in one place (the documentation site).
3. Keeps trace-related content co-located under `FAST25-release/`.

## PR Content

### README improvements
- **Overview**: Remove the redundant architecture diagram and long narrative; replace with a shorter, component-focused description (Transfer Engine, Mooncake Store, Mooncake EP & PG).
- **Getting Started** (formerly Quick Start): Keep only essential `pip install` commands; link to the docs for prerequisites, source builds, deployment, and other accelerator backends.
- **AI Assistant Skills**: Collapse the skills table and plugin install instructions into a `<details>` block to reduce visual clutter.
- **Open Source Traces**: Move trace JSON samples into `FAST25-release/README.md`; summarize traces in the README and link to `FAST25-release`, plus the KV Cache Size Calculator and Hit Rate Simulator tools.
- **Citation**: Surface the FAST'25 paper as the primary citation; move other papers into a collapsible "More" section.

### Documentation sync
- Move the "Before using Mooncake" prerequisites and expanded installation notes (CUDA 13, NPU, package variants, runtime dependencies) from the README into `docs/source/getting_started/quick-start.md`.

### New file
- Add `FAST25-release/README.md` with trace sample format and release notes (content previously inline in the root README).

## Changes

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `README.md` | ~132 lines changed (net reduction) |
| `docs/source/getting_started/quick-start.md` | +35 lines (prerequisites & install details) |
| `FAST25-release/README.md` | +17 lines (new) |

This PR streamlines the README by making the **Mooncake Store**, **SGLang Integration**, and **vLLM Integration** sections more concise and scannable, while keeping detailed information available in collapsible sections.

- Removed outdated benchmark tables and long-form community quotes from the main README flow.

**vLLM Integration**
- Updated the guide link to the [vLLM integration index](https://kvcache-ai.github.io/Mooncake/getting_started/examples/vllm-integration/index.html).
- Replaced legacy PR references, dated update notes, and the v0.2 performance table with a concise summary and collapsible details.
- Documented current capabilities: disaggregated prefill-decode serving (`MooncakeConnector`), distributed KV cache pooling (`MooncakeStoreConnector`), and vLLM-Omni stage communication.

body:
Previously, a replica could contain multiple slices. It has now been simplified so that each replica contains only one slice.
This simplification makes it easier to implement future replica management features, such as high availability and SSD offloading.

This PR mainly modifies the server-side code. The client side is more complex and affects many components, so it will be refactored gradually in future updates.

title: [Bugfix][Store] Register ShmHelper memory with SPDK for NoF zero-copy transfers
body:
## Description
fix: https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/issues/3736
Implement NOF integration with SGLang, SPDK's RDMA transport can only DMA from SPDK-registered memory. The host pool allocated via ShmHelper (memfd+mmap) was never registered, so NoF (NVMe-oF) put/get passing user buffers directly fails with "spdk_rdma_get_translation: No translation for ptr".

Register the mapping with spdk_mem_register in allocate() (USE_NOF only) and unregister before munmap in free()/cleanup(). Registration failure is non-fatal so non-NoF paths are unaffected. A dedicated ShmSegment::spdk_registered flag tracks SPDK registration, keeping the existing `registered` flag (used by DummyClient for IPC registration) untouched.

This PR fixes an issue where SGLang's MooncakeHostTensorAllocator triggers a No translation for ptr error under Mooncake NoF mode. The allocator uses MooncakeHostMemAllocator → ShmHelper (memfd+mmap), but the allocated memory was not registered with SPDK, so RDMA transport cannot access the buffer. The patch adds spdk_mem_register()/spdk_mem_unregister() to ShmHelper's allocate/free paths to enable NoF zero-copy transfers for SGLang.

title: [Store] Structure S3ClientConfig environment settings
body:
## Description

Converges Mooncake Store's existing S3 client environment settings under a private `S3ClientConfig` as part of #3809.

- Groups the eleven existing `MOONCAKE_AWS_*` variables in the common environment catalog using their semantic string, boolean, and `int64_t` types.
- Loads the values through typed `Environ::ReadOr()` and caches the resolved config once from `S3Helper::InitAPI()` for the process lifetime.
- Removes the S3-specific getters, backing fields, constructor reads, and singleton-coupled test from the global `Environ` object.
- Preserves all existing variable names, defaults, literal string behavior, shared boolean/integer parsing, invalid-value warnings, explicit endpoint/bucket/region argument precedence, credential redaction, and restart/reinitialization caching behavior.
- Keeps checksum-mode parsing beside the AWS SDK types. An unset or explicitly empty Mooncake checksum setting still leaves the AWS SDK default unchanged, preserving the compatibility correction reviewed in #2649.
- Adds focused config tests for defaults, all populated settings, explicitly empty strings, invalid typed-value fallbacks and diagnostics, environment restoration, and independent loader reads.

Open PR #1538 is a broad cross-module migration toward a larger global `Environ` singleton. This PR is the narrow Store-only owner migration required by the current #3809 rules: it removes S3-specific global state, keeps the config header private, and does not change Transfer Engine or other component settings.

Open PR #2205 proposes a new checksum compatibility switch and still targets the pre-#3587 S3 helper path. This PR does not introduce that variable or adopt its behavior; if #2205 is revived, its behavior can be layered onto `S3ClientConfig` separately.

title: [Store] Add best_fit allocation strategy for RL data-plane offload, with trace tooling
body:
## Description

**Problem.** Under RL data-plane offload, large puts fail with `NO_AVAILABLE_HANDLE` while the cluster still reports plenty of free space. The cause is the object mix, not the amount of free memory.

Captured from a real RL trainer running with `--object-store-backend mooncake` (40 steps, 1360 puts, 1.28 GiB), the distribution is strongly bimodal with an empty middle:

| Size octave | Objects | Share of objects | Share of bytes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 256 B - 512 B | 440 | 32.4% | 0.01% |
| 512 B - 1 KiB | 120 | 8.8% | 0.00% |
| 1 - 2 KiB | 40 | 2.9% | 0.00% |
| 2 - 4 KiB | 560 | 41.2% | 0.09% |
| 8 - 16 KiB | 80 | 5.9% | 0.05% |
| **8 - 16 MiB** | **120** | **8.8%** | **99.84%** |

Nothing lands between 16 KiB and 8 MiB. Each Arrow buffer of a bundle is stored as its own object, so every step writes three payload buffers of 10.5 to 12.4 MiB carrying essentially all the bytes, plus 31 metadata buffers taking ten discrete values between 256 B and 9896 B. Everything is removed explicitly one to three steps later; eviction never runs. The payload sizes are data-driven -- 120 samples take 80 distinct values spanning 18.1% -- so they cannot be aligned to allocator size classes from the client side.

Replayed at scale against a live `mooncake_master` (8 segments, 16320 puts per run, eviction disabled, `--v=1`), the first failure looks like this:

```
key=.../step25-shard2/buffer/non_tensor_batch.loss_masks.data, value_length=11672576,
segments=8, total_free=176076536, largest_free=10485760,
error=NO_AVAILABLE_HANDLE, action=put_start_alloc_failed
```

86.2% of reserved capacity in use, **168 MiB still free -- 15x the request -- but the largest contiguous hole is 10.0 MiB against an 11.1 MiB request**. Every failure in every run is in the 8 to 16 MiB class; every KB-class put succeeds.

**Mechanism.** `OffsetAllocator` reserves the rounded-up size class rather than the requested size, and `getLargestFreeRegion` reports the floor of the highest non-empty bin. At `MANTISSA_BITS = 3` the bins above 8 MiB are 8, 9, 10, ... MiB, so an 11.1 MiB request needs a 12 MiB hole. When the spreading strategies scatter payloads evenly, the KB metadata objects interleave with them and every segment converges on holes around 10 MiB while none holds 12 MiB. The observed `largest_free` at failure lands exactly on a bin floor every time -- at 8 x 147 MiB it is 10485760 (10 MiB) at M = 3, 11534336 (11 MiB) at M = 4 and 10747904 (10.25 MiB) at M = 5, each the bin step for its mantissa width -- which is that mechanism showing through.

**`MANTISSA_BITS` (#3787) is not the lever.** Raising it does buy real space: per-object rounding waste on this trace drops from 5.26% (M = 3) to 2.37% (M = 4), 1.17% (M = 5) and 0.53% (M = 6). But it does not move the point where failures disappear, because holes and rounded-up requests scale together:

| | M = 3 (current) | M = 4 | M = 5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rounding waste on this trace | 5.26% | 2.37% | 1.17% |
| Failed puts, `best_fit`, 8 x 147 MiB | 16 | 3 | 4 |
| Reserved occupancy at first failure | 88.9% | 87.5% | 89.8% |
| Smallest segment size with zero failures | 153 MiB | 156 MiB | 152 MiB |

M changes how much RAM a unit of data costs; it does not raise the occupancy ceiling. Changing it is also a persistence-format break (`m_usedBins` width and `NUM_LEAF_BINS` are serialized), so it belongs in its own RFC. Full analysis: #RFC.

**Fix.** A `best_fit` allocation strategy (`--allocation_strategy=best_fit`, off by default): each replica goes to the segment whose largest contiguous free region is the smallest one that still fits, so small objects fill partially used segments and large regions survive for large objects.

On this workload, measured against a live master, `best_fit` reaches zero failed puts with **7.3% less memory** than the spreading strategies need (153 MiB per segment versus 165 MiB), and below that threshold it fails 2 to 3 times less often at every capacity. The tracing and replay tooling used to find and verify this is included.

### Changes

| Area | File | Change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Strategy | `include/allocation_strategy.h` | `BestFitAllocationStrategy` on top of `AllocateRanked`, slack-based score |
| Strategy | `include/allocation_strategy.h` | `AllocateRanked`: `rank_all_segments` flag (default off), `stable_sort` for ties |
| Wiring | `include/types.h`, `include/master_config.h`, `src/master.cpp` | `BEST_FIT` enum, `best_fit` parsing, flag help |
| Docs | `docs/source/design/store/mooncake-store.md` | Strategy table row and usage guidance |
| Tests | `tests/allocation_strategy_test.cpp` | BestFit in the parameterized matrix, 2 new tests |
| Master logs | `src/master_service.cpp` | `VLOG(1)`: `put_start_allocated`, `put_start_alloc_failed`, `remove_object`, `evict_object` |
| Bench | `benchmarks/variable_length_allocation_bench.cpp` (new) | Variable-length workload: octave size pattern, large-allocation probe, size and event replay, strategy comparison, traffic skew. `allocation_strategy_bench.cpp` keeps the fixed-size workloads and is untouched |
| Tools | `benchmarks/extract_alloc_trace.py` (+ test) | Master log to size file, event log, histogram; keyed on `put_start_allocated` so rejected puts are not replayed as allocations |
| Tools | `mooncake-rl/examples/rl_dataproto_trace_driver.py` | Multi-rank RL load generator; `verl` DataProto and `miles` per-buffer workloads, `put`/`put_parts` paths |
| Docs | `benchmarks/README.md` | Capture and replay workflow |

### Strategy details

- Segments whose allocator cannot report a largest free region (cachelib) rank last; segments too small for the request rank after those and are only tried as a fallback.
- `rank_all_segments` exists because best-fit needs the global tightest fit, not a 6x sample. Existing callers keep the sampled behavior.
- `stable_sort` keeps the random start order among equal scores so ties stop favoring low segment indices. This also applies to `free_ratio_first`.
- Cost: one mutex-protected bin lookup per segment per allocation, linear in the segment count.

### Trade-off, measured on the captured trace

Offline replay of the recorded event log, 8 segments x 152 MiB, 16320 puts, uniform segment sizes, median of 5 runs:

| Metric | random | free_ratio_first | best_fit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Failed puts | 23 | 28 | **1** |
| Fragmentation p50 | 0.419 | 0.405 | **0.194** |
| p99 allocation latency | 1115 ns | 1430 ns | 1627 ns |
| Write skew, whole run (max/mean) | 1.06 | 1.03 | 1.06 |
| Write skew inside a 200-put window | 3.25 | 3.11 | 4.92 |
| Per-segment utilization stddev | 0.099 | 0.042 | 0.175 |

`best_fit` halves fragmentation and cuts failed puts by more than an order of magnitude, at about 45% higher p99 allocation latency and a markedly less even instantaneous write distribution. Long-run bytes per segment stay balanced, but deployments bound by per-segment bandwidth should measure before switching.

## Module

- [x] Mooncake Store (`mooncake-store`)

## Type of Change

- [x] New feature
- [ ] Refactor
- [ ] Breaking change

- [x] Other (benchmark and diagnostics tooling)

## How Has This Been Tested?

**Test commands:**
```bash
cmake -S . -B build -DBUILD_UNIT_TESTS=ON -DBUILD_BENCHMARK=ON
cmake --build build --target allocation_strategy_test \
  variable_length_allocation_bench allocation_strategy_bench mooncake_master -j
./build/mooncake-store/tests/allocation_strategy_test
python3 -m unittest mooncake-store/benchmarks/test_extract_alloc_trace.py

# 1. reproduce the workload against a real master, one lane per strategy
./build/mooncake-store/src/mooncake_master --v=1 --memory_allocator=offset \
  --allocation_strategy=best_fit --eviction_ratio=0 \
  --eviction_high_watermark_ratio=0.95 --log_dir=logs &
# 0.1494 GiB = 153 MiB per segment, the point where best_fit stops failing
python3 mooncake-rl/examples/rl_dataproto_trace_driver.py --workload miles \
  --ranks 8 --keep_steps 3 --steps 60 --segment_gib 0.1494 \
  --local_buffer_mib 128 --target_multiple 1e9

# 2. extract the trace from that master's log and replay it offline
python3 mooncake-store/benchmarks/extract_alloc_trace.py logs/mooncake_master.INFO \
  -o rl_sizes.txt --events rl_events.txt
./build/mooncake-store/benchmarks/variable_length_allocation_bench \
  --trace_events=rl_events.txt \
  --segment_capacity=152 --segment_counts=8 --replica_counts=1 \
  --strategies=random,free_ratio_first,best_fit

# 3. synthetic variable-length pattern, no trace needed
./build/mooncake-store/benchmarks/variable_length_allocation_bench \
  --segment_capacity=4096 --segment_counts=16 --replica_counts=1 \
  --prefill_pct=70 --release_prob=1.0 \
  --num_allocations=20000 --probe_mib=1280
```

**Unit tests**

| Suite | Result | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `allocation_strategy_test` | 88 / 88 | `BEST_FIT` added to the parameterized matrix |
| `BestFitPrefersTightestSegment` | pass | 3, 20, 40 MiB requests land on the tightest fitting segment |
| `LargestFreeRegionIsLargestSatisfiableRequest` | pass | `allocate(largest)` succeeds, `allocate(largest + 1)` fails |
| `test_extract_alloc_trace.py` | 6 / 6 | Keys with commas, remove and evict parsing, histogram; a put rejected with `OBJECT_ALREADY_EXISTS` yields one allocation, and an `UpsertStart` allocation with no begin record is still counted |

**End-to-end on a real `mooncake_master`**, 8 segments, 16320 puts per run, `--memory_allocator=offset`, eviction disabled, one run per cell. Failed puts:

| Segment size | Cluster | random | free_ratio_first | best_fit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 165 MiB | 1.29 GiB | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 162 MiB | 1.27 GiB | 1 | 3 | **0** |
| 159 MiB | 1.24 GiB | 11 | 5 | **0** |
| 156 MiB | 1.22 GiB | 20 | 16 | **0** |
| 153 MiB | 1.20 GiB | 16 | 13 | **0** |
| 152 MiB | 1.19 GiB | 6 | 20 | 2 |
| 147 MiB | 1.15 GiB | 47 | 39 | **16** |
| 143 MiB | 1.12 GiB | 54 | 51 | **25** |
| 139 MiB | 1.09 GiB | 55 | 55 | **32** |
| 135 MiB | 1.05 GiB | 82 | 78 | **51** |

`best_fit` reaches zero failures at 153 MiB per segment; `random` and `free_ratio_first` still fail at 162 MiB and only clear at 165 MiB. Same workload, same zero-failure guarantee, **7.3% less memory**. Below that threshold `best_fit` fails 2 to 3 times less often at every size.

These are single runs, and the two spreading lanes are noisy between 152 and 162 MiB (`random` scores 6 at 152 MiB but 16 to 20 just above it) because segment choice is randomized per run. The threshold separation is well outside that noise; the individual counts in that band are not. Zero evictions in every run, so eviction is neither masking nor causing anything.

**Offline replay of the same trace (bench)**, uniform segments, failed puts as median of 5 runs (min - max in parentheses):

| Segment size | random | free_ratio_first | best_fit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 152 MiB | 23 (21 - 45) | 28 (18 - 42) | **1 (0 - 1)** |
| 147 MiB | 107 (69 - 121) | 80 (79 - 92) | **20 (17 - 36)** |
| 143 MiB | 117 (107 - 146) | 114 (106 - 122) | **38 (30 - 42)** |

Same ordering as the live runs, and the same signature: all failures in the 8 to 16 MiB class, `largest_free` at failure pinned at 10 to 11 MiB. The replay is harsher than the live master because it packs a fixed trace into fixed segments with no client-side retry.

**Trace extraction**

Keyed on `put_start_allocated`, the extracted event log balances exactly -- 16320 puts against 16320 removes on a 16320-put run. Keying on `put_start_begin` instead yields 15984 puts against 15968 removes, because `put_start_begin` is logged before the duplicate-key and quota checks and `UpsertStart` logs no begin record at all; the 16 extra puts are requests that reserved nothing but would own a lifetime in the replay.

**Other checks**

| `allocation_strategy_bench` | byte-identical to `main`; the variable-length workload lives in its own binary |
| Driver, both workloads and both write paths, real master | 60-step runs, 16320 puts and removes each |

title: [Bugfix][Store] Poll TENT batches with event completion enabled
body:
## Description

With `USE_EVENT_DRIVEN_COMPLETION=ON` and `MC_USE_TENT=1`, Store's `wait_for_completion()` casts a native TENT batch to classic `Transport::BatchDesc`. Their layouts differ, so the completion flags and synchronization objects are invalid. The new TCP regression reports `TRANSFER_FAIL` on a normal READ before this fix.

Restrict the condition-variable branch to the classic engine and let TENT use Store's existing status-polling loop. Classic notification semantics and the 60-second deadline are preserved. The production change is one runtime guard and the corresponding fall-through/return; most changed lines are indentation. Add a real two-engine READ/WRITE test and a CTest entry that explicitly selects TENT.

Related: #4070 separately migrates Store to the native TENT API; it does not fix this completion wait. No equivalent open fix was found.

## Module

- [x] Mooncake Store (`mooncake-store`)
- [x] CI/CD

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix

## How Has This Been Tested?

Ubuntu 24.04, GCC 13.3, Release, `WITH_TE=ON WITH_STORE=ON USE_TENT=ON USE_CUDA=OFF USE_EVENT_DRIVEN_COMPLETION=ON BUILD_UNIT_TESTS=ON`.

```bash
cmake --build build --target transfer_task_test -j 1
```

title: [CI] Make the Go store integration link self-contained again
body:
## Description

Fixes the Go store integration job in the nightly (#4145). Once the job reached the Go store tests it failed at the final link, and fixing only that would have left it red two more times. Three independent breakages, all in how the job links and wires its own services:

1. `libmooncake_store.a(oss_adapter.cpp.o): undefined reference to symbol 'EVP_sha256@@OPENSSL_3.0.0'` / `libcrypto.so.3: error adding symbols: DSO missing from command line`. The OSS adapter (#3714) signs requests with OpenSSL HMAC, and static archives carry no transitive deps, so the Go link needs `-lcrypto` whenever the adapter is compiled in. Gated on the `MOONCAKE_OSS_ADAPTER_ENABLED` CMake cache marker, so builds without the adapter are untouched.
2. Undefined references to `mooncake::LocalSsdManager::{GetUsage,ConsumeRemoveAll,ReportCapacity}` from `master_service.cpp` (inside `libmooncake_store.a`). `LocalSsdManager` lives in its own static archive under `local_ssd/` that the link line never named. Now linked inside the static group when the archive exists, so cyclic references resolve and older trees without the directory keep working.
3. With both libraries present the test binary links but every case fails at client creation: the transfer engine publishes `rpc_meta` with `PUT http://127.0.0.1:8080/metadata?...` and gets connection refused. `integration_test.go` documents `mooncake_master --enable_http_metadata_server=true` as the run requirement, but the script started its master without the flag. Older green nightlies only passed because an unrelated shared master from an earlier step in the same job happened to serve 8080; that shared master no longer exists here (09-04 logs show `enable_http_metadata_server=1` on `nightly_test_cluster`, 09-15 shows no http-enabled master at all). The script's own master now serves http metadata, making the job self-contained.

`mooncake-store/go/build.sh` gets the same two link fixes for users building the Go bindings by hand.

title: [Store] Add durable awaiter to OrderedOpLogWriter
body:
## Description

Refs #3808 (W02).

Add `OrderedOpLogWriter::AwaitDurable(sequence)` as an `async_simple::Future<ErrorCode>` interface. It returns immediately without blocking a worker thread, so RPC callers can suspend with `co_await` in a later integration.

Waiters are registered under the writer mutex in a sequence-ordered table. When the durable prefix advances, only covered waiters are extracted; their promises are fulfilled outside the mutex. Duplicate waiters for the same sequence are supported. Completion is independent of durable callback execution.

An already-covered sequence returns an immediately ready `OK` future, including a prefix restored from storage or covered before terminal failure or Stop(). Otherwise, terminal failure completes remaining waiters with the exact latched W03 error before invoking the terminal callback. Stop() completes remaining waiters with `UNAVAILABLE_IN_CURRENT_STATUS`, including before the writer starts.

This change stays within the writer API and its tests. Lifecycle barriers and Put/Upsert integration remain separate roadmap work. The asynchronous interface addresses the waiting-mechanism feedback in [the review comment](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/4141#issuecomment-5693298488).

title: fix(rdma): rank link-local GID below any network-backed IPv4 in auto-GID
body:
## Problem
Fixes #2747. On routed RoCEv2 fabrics using RFC1918 addressing (e.g.
10.0.0.0/8), auto-GID selection picks a non-routable link-local GID over the
routable IPv4 GID, so cross-node QPs never reach RTR and transfers fail.

The routable IPv4 GID is flagged as an overlay by `isOverlayIPv4` (10/8,
172.16/12, 100.64/10) and lands in `kNetworkDegraded`; a network-backed
link-local GID also landed in `kNetworkDegraded`, so the stable tie-break on
ascending `gid_index` chose the link-local GID.

## Fix
Introduce a dedicated `kNetworkLinkLocal` class ranked strictly below every
network-backed IPv4 class, so a link-local GID is chosen only when no
network-backed IPv4 GID exists. Wired into the priority table, the string
helper, and `autoGidStateFromSelection` (still `GID_WITH_NETWORK`).

Only the auto-GID path (`gid_index < 0`) is affected; explicit-index
deployments are unchanged.

## Testing
- Unit: existing `rdma_gid_probe_test.cpp` cases still pass; added an ionic
  regression (network-backed link-local vs network-backed overlay-IPv4 → IPv4
  wins) plus a reversed-order variant.
- HW `transfer_engine_bench`, auto-GID (no explicit index), two fabrics:
  - routed RoCEv2 (10.102.x.x): **before** → selects link-local GID[0], transfer
    fails at RTR; **after** → selects routable GID[1] (10.102.x.x), completes
    (~48 GB/s).
  - flat-L2 (exposes a normal routable IPv4 GID): selection unchanged, no
    regression (~41 GB/s before and after).

title: [Bugfix] Honor MC_FORCE_HCA before automatic GPU P2P fallback
body:
## Description

Honor `MC_FORCE_HCA` before the automatic no-HCA GPU P2P fallback in the classic Transfer Engine.

When cross-node GPU P2P is compiled and topology discovery returns zero HCAs, `force_gpu_p2p || no_hca` currently selects NVLink/MUSA before reaching the RDMA branch, even with `MC_FORCE_HCA=1`. This bypasses the fail-fast intent introduced in #1259.

Change the automatic fallback to `no_hca && !force_hca`. With no HCA and no explicit GPU transport override, forcing HCA now reaches RDMA initialization, where an unavailable RNIC is reported as an error. Explicit `MC_FORCE_MNNVL` / `MC_FORCE_MUSA` and `MC_INTRANODE_NVLINK` precedence is unchanged; this PR does not redefine conflicting force flags.

Source-level reproduction: classic auto-discovery, GPU P2P compiled, zero HCAs, `MC_FORCE_HCA=1`, and `MC_FORCE_TCP`, `MC_FORCE_MNNVL`, `MC_FORCE_MUSA`, `MC_INTRANODE_NVLINK` unset. No hardware reproduction is claimed.

## Description

Fixes an intermittent unit-test race in `RuntimeQueueDispatch.ProgressWorkerRefillsWindowFromTransportNotify` (same class as #3459 / #3460).

title: [Store] Freeze restored snapshot test eviction worker
body:
## Description

The restored MasterService starts an eviction worker before the snapshot test can freeze it. When `EvictObject` leaves memory above the watermark with expired leases, that worker changes replica metadata before the second snapshot and state comparison. In the failing PR #4142 CI run, the restored worker evicted 1042 replicas and the metadata snapshot shrank from 737277 to 723791 bytes.

Set the restored instance's memory eviction watermark to 1.0 before construction, then stop and join its eviction worker before snapshot comparison, matching the original instance's existing freeze. This prevents watermark eviction during startup as well as subsequent worker mutations during comparison. Uses the upstream `MasterServiceTestPeer` accessors; only the shared snapshot test fixture changes.

title: [Bugfix] Register SSD replicas per owner after client restart
body:
## Description

Fix a bug where a **restarted client's SSD (local-disk) replica registration could be silently dropped**, leaving offloaded objects with no disk replica once the old owner is swept.              
                                                                                                                                                                                                     
  When a client crashes and restarts, it comes back with a **new UUID** but the same on-disk files and RPC endpoint. On restart it rescans its SSD objects and re-reports them to the master (via    
  `NotifyOffloadSuccess`, or `AddReplicaForRetainedClient` on the retained-client path). At that moment the **old owner's disk replicas may still be registered**, because owner cleanup happens     
  through the heartbeat/liveness lifecycle rather than immediately.                                                                                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                     
  Both registration paths deduplicated existing disk replicas by **storage medium** (`Replica::fn_is_local_disk_replica`) — i.e. "does this object already have *any* local-disk replica?". So while 
  the old owner's replica was still present, the new owner's report was treated as already-existing and effectively discarded. Once the old owner was later swept, the object was left with **no disk
  replica at all**, even though the new client had already reported it — forcing another rescan (or a memory-replica fallback) to recover.

### Fix                                                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                     
  Deduplicate by **owner (`client_id`)** instead of by medium, in both paths (`master_service.cpp`):                                                                                                 
  - `AddReplicaForRetainedClient`                                                                                                                                                                    
  - `NotifyOffloadSuccess`                                                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                     
  A disk replica is now treated as "already registered" only when the **same owner** already has one:                                                                                                
  - Repeated rescan batches from the **same owner** stay idempotent (the descriptor's endpoint/size is refreshed in place).                                                                          
  - Replicas from **different owners coexist** until the old owner is removed by its normal lifecycle cleanup.                                                                                       
  - The restarted owner's registration is no longer lost.                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                     
  A key or RPC endpoint cannot prove that two owners share a disk, so owner identity (`client_id`) is the only safe dedup key.

title: [Store] Add immutable bucket allocator for DFS replicas
body:
## Description

This PR implements the DFS immutable Bucket allocator proposed in:

- RFC: https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/issues/3641

It introduces a pluggable `GlobalAllocatorInterface` for DFS replica allocation while preserving the existing `DfsGlobalAllocator` as the default `shard` implementation.

A new `ImmutableBucketAllocator` can be selected with:

```bash
MOONCAKE_DFS_ALLOCATOR_TYPE=bucket
```

The Bucket allocator stores objects as append-only immutable entries. Bucket files are created on demand, sealed metadata is persisted for standalone restart recovery, and physical space is reclaimed by evicting complete Buckets in LRU order.

The existing `DistributedFSDescriptor` wire format is unchanged. In Bucket mode, the existing `shard_idx` field carries the Bucket ID, preserving descriptor serialization compatibility.

### Main changes

#### Pluggable DFS allocator

- Extract `GlobalAllocatorInterface` as the Master-facing DFS allocation contract.
- Adapt the existing fixed-shard `DfsGlobalAllocator` to implement the interface.
- Keep `shard` as the default allocator with its existing behavior.
- Add `ImmutableBucketAllocator` following the terminology used by RFC #3641.

#### Immutable Bucket allocation

- Create Bucket files dynamically as capacity is needed.
- Store each key and value as one aligned, append-only entry.
- Never overwrite or reuse an entry in place.
- Allow a batch allocation to be packed across multiple Buckets.
- Roll back incomplete batch reservations without publishing invalid descriptors.
- Reclaim Bucket space when allocation is exhausted.

#### Metadata and recovery

- Persist one metadata snapshot for each sealed Bucket.
- Restore committed entries from sealed Bucket metadata after a standalone Master restart.
- Exclude pending and tombstoned entries from recovery.
- Remove the former append-only metadata log and rename-based publication flow.
- Conservatively handle corrupt metadata, orphan files, interrupted eviction, and incompatible configuration.

The active Bucket is intentionally not persisted. After an abrupt restart, it is discarded, while committed entries in sealed Buckets are recovered.

#### Bucket-level LRU eviction

- Track access at Bucket granularity.
- Exclude the active Bucket and Buckets containing processing entries from eviction.
- Validate leases and pin state before removing any replica.
- Remove all eligible replicas from Master metadata before deleting Bucket files.
- Abort the entire Bucket eviction if any entry is still protected.
- Trigger reclamation both at configured watermarks and on allocation exhaustion.

#### Batch I/O and direct reads

- Add packed Bucket `BatchWrite`.
- Group `BatchRead` requests by Bucket and process independent Buckets in parallel.
- Optionally merge adjacent entries into bounded reads.
- Add POSIX `O_DIRECT` reads with aligned pooled staging buffers.
- Fall back to buffered POSIX reads when the filesystem rejects `O_DIRECT`.
- Treat short reads, zero progress, EOF before the requested range, and partial failures as errors.
- Preserve the existing HF3FS adapter-specific read path.

#### Master and Client integration

- Integrate allocator selection into Master and Client initialization.
- Add Bucket batch reservation and asynchronous write completion.
- Copy or stage caller-owned buffers before asynchronous writes so they can be safely reused.
- Keep DFS replicas in `PROCESSING` until the write succeeds and the Master commits them.
- Revoke failed writes so incomplete data is never published as readable.
- Drain queued writes during Client shutdown.

#### Configuration and administration

The following settings are introduced or documented:

```text
MOONCAKE_DFS_ALLOCATOR_TYPE=shard|bucket
MOONCAKE_DFS_BUCKET_CAPACITY
MOONCAKE_DFS_MAX_BUCKET_COUNT
MOONCAKE_DFS_BATCH_READ_THREADS
MOONCAKE_DFS_BATCH_READ_MERGE_ENABLED
MOONCAKE_DFS_DIRECT_READ_ENABLED
```

The active Bucket limit can be changed online through:

```http
PUT /api/v1/dfs/max_bucket_count
Content-Type: application/json

{"max_bucket_count": 512}
```

The endpoint validates the JSON type and range. Values must be in `[1, INT32_MAX]`, and the endpoint returns a conflict response when the active allocator is not the Bucket allocator.

Lowering the limit below the current Bucket count does not delete existing Buckets immediately. It prevents additional Bucket creation until the count falls below the configured limit.

### Compatibility

- `shard` remains the default allocator.
- Existing shard allocation semantics are preserved.
- `DistributedFSDescriptor` serialization is unchanged.
- This PR builds on the DFS replica support already present in the community tree; it does not reintroduce the original DFS POSIX implementation.
- DFS prefetch, session object cache, monitoring metrics, persistent asynchronous H2D streams, Transfer Engine changes, and hardware-specific adaptations are intentionally out of scope.

### Known limitations

- Recovery covers sealed Buckets only; the active Bucket is discarded after an abrupt restart.
- Bucket recovery is for a standalone Master reopening the same DFS root.
- DFS remains incompatible with Master snapshot restore, oplog recovery, standby restore, and HA failover.
- Asynchronous Bucket writes do not currently provide a persistent retry queue, request cancellation, DFS-specific timeout, or `fsync` durability guarantee.
- A complete object must fit within one Bucket.

title: [Store] Extract per-object metadata and runtime state headers from MasterService
body:
## Description

Moves the per-object metadata envelope and the per-key runtime state records out of `MasterService` into their own headers:

| New header | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `mooncake-store/include/object_metadata.h` | `ResolvedSoftPinRequest`, `ObjectMetadata` (with its nested `SoftPinEvaluation`, `PendingSoftPinAction`, `DynamicReplicaRecord`) |
| `mooncake-store/include/object_runtime_state.h` | `DynamicReplicaPending`, `ReplicationTask`, `OffloadingTask`, `PromotionQueueResult`, `PromotionCandidateReason`, `PromotionCandidate`, `PromotionTask` |

These are per-object types, but they are declared inside the service that owns the metadata shard tables. Anything that needs one of them pulls in the whole service header and the quota/HA machinery behind it, and the object's own state cannot be moved out of the shard tables while its declarations live there. RFC #3670 moves metadata ownership from shards to tenants and narrows the mutation boundary from one shard lock to one object lock; separating the types is the step that makes that move expressible.

`object_runtime_state.h` names the records after what they are rather than after their consumer.

No behavior change. The declarations are unchanged apart from the dedent and the `clang-format` re-wrap that follow from leaving their old nesting, and the `MasterService::` qualification dropped where these types are named.

Changes on top of the move:

- `ResolvedSoftPinRequest::ttl_ms` and `PendingSoftPinAction::ttl_ms` become `std::chrono::milliseconds ttl`, and `ComputeSoftPinDeadline` takes that duration rather than a raw `uint64_t`. The rep-range guard it carried is unreachable once the parameter is a duration, so it is gone; the config-facing `uint64_t` values are converted at the boundary in `ResolveSoftPinRequest`.
- `PendingSoftPinAction::eligible_replica_ids` is a `std::unordered_set<ReplicaID>`. The only question asked of it is membership, once per replica on two paths, so the set states that directly and neither query scans.
- The `object_metadata.h` module comment now says what actually guards the envelope: it has no ownership lock, and the internal spin lock it does carry covers only `lease_` and `soft_pin_timeout`.
