title: [Store] Decouple NoF data path from SPDK behind neutral interfaces
body:
## Description Related RFC #3397 Decouple Mooncake Store's NoF (NVMe-oF) data path from SPDK behind two neutral interfaces, and fix #3131 along the way. **Before**: all NoF traffic funneled into the `SpdkWrapper` Meyers singleton (env init + qpair cache + I/O + DMA alloc + probe in one class). SPDK types leaked through its header, and 38 SPDK/DPDK static libs propagated as PUBLIC link requirements to client/master/bench. **After**: - Two role interfaces under `include/nof/`: `NVMeoFInitiator` (byte-oriented I/O behind an opaque `NofSegmentHandle`) and `DmaBufferAllocator`. - SPDK implementations live in the new `mooncake_nof_spdk` static lib (pimpl — SPDK types confined to one `.cpp`, SPDK/DPDK libs linked `PRIVATE`). - Instances come from `CreateNofRuntime()` — the only `#ifdef USE_NOF` site naming SPDK types — and are injected via `shared_ptr`. The SPDK env initializes lazily on first use and is owned by a refcounted guard. - `register_buffer` now also registers user buffers with the SPDK RDMA translation table (process-global registry, per-2MB-page refcount, TE rollback on failure) — **fixes #3131**. Requires SPDK ≥ 22.05; a CMake probe warns on older versions. No wire-protocol / RPC / Python ABI changes. Non-NoF builds keep the exact original behavior (allocator injected as `nullptr` → original protocol → VRAM → `aligned_alloc` order). ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph B["Before — everything funnels into one singleton"] TS1["TransferSubmitter / worker pool"] -->|GetInstance ×6| SW["SpdkWrapper (Meyers singleton):
env init · qpair cache · IO · DMA alloc · probe"] RC1["RealClient::setup"] -->|eager InitializeEnv| SW CB1["ClientBufferAllocator / utils"] -->|use_spdk_dma flag| SW MS1["Master heartbeat probe"] --> SW SW -.->|SPDK types in header,
38 SPDK/DPDK libs PUBLIC| L1["leaks into client / master / bench"] end subgraph A["After — interface split + dependency injection"] RC2["RealClient::setup"] -->|CreateNofRuntime:
only USE_NOF ifdef| F["NofRuntime factory"] F --> NI["NVMeoFInitiator «interface»"] F --> DA["DmaBufferAllocator «interface»"] NI -.pimpl.- SI["SpdkInitiator::Impl — SPDK confined
to one .cpp, libs PRIVATE"] DA -.-> SA["SpdkDmaAllocator /
SystemDmaAllocator"] TS2["TransferSubmitter / NofWorkerPool"] -->|injected shared_ptr| NI CB2["ClientBufferAllocator"] -->|injected; nullptr when NoF absent| DA MS2["Master heartbeat probe"] --> NI end ``` Lifetime and registration fixes riding along: ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph LIB["mooncake_nof_spdk — the only SPDK-aware code"] G["SpdkEnvGuard:
lazy, refcounted,
init/fini serialized"] R["NofPageRegistry: process-global,
per-2MB-page refcount,
-EBUSY → external page"] Q["ctrlr/ns/qpair cache:
same endpoint → same qpair,
connect outside mutex"] G --- R G --- Q end RB["RealClient::register_buffer"] -->|1. TE register OK| R R -->|2. RegisterMemory fail → roll back TE| RB W["NofWorkerPool"] -->|SubmitIO bytes /
PollCompletion| Q ``` Also fixed in passing: `io_count` was a raw pointer to a worker-thread stack variable (now `shared_ptr>`); a failed `SubmitIO` leaked its sub-task pool slot (now returned); the probe context recycle race; `OpenSegment` blocked a global mutex during NVMe-oF connect. ### Upgrade notes for existing NoF users No breaking configuration or API changes: build flags (`-DUSE_NOF=ON`), existing env vars (`MC_NOF_*`, `MC_NVME_*`, `MC_STORE_NUMA_SOCKET_ID`), transport strings, and the Python ABI are all unchanged. One optional env var is added. Behavioral differences to be aware of: - **New optional `MC_NOF_BACKEND`** (`spdk` by default, case-insensitive): selects the NoF backend pair. Set it to `none` to disable NoF at runtime in a `USE_NOF` build — one binary can be deployed on nodes without a working SPDK/hugepage environment. Unrecognized values fall back to `spdk` with a warning. Note the master process honors it too (with `none`, heartbeat probes fail and NoF segments are unmounted after the threshold). - **SPDK env init is now lazy.** `RealClient::setup` used to initialize the SPDK env eagerly and fail when hugepages were missing — even for clients that never touch NoF. Setup now always succeeds; a broken SPDK env surfaces as an error on the *first NoF operation* instead. Keep configuring hugepages before NoF traffic, as the deployment guide says. - **`register_buffer` registers with SPDK automatically** — no extra call or parameter. The buffer must be block-size aligned (existing hard gate) and must live in hugepage-backed memory (2MB hugetlb). The pointer itself need not be 2MB-aligned — a non-aligned buffer is registered by its containing 2MB pages (logging a `RegisterMemory` warning); but 4KB-backed malloc memory fails inside SPDK's `spdk_mem_register` with paddr-misalignment `-EINVAL`. - **The #3131 fix needs SPDK ≥ 22.05** (`spdk_mem_register`). Older SPDK still builds (with a CMake warning) and behaves exactly as before — i.e. NoF-over-RDMA writes from unregistered user buffers keep failing with "No translation". ### Use cases **1. Pure-NoF write to the SSD pool** (the #3131 scenario — now works over RDMA): ```python from mooncake.store import MooncakeDistributedStore, ReplicateConfig store = MooncakeDistributedStore() store.setup(...) # protocol="rdma", local_buffer_size > 0 — see deployment guide # Now also registered with SPDK's RDMA translation table (automatic): store.register_buffer(buf_ptr, buf_size) config = ReplicateConfig() config.replica_num = 0 # no DRAM replica config.nof_replica_num = 1 # NoF SSD replica only store.batch_put_from(keys, buffer_ptrs, sizes, config) ``` Requirements: `USE_NOF=ON` build against SPDK ≥ 22.05; the buffer must be block-size aligned (existing hard gate) and must be hugepage-backed (2MB hugetlb). The pointer itself need not be 2MB-aligned — `register_buffer` normalizes it to its containing 2MB pages, logging a `RegisterMemory` warning — but 4KB-backed malloc memory fails inside SPDK's `spdk_mem_register` with paddr-misalignment `-EINVAL`. **2. One binary, deployed everywhere** — nodes without hugepages/SPDK no longer need a separate build: ```bash export MC_NOF_BACKEND=none # NoF disabled at runtime; the rest works as usual ``` **3. Standard SSD-pool deployment** (master + store service + `spdk_tgt_create` + `mooncake_ssd_register`): unchanged — see `docs/source/deployment/ssd/nvmf-ssd-deployment-guide.md`. **4. Custom/test initiator injection** (C++): any `NVMeoFInitiator` implementation can be injected — directly into `NofWorkerPool`, or via the new tail parameter of `Client::Create(...)`. The alignment gate, QoS, and worker loop run unchanged against it; `nvmeof_initiator_test` exercises the full pool this way without SPDK. ### What if the backend is not SPDK later? That swap is the point of the split. A non-SPDK backend implements `NVMeoFInitiator` (and optionally `DmaBufferAllocator`) and plugs into `CreateNofRuntime()` — the single place that names SPDK types. Callers (`NofWorkerPool`, `RealClient`, master probe) do not change. Backend differences are advertised through `NofCapabilities`: e.g. a backend without an RDMA translation table returns `requires_memory_registration = false` and its `RegisterMemory` is a no-op `OK`. The new test suite already runs the worker pool against a non-SPDK `MockInitiator`, proving the seam. Backend selection exists from day one as one env var choosing a matched Initiator+Allocator pair: `MC_NOF_BACKEND=spdk` (default) or `none` (runtime-disable NoF in a `USE_NOF` build). Adding a backend is one enum value + one factory branch + one env value — deliberately no plugin machinery before a second backend exists. ## Module - [x] Mooncake Store (`mooncake-store`) - [x] Docs ## Type of Change - [x] Bug fix (#3131) - [x] Refactor ## How Has This Been Tested? **Test commands:** ```bash cmake --build build -j # USE_NOF=OFF: 0 errors, 0 warnings ./build/mooncake-store/tests/nvmeof_initiator_test # new mock-initiator suite ./build/mooncake-store/tests/transfer_task_test ./build/mooncake-store/tests/client_buffer_test ``` **Test results:** - [x] Unit tests pass (nvmeof_initiator_test 4/4, transfer_task_test 11/11, client_buffer_test 16/16) - [ ] Integration tests pass (if applicable) - [x] Manual testing done (describe below) ⚠️ `USE_NOF=ON` build and runtime NoF validation still pending — requires a machine with SPDK + an NVMe-oF target. Will run before marking ready (incl. non-2MB-aligned hugepage-slice registration and NoF-over-RDMA pure-NoF write from #3131's repro). ## Checklist - [x] I have performed a self-review of my own code - [x] I have formatted my code using `./scripts/code_format.sh` - [x] I have run pre-commit on the files changed in this PR and all hooks pass *(local pre-commit 2.17 too old for the repo config; ran the equivalent hooks manually: clang-format via `code_format.sh --staged`, whitespace/EOF checks)* - [x] I have updated the documentation (if applicable) - [x] I have added tests to prove my changes are effective - [ ] For changes >500 LOC: I have filed an RFC issue *(design doc exists; will file/link the RFC issue before undrafting)*

title: [Store] Add HealthCheck RPC and /readyz probe for master RPC readiness
body:
## Description

### Background

A production incident (#3940) observed a window where the master's RPC plane became fully unresponsive: when a store client's lease expired, the master's `ClientMonitorThreadFunc` synchronously invoked `ClearInvalidHandles` → `ClearStaleHandles` to sweep all keys/replicas owned by that client. During the sweep, `ClearStaleHandles` held the metadata shard write lock, while data-plane RPCs such as `PutStart` / `Get` need the same shard's read lock — blocking all data-plane RPCs and driving inference-engine get/put throughput to zero for minutes.

In a K8s deployment, operators want a readinessProbe to automatically remove a blocked master from Service endpoints and shift traffic to a healthy standby, plus Prometheus alerts to surface the condition. But every existing liveness/readiness mechanism fails against this "process alive, port listening, RPCs fully blocked" scenario:

| Probe method | Behavior during the block | Detects? |
|---|---|---|
| `tcpSocket 50051` | socket is up, TCP handshake succeeds | No (false green) |
| `httpGet /health` (admin port 9003) | admin thread takes no shard lock, always 200 | No (false green) |
| `Ping` RPC | takes only `client_mutex_` shared lock, not a shard lock, returns normally | No (false green) |
| `ServiceReady` RPC | returns the version string, takes no lock | No (false green) |

Root cause: `Ping` takes only the `client_mutex_` shared lock (`MasterService::Ping`), `ServiceReady` takes no lock, and `ClearInvalidHandles` releases `client_mutex_` before calling `ClearStaleHandles` — none of these contend with the shard write lock, so none can be blocked by the sweep. Reliably detecting this condition requires a probe RPC that **contends for the shard read lock**.

### Design

Add a new public RPC `HealthCheck` that walks all metadata shards (`kNumShards = 1024`) probing read-lock availability, paired with an in-process self-probe thread, Prometheus metrics, and a `/readyz` endpoint. **No existing RPC interface is modified** — `Ping` / `ServiceReady` / `ExistKey` keep their signatures and behavior; `HealthCheck` is purely additive.

#### 1. New RPC `HealthCheck`

Signature (`WrappedMasterService` / `MasterService`, no parameters):

```cpp
struct HealthCheckResponse {
    bool ok;               // true if all shards acquired the read lock within budget
    uint64_t shards_checked;
    uint64_t shards_blocked;
};
tl::expected<HealthCheckResponse, ErrorCode> HealthCheck();
```

Algorithm:

- Walk all 1024 shards serially, calling `try_lock_shared()` (non-blocking) on each shard's `mutex`.
- Acquire-and-release: hold at most one read lock at a time, so writers on other shards are not blocked — interference is negligible. Proceed to the next shard immediately.
- When a shard's write lock is held by a long-running sweep, `try_lock_shared` fails → retry with ~10ms backoff until success or **global budget exhaustion**.
- Global budget `kShardLockBudget` (default 2s, below the probe timeout of 3s).
- All shards acquired within budget → `ok=true, shards_checked=1024`; any shard exceeds budget → return `ok=false, shards_blocked=<first blocked shard index>`.
- Read-only, no OpLog, no side effects; works in both HA and non-HA modes. Under normal load 1024 non-contended `try_lock` calls complete in < 5ms; only a shard held for seconds triggers failure.

> Rationale for walking all 1024 shards rather than a single key: a single key hits only one shard (`key % kNumShards`), so the chance of landing on the shard currently being swept is ~1/1024. With a 5s probe interval over a 7-minute window that is under 10% — it would mostly miss. `HealthCheck` covers all shards in one pass for a reliable verdict.

Register with one line in `RegisterRpcService`:

```cpp
server.register_handler<&mooncake::WrappedMasterService::HealthCheck>(
    &wrapped_master_service);
```

#### 2. Self-probe thread (RPC probe)

Add an independent `rpc_probe_thread_` to `MasterAdminServer` (which already runs a 10s metrics-reporting thread):

- Period `rpc_probe_interval_seconds` (default 5s); runs only when `service_available_` is true.
- Calls `HealthCheck` against `rpc_address:<rpc_port>` with timeout `rpc_probe_timeout_seconds` (default 3s). The probe target uses the RPC server's actual bind address: `0.0.0.0`/`::` is normalized to `127.0.0.1`; otherwise `rpc_address` is used directly (when bound to a specific IP, `127.0.0.1` is unreachable).
- Uses TCP (the TCP listener stays on `rpc_port` even when the RPC server enables RDMA).
- Results cached under atomic guards: `rpc_probe_ok_`, `rpc_probe_latency_ms_`.
- **HA guard**: on a standby, `service_available_=false` (RPC server not started) → the probe thread skips → `/readyz` returns 503 directly, which is correct.

#### 3. Prometheus metrics + `/readyz`

New metrics in `MasterMetricManager`:

| Metric | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `mooncake_master_rpc_responsive` | gauge | 1 = probe completed within timeout, 0 = timed out |
| `mooncake_master_rpc_probe_latency_ms` | gauge | Latency of the most recent probe |
| `mooncake_master_rpc_probe_failures_total` | counter | Cumulative failed probes |

New `GET /readyz` on `MasterAdminServer`: `service_available_ && rpc_probe_ok_` → HTTP 200; otherwise HTTP 503. It only reads cached state — the admin thread takes no shard lock, so it returns instantly. The existing `GET /health` is unchanged (process liveness, always 200).

#### 4. Configuration (new gflags, all tunable)

```
--enable_rpc_health_probe    (default true; when false, no probe thread starts and /readyz degrades to /health semantics)
--rpc_probe_interval_seconds (default 5)
--rpc_probe_timeout_seconds  (default 3)
```

### Design Rationale

- **Add rather than modify existing interfaces**: `Ping` / `ServiceReady` have callers relying on their current semantics (no shard lock, always fast). Changing their lock behavior would break client contracts. `HealthCheck` has a clear purpose ("all-shard read-lock liveness") and is probe-only — purely additive, zero regression risk.
- **RPC rather than in-process call**: calling `service_->HealthCheck()` in-process saves the RPC client but bypasses the dispatch path, so it cannot detect "RPC worker pool exhausted by blocked RPCs" — a secondary symptom. Going over RPC exercises the full accept → dispatch → handler path, giving the most faithful readiness verdict — under pool exhaustion `HealthCheck` itself is delayed and judged unavailable, which is the desired behavior.
- **All shards rather than a single key**: `kNumShards = 1024`; a single-key probe hits ~1/1024, unable to reliably catch a specific shard's long-held write lock.
- **Readiness vs liveness separation**: `/readyz` (drives readinessProbe; failure only removes traffic, no restart) answers "can it serve"; `/health` (drives livenessProbe; failure restarts) answers "is the process alive". Do not use "RPC timeout" to trigger liveness restarts — it would interrupt a legitimate sweep, re-scan after restart, and likely recur.

### Known Limitations

- `HealthCheck` has no Python binding. The self-probe is an in-process C++ behavior needing no Python; a Python client wrapper for the public `HealthCheck` RPC is left as follow-up.
- This PR only addresses "detect / drain traffic"; it does not fix the root cause. The root-cause fix (sweep duration under the shard write lock in `ClearStaleHandles`) is Approach A in #3940 and should proceed separately.
- The probe thread occupies one admin thread; `/readyz` itself only reads cached state and takes no shard lock, so it never delays under blocking.

### Testing

**New unit tests:**

- `HealthCheckReturnsOkWhenNoLockHeld`: with no shard write lock held, `HealthCheck` returns `ok=true, shards_checked=1024, shards_blocked=0`, completing in milliseconds.
- `HealthCheckDetectsShardWriteLockHeld`: the test fixture takes a write lock on shard 0 and holds it past the budget (2s); `HealthCheck` returns `ok=false` with `shards_blocked=0` (the first blocked shard); after releasing the lock, `HealthCheck` recovers to `ok=true, shards_checked=1024`.

> An integration test for the `/readyz` endpoint (`ReadyzReflectsProbeResult`) requires standing up a coro_rpc server + admin server + probe thread simultaneously, which is too heavy for the `master_service_test` unit tests; left as follow-up (can live in `master_admin_service` integration tests or e2e coverage). The `/readyz` logic is simple (read `service_available_ && rpc_probe_ok_` cache → 200/503) and is indirectly covered by the two `HealthCheck` tests.

title: [Misc] Apply ruff-format to Python sources and clear ruff check debt
body:
## Description

Clears the repository-wide Python formatting and lint debt so the existing **strict, whole-file** gates can stay in place.

On `main` (`430c6e74`):

- **69 of 265** non-vendored Python files were not `ruff format`-formatted.
- `ruff check` reported **40** pre-existing findings across 18 files, 31 of them in the files above.

Both the `python-lint` CI step and the `ruff-format` pre-commit hook operate on whole files, so any PR touching one of those files failed on hunks it never wrote (`mooncake-wheel/mooncake/structured_object_store.py` alone carries 96 pre-existing format hunks), while `pre-commit run --files <file>` rewrote hundreds of unrelated lines. That is the situation #3567 is working around with a bespoke changed-lines checker; once this lands, the workaround is unnecessary and #3567 can go back to `ruff format --check`.

This PR deliberately **does not change CI policy and does not relax any check** — local pre-commit and CI keep enforcing whole files, and they now agree.

### Commits

1. `46749bef` — `[Misc] Apply ruff-format to Python sources` (69 files, +3431/−2139)

   Pure `ruff format` 0.6.9 output, i.e. the version pinned in `pyproject.toml`, `.pre-commit-config.yaml` and CI. The only content-level changes are Ruff's docstring normalizations (trailing whitespace inside docstrings, docstring indentation); string constants, comments and `ruff check` results are otherwise identical. This commit is listed in `.git-blame-ignore-revs`.

2. `4d88638c` — `[Misc] Ignore the ruff-format commit in git blame`

   Adds `.git-blame-ignore-revs` plus a short note in `CONTRIBUTING.md` explaining how to enable it locally.

3. `1826d3ed` — `[Misc] Clear pre-existing ruff check findings` (18 files, +41/−45)

   Required, because 31 of the 40 findings were in files touched by commit 1, so the lint step would otherwise still fail for this PR itself. 23 are `ruff check --fix` autofixes; the rest were reviewed by hand (details in the commit message and below):

   - `import mooncake.pg` in `mooncake-ep/benchmarks/legacy_buffer_perf.py` is kept with `# noqa: F401`: the import registers the process-group backend, so removing it would change behavior. A pre-existing precedent exists in `mooncake-ep/benchmarks/ep_benchmark/run_ep_benchmark.py`.
   - The availability probes in `mooncake-wheel/tests/test_spdk_tgt_create.py` and `scripts/test_engram_store.py` (import after `sys.path` setup) keep their imports with `# noqa`.
   - Removed the shadowed duplicate `TestClass.serialize_into`; the surviving no-argument definition is the one Python already bound, so behavior is unchanged.
   - Moved module-level imports in `mooncake-rl/examples/rl_samples.py` and `mooncake-wheel/tests/test_put_get_tensor.py` into the import block, placed the `scripts/test_drain_http_api.py` docstring above `from __future__ import annotations`, narrowed a bare `except` to `(TypeError, ValueError)`, and renamed an ambiguous `l` loop variable.

title: [Store] Stabilize HA under OpLog pressure
body:
Related to #3808

## Why

Sustained OpLog pressure exposed two independent HA failures. OpLog queue
saturation could request repeated eviction passes. The leader also shared one
etcd client with Store traffic, so resetting that client closed the leadership
keep-alive stream.

## What

- Stop retrying a full eviction pass after OpLog queue saturation.
- Give each leadership lease keep-alive its own etcd client.
- Keep active lease streams alive when the general Store etcd client resets.
- Update HA tests to require reset isolation.

## How

Batch eviction consumes one pending allocation-pressure request. It restores
that request only when the pass made no progress, ended without an OpLog error,
and still found evictable objects.

The Go etcd wrapper creates one client for each blocking lease keep-alive.
General Store reset still replaces the Store client and cancels its watches and
maintenance sessions. It does not cancel leadership keep-alive. Explicit lease
cancel and coordinator shutdown remain the normal stop paths.

## Test

- The reset-isolation regression failed before the fix because Store client
  reset closed the keep-alive channel.
- The two focused leadership tests passed 20 consecutive runs.
- The full etcd HA test binary passed all 14 tests.
- Go tests with the race detector passed.
- The queue-saturation regression passed 20 consecutive runs.
- Eight related eviction tests passed.
- `MasterServiceTest.PutStartExpiringTest` passed.
- One full HA test run passed all 93 tests.
- Pre-commit and `git diff --check` passed.

A sustained downstream deployment test confirmed that the target cache
collapse did not recur. Active-master deletion promoted the standby, and the
replacement standby caught up. Environment, image, traffic, hardware, and
performance details are intentionally omitted.

The Ubuntu 22.04 wheel job failed in
`test_ssd_offload_in_evict.py::test_concurrent_stress`. The unchanged base
commit failed in the same job and test. All other CI jobs passed.

This PR does not address the separate durable mutation barrier in #3808. It
must not be treated as the complete production-readiness gate for that roadmap.

## Ablation

- Existing shared-client behavior failed because reset closed the lease stream.
- A dedicated client alone failed because reset still canceled the lease
  context.
- Removing reset cancellation alone failed because closing the shared client
  still closed the stream.
- The combined lease design passed the reset and leadership checks.
- Always clearing the eviction request stopped the retry, but it failed
  `PutStartExpiringTest`. Conditional restore passed that test and the
  queue-saturation test.

title: [CI/Build] Fix the USE_NOF build and NoF e2e on Ubuntu
body:
Fixes #4072.

## Description

A `USE_NOF` build cannot be produced or exercised out of the box by following the documented build path. On a clean Ubuntu 22.04 host the documented steps fail at four points; this PR fixes all of them:

| # | Failure | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | SPDK `./configure --with-rdma` aborts: `--with-rdma requires libverbs and librdmacm` | invoke SPDK's `./scripts/pkgdep.sh --rdma` from the optional `INSTALL_SPDK` branch; it installs `librdmacm-dev` without changing common dependencies |
| 2 | Linking fails: `cannot find -lisal`, `cannot find -lelf` | install `libelf-dev` in the Ubuntu/Debian `INSTALL_SPDK` branch; take isa-l from SPDK's build tree via `-L${SPDK_ISA_L_LIB_DIR}` (the same library SPDK itself links), instead of installing a second `libisal.a` into `/usr/local/lib` |
| 3 | `make mooncake_master` fails: undefined `SpdkWrapper::GetInstance()` / `ProbeNofSegment()` / `SpdkControllerConfig::FromEnvironment()` | add the wrapper sources, the controller options parser, the SPDK/DPDK include directories and `${SPDK_STATIC_LIBS}` to the reduced master library |
| 4 | NoF e2e aborts with `ImportError: libasio.so: cannot open shared object file` | export `$BUILD_DIR/mooncake-common` on `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` in the e2e script |


## Module

- [x] Mooncake Store (`mooncake-store`)
- [x] CI/CD

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix

## How Has This Been Tested?

**Reproduction environment:** Ubuntu 22.04.5, gcc 11.4.0, cmake 3.22.1 and branch master.

**Test commands:**

```bash
sudo bash dependencies.sh --with-spdk

mkdir build && cd build
cmake .. -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DUSE_NOF=ON -DBUILD_BENCHMARK=ON
make -j28 nof_worker_pool_bench
make -j28 mooncake_master

ln -s ~/spdk ../extern/spdk
BUILD_DIR=$PWD CLIENT_GLOBAL_SEGMENT_SIZE=0 CLIENT_MEMORY_REPLICA_NUM=0 \
    bash ../mooncake-store/tests/e2e/run_nof_heartbeat_tcp_e2e.sh
```

**Test results:**

- [x] Manual testing done (describe below)

Checks for the isa-l link path, originally run on `edbb692b` (Ubuntu 22.04.5, gcc 11.4.0, cmake 3.22.1,
SPDK v23.01.1 built by `dependencies.sh --with-spdk`). The distro `libisal-dev` package was
**installed** and `/usr/local/lib/libisal.a` was moved out of the way, so nothing but SPDK's
bundled library could satisfy `-lisal`:

| Action | Result |
| --- | --- |
| rename `extern/spdk/isa-l/.libs/libisal.a` away, re-run `cmake` | `CMake Error at mooncake-store/src/CMakeLists.txt:302 (message): isa-l not found at .../extern/spdk/isa-l/.libs/libisal.a. Run \`sudo bash dependencies.sh --with-spdk\`, or set -DSPDK_ISA_L_LIB_DIR.` |
| restore it, re-run `cmake` | `-- Configuring done` / `-- Generating done` |
| with `libisal-dev` installed, relink | link line carries `-L.../extern/spdk/isa-l/.libs -lisal`; `nof_worker_pool_bench` links 50 isa-l symbols statically and has no `libisal` entry in `DT_NEEDED` |
| remove `libelf-dev`, relink | `/usr/bin/ld: cannot find -lelf: No such file or directory` |
| install `libelf-dev`, relink | `[100%] Built target nof_worker_pool_bench` |

`/usr/local/lib` no longer receives a `libisal.a`, so nothing is copied over a distro or
user-installed isa-l there, and the link does not depend on the distro `libisal.so` even when that
package is installed.

Mechanism check run locally (synthetic CMake project linking a stub `libisal.a`, no SPDK build

title: [Store] Make re-offload of persisted keys an idempotent skip in BatchOffload
body:
## Description

Fixes #2827.

Under stress or retry the same keys get offloaded again, and today that fails the whole batch: `PrepareEviction` rejects any write key already visible in `object_bucket_map_` or `pending_write_keys_`, and the commit phase repeats the same all-or-nothing check. One duplicate key therefore kills every fresh key in the same bucket, and the error propagates out of `FileStorage` as a persist failure. `GroupOffloadingKeysByBucket` already skips persisted keys under `offloading_mutex_`, but its `IsExist` check and the commit under `mutex_` sit on different locks with `BuildBucket`/`WriteBucket` disk I/O in between, so a racing duplicate still reaches this path. This was the residual window discussed in the issue with @LujhCoconut: grouping is the fast path, this change is the correctness net under `mutex_`.

The change makes re-offload behave like Put, an idempotent no-op:

- `PrepareEviction` moves duplicates into a new `skipped_keys` list instead of rejecting the batch, and only registers the genuinely new keys in `pending_write_keys_`.
- The commit phase skips those keys (plus anything committed since, as defense in depth) and inserts only the rest into `object_bucket_map_`. The complete handler and the rollback path only ever see newly committed keys, so Master is never notified twice for the same key.
- A batch where every key is already persisted succeeds without invoking the complete handler; the redundant bucket file is cleaned up exactly as the old rejection path did.
- A key that is pending eviction still fails the batch. Skipping there could drop the only replica once eviction lands, so loud failure stays the right behavior.

This intentionally changes the duplicate contract from whole-batch atomic rejection to skip-and-commit, per the semantics aligned in the issue. The three Phase 0 duplicate tests and the reentrant pending-write test are updated to the new contract; the partial-batch test now also asserts that the handler only receives the newly committed key and that the new key reads back its own value.

title: [Bugfix][TENT] Fix VMM teardown order in MNNVL transport
body:
Follow-up to the teardown-order fix in #2380 (classic NVLink transport), applied to the TENT MNNVL transport.

As called out by @alogfans in #2380, the CUDA VMM teardown sequence should be `cuMemUnmap` -> `cuMemRelease` -> `cuMemAddressFree`, to match the cleanup order used elsewhere. This PR applies the same order to three sites in `mnnvl_transport.cpp`:

- `MnnvlTransport::allocateLocalMemory` -- `cudaGetDeviceCount` failure path
- `MnnvlTransport::allocateLocalMemory` -- `cuMemSetAccess` failure path
- `MnnvlTransport::freeLocalMemory` -- main teardown path

Each site now unmaps, releases the physical allocation handle, then frees the VA range, with a comment marking the teardown order (same wording as #2380).

**Left unchanged** (matching the #2380 ruling):
- The `cuMemMap` failure path: the map never succeeded, so there is no mapping to tear down and the `cuMemAddressFree`/`cuMemRelease` order is irrelevant.
- Existing single-release sites (EGM export branch, `cuMemAddressReserve` failure path, creator-reference drop after mapping).

No functional-path change -- only error paths and teardown ordering.

title: [Bugfix][TENT] Take the handler map lock when serving an RPC
body:
## Description

`CoroRpcAgent::registerFunction()` writes `func_map_` under `func_map_mutex_`, but `process()` read it with a bare `find()` on the io_context thread. A registration after `start()` therefore races a rehash against every in-flight lookup: a data race, and with more than one server thread a lookup can miss or crash. It has held up only because `ControlService` registers everything before `start()`; nothing enforced that.

`process()` now takes the mutex for the lookup, copies the `Handler` out and releases before the coroutine can suspend, so the lock never spans a `co_await`. `registerFunction()` uses a `lock_guard`. Cost is one uncontended mutex per control-plane RPC; the data path does not pass through here.

- 10-second measurement

| Configuration | Throughput | Avg transfer latency | P99 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 rail | 2.526 GB/s | 26.56 ms | 35.33 ms |
| 2 rails | 4.917 GB/s | 13.65 ms | 17.72 ms |

The two-rail configuration improved single-transfer throughput by 94.6%.

Payload correctness was verified separately with `tebench --op_type=mix --check_consistency=true` using 4 MiB transfers over two rails. The full-buffer comparison completed without mismatch.

**Test results:**

- [x] Unit tests pass
- [x] Integration tests pass
- [x] Manual dual-host testing done

### Follow-up Store validation — 2026-09-11

On two H20 VMs, Store host-memory READs benefited from the existing static multi-rail implementation with **4 HP workers per endpoint and 4 total persistent lanes per peer** in both configurations. This follow-up changes no runtime mechanism or defaults.

Three interleaved repetitions per configuration, with a 2-second warmup and a 20-second timed phase. Values below are medians; throughput brackets contain the full minimum–maximum range. GB/s is decimal.

| Request / batch | Concurrency | HP one rail, GB/s [min, max] | HP two rails, GB/s [min, max] | Throughput change | Client CPU cores, one → two |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 8 MiB | 1 | 2.267 [2.237, 2.283] | 3.458 [3.429, 3.481] | 52.5% | 1.665 → 2.004 |
| 8 MiB | 4 | 6.518 [6.516, 6.542] | 10.838 [10.717, 10.915] | 66.3% | 5.098 → 6.739 |
| 4 KiB | 1 | 0.02706 [0.02655, 0.02721] | 0.02690 [0.02619, 0.02741] | -0.6% | 0.906 → 0.913 |
| 4 × 512 KiB | 4 | 6.251 [6.086, 6.298] | 6.394 [6.251, 6.408] | 2.3% | 5.570 → 5.576 |

For 8 MiB, client p99 fell from 4.863 to 3.076 ms at concurrency 1 and from 7.171 to 4.928 ms at concurrency 4. These are medians of each run's sampled quantile, not pooled quantiles. Client CPU increased by 20.3% and 32.2%, respectively, despite keeping the configured worker and lane counts fixed. CPU cores are client process CPU seconds divided by measured wall time; they exclude the holder, master and whole-host interrupt work. Small READs showed no material benefit, and the 4 × 512 KiB batch ranges overlap. Three repetitions do not establish statistical significance or universal scaling.

**Correctness and rail usage:**

- All 33 timed Store cases completed without request failures or misses. Each case first verified all 32 objects byte-for-byte; byte verification was disabled during timing.
- All 24 HP cases had exact payload-byte agreement between successful Store reads and per-process TCP_INFO deltas after subtracting protocol headers. All six dual-rail 8 MiB cases split payload 50% / 50% between the two rails.
- The #3987 / #3988 follow-up check used four logical peers, each with four lanes (two per rail): client connections went 16 → 0 → 16 across a 2-second idle threshold and reconnection. All 64 patterned READs before and after idle passed. The four server engines shared one server process; this checks connection behavior rather than multi-server throughput scaling.

**Workload and fixed conditions:**

- Reused the `mooncake-store/benchmarks/store_kv_bench.py` `get_into` / `batch_get_into` read path through a local validation driver for separate prepare, verify, warmup and timed phases. The dataset was synthetic resident KV in a remote 1 GiB holder segment. The client had no global segment, a 128 MiB local buffer, 32 objects, I/O depth 1 per job, and 1 or 4 jobs.
- HP source-bound routes used one or two interfaces in NUMA 0. Both processes were allowed CPUs 0–89 in NUMA 0; this affinity is not a four-core CPU cap. RPC threads stayed at four. No system route or NIC tuning was changed. The H20 GPUs were unused.
- Ubuntu 22.04 / GCC 11 / Python 3.10, Release without LTO; CUDA and TENT metrics disabled. The entire matrix used the same binaries. Standard TCP reference cases were included in the 33-case total, but used a different outbound interface, so the performance claim above compares HP one rail with HP two rails.
- The three repetition orders were TCP → HP1 → HP2, HP2 → HP1 → TCP, and HP1 → TCP → HP2. The batch case compared HP1 / HP2 only. Latency was sampled every seven requests.

**Source provenance:** This is a later combined validation candidate, `ea02043fc9cf0f5d65c67d1d1ee8e4cbf0b2b05c`, based on `32c4b93880eeaa63606fcb0dee78ac38364bc27e` (already containing #3987 and #3988), with changes from #4001, #4002, #4005, #4006 and #4007 plus the two-line Python guard fix subsequently submitted as #4051. This is not a measurement of this PR's original head or unmodified upstream main. The candidate was held fixed between the one- and two-rail cases.

The results support large remote Store host-memory READs in this setup. They do not measure GPU-memory transfers, model-inference TTFT or production workload gains. The full raw archive remains local; all 34 raw result files (33 Store cases plus the multi-peer check) were matched to the controller results. Archive SHA-256: `4d9f13747ef353c2b531af061849c7ba4363483f0571e5b38441a78bf69f3e50`.

### Current upstream main validation — 2026-09-14

Retested **unmodified upstream main `202ad9c89e1814f0273c605cc12b3ccb1c8117c6`** on the two H20 VMs. The runtime code and defaults were unchanged for this validation. As above, both configurations used four HP workers per endpoint, four total lanes per peer, four RPC threads, the Store host-memory `get_into` / `batch_get_into` path, 32 resident objects, a 2-second warmup and a 20-second timed phase. Three interleaved repetitions compared HP1→HP2, HP2→HP1, then HP1→HP2 using the same binaries. GPUs were unused.

With both endpoints allowed CPUs 0–89:

| Request / batch | Concurrency | One rail, GB/s [min, max] | Two rails, GB/s [min, max] | Change | Client CPU cores, one → two |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 8 MiB | 1 | 2.206 [2.119, 2.207] | 3.293 [3.266, 3.334] | +49.3% | 1.675 → 2.014 |
| 8 MiB | 4 | 6.205 [6.136, 6.405] | 10.709 [10.313, 10.790] | +72.6% | 5.092 → 6.847 |
| 4 KiB | 1 | 0.02668 [0.02641, 0.02724] | 0.02666 [0.02649, 0.02678] | −0.1% | 0.913 → 0.915 |
| 4 × 512 KiB | 4 | 6.210 [6.158, 6.241] | 6.197 [6.018, 6.216] | −0.2% | 5.746 → 5.675 |

For 8 MiB, median sampled p99 was 5.071→3.601 ms at C1 and 7.738→5.096 ms at C4. Client CPU means process CPU seconds / wall seconds, excluding the holder, master and whole-host interrupt work.

**CPU budget boundary:** six cases restricted both endpoints to CPUs 0–3. The guest topology reports two cores with two SMT threads each. C4 8 MiB throughput was 3.653 [3.650, 3.689]→3.661 [3.646, 3.729] GB/s (+0.2%). A six-case follow-up kept four logical CPUs but spread them across four distinct guest core IDs (0,2,4,6, one thread each): 4.332 [4.095, 4.521]→4.249 [4.249, 4.345] GB/s (−1.9%). Neither restricted configuration showed a clear two-rail throughput benefit; ranges overlap. Guest core IDs do not establish exclusive physical-core allocation. The wide-affinity gain requires CPU headroom in this setup; fixed worker counts alone do not impose a four-CPU process budget.

**Validation:** all 14 relevant CTest targets and all 36 timed Store cases passed. Every case first verified all 32 objects byte-for-byte. All 36 HP TCP_INFO payload checks matched successful Store bytes, and all 12 dual-rail 8 MiB cases split payload equally. The four-logical-peer check again passed 64 patterned READs and connection retirement/reconnection 16→0→16. As above, these peers shared one server process.

All 37 raw result JSONs matched their controller records, and both endpoints' actual CPU affinity was checked. Raw archives remain local:

- Main matrix: `53f94913b8314ed0225aec5f6859eda44b47d0667fa351db362ead4f99d5611e`.
- Four-distinct-guest-core follow-up: `dce9eb1b6c41b0efbf68a9a36107c8130b165a233631155dccf0fa2f7960a849`.

These results support large remote Store CPU-memory READs under the measured conditions. Small and CPU-constrained workloads showed no clear throughput gain. This is not a cross-version regression comparison, a GPU-memory transfer measurement or an inference TTFT claim.


## Store buffer-layout replay (2026-09-16)

Completed 18 additional two-host cases on the same frozen, unmodified main `202ad9c89e1814f0273c605cc12b3ccb1c8117c6`, using the previously validated binaries. This replays host KV buffer shapes from the audited SGLang path, with a selected BF16/page64 DeepSeek-V3 object of 4,497,408 bytes (4.289 MiB). It is a Store API replay, not a model inference run.

Both endpoints used 4 workers, 4 total lanes per peer, affinity 0–89, C1 and 32 resident objects. Each point verified all 32 objects, warmed up for 2 seconds and measured for 20 seconds. Three interleaved repetitions used HP1→HP2, HP2→HP1, HP1→HP2.

| Destination layout | One rail GB/s [min,max] | Two rails GB/s [min,max] | Change | Client CPU cores, one → two | Sampled p99 ms, one → two |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Page-first, one contiguous buffer | 2.777 [2.715,2.785] | 4.621 [4.602,4.793] | +66.4% | 1.820 → 2.417 | 2.150 → 1.330 |
| Layer-first, 61 scattered 72 KiB buffers | 1.291 [1.286,1.294] | 1.274 [1.260,1.277] | −1.3% | 1.772 → 1.740 | 4.818 → 4.866 |
| Contiguous 61-buffer control | 2.669 [2.613,2.697] | 4.504 [4.496,4.569] | +68.8% | 1.809 → 2.352 | 2.274 → 1.308 |

Numbers are medians of three runs; GB/s is decimal. CPU covers the client process only. Latency samples one in seven requests. This used a different host pair from September 14, so absolute rates are not a cross-version comparison.

All 18 payload/wire-count checks passed, and every raw result matched its controller record. Page-first and contiguous multi-buffer emitted 1→2 wire READs per Store call; scattered layer-first emitted 61 with either rail count. Dual-rail contiguous payload split equally, and scattered payload differed by at most one 72 KiB request between rails. Thus the scattered workload did use both rails without a throughput benefit. All 36 endpoint configurations and CPU affinities were independently checked, as were the seven runtime file hashes on each host.

This confirms the benefit depends on the contiguous request shape, not just total object size. The contiguous multi-buffer control retains the API form while restoring adjacency/merging; the scattered layout changes both locality and request count, so the experiment does not isolate a single bottleneck. No packing, scheduling, split-threshold or other production change was made. No GPU transfer or TTFT improvement is claimed; changing application layout still needs its conversion costs evaluated.

Raw archive remains local, SHA256 `c9b817c3653d70ddaf2a220a7a7260d3afc8ae84bfd28d5f74313b3b6efdd9be`. Both endpoints were cleaned up and reservations released.

title: [TE][Store] Make P2P handshake + WaitForTransfers robust at large-scale DEP (32+ peer mesh)
body:
## Description

In **P2P-handshake** mode, when the peer mesh grows past ~30 transfer engines (e.g. vLLM with `DP=32 × EP=32` on 8 GB200 nodes, ~1000 pair-wise RDMA connections), three small but compounding bugs in the handshake / transfer path turn the first benchmark batch into a permanent stall:

| Setup | External-cache hit rate | Total throughput |
|---|---|---|
| 2-node / 4-node DEP (small mesh) | ~66 % | works |
| **8-node × DP=32 × EP=32 (this PR's target)** | **0.00 %** baseline → **64.41 %** with this PR | **21–35 k tok/s baseline → 79.4 k tok/s** with this PR |

Same recipe, same model, same code path — the only difference is mesh size. Smaller meshes never hit the chain because the thundering herd never forms.

## The chain (and what each fix breaks)

When the first transfer fires, every active engine concurrently triggers lazy QP setup with every peer. ~1000 pair-wise handshakes arrive within ~50 ms. Then:

1. **Listener saturation.** `SocketHandShakePlugin::startDaemon` runs the entire pipeline (`accept → callback → writeString → shutdown(SHUT_WR) → blocking read() waiting for client half-close → close`) on a single thread. Under the burst the queue can't drain in time; client-side reads return empty / partial bodies and surface as `malformed json format` / `unexpected handshake message type`.
   → **Fix: hand each accepted connection to a bounded worker pool** (`transfer_metadata_plugin.cpp`). The listener thread only does `accept()`; a fixed pool of workers (default 8, tunable via `MC_HANDSHAKE_WORKERS`, capped at 256) runs the per-connection pipeline. A 4096-deep backlog provides backpressure — at saturation the newest connection is dropped and the client retries, which beats unbounded memory growth. The destructor drains the workers and closes leftover fds cleanly.

2. **Single-shot RPCs.** `sendHandshake` / `sendNotify` / `getSegmentDesc → exchangeMetadata` issue exactly one TCP round-trip; any transient `ECONNREFUSED` (peer hasn't called `listen()` yet) or short read propagates straight up as a hard failure.
   → **Fix: bounded retry with exponential backoff** (`transfer_metadata.cpp`):

   | RPC | Attempts | Backoff | Total sleep budget |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | `sendHandshake` | 4 | 100/200/400 ms | ~700 ms |
   | `sendNotify` | 4 | 100/200/400 ms | ~700 ms |
   | `exchangeMetadata` (active side only) | 3 | 100/200 ms | ~300 ms |

   The passive `receivePeerMetadata` callback intentionally stays single-shot — it runs inside the listener path and blocking it would stall concurrent handshakes. Longer-lived recovery stays with the worker pool's slice-level retry.

3. **Per-future timeouts compound.** `WaitForTransfers` calls `pending_transfers[i].get()` in a straight loop. Each `get()` has its own 60 s internal timeout; with 62 ops per batch the worst-case wait is 62 × 60 s ≈ 62 min per BatchPut, during which the two-phase PUT never reaches `BatchPutEnd` / `BatchPutRevoke` and master accounting stalls. Once the original op finally times out and revokes, the benchmark window is over.
   → **Fix: cap the total wait at the batch level** (`client_service.cpp`). The per-op timeout is now a shared constant (`TransferEngineOperationState::kTimeoutMs`) and the batch wait reuses the same value — transfers in a batch run concurrently, so no healthy batch needs to wait longer than one operation timeout. Ops still unready past the cap are recorded as failed via the existing path, so every op always reaches `FinalizeBatchPut` in a definitive state.

## Why each fix matters in isolation

Any **one** of bugs 1–3 in isolation is survivable — the system would limp along. Together they create a one-way street into "reserved-but-never-committed" master state that other ranks then read as "key already exists" via `batch_is_exist` and skip storing themselves. Net effect: `master_batch_put_end_total` stays at 0 for the whole run.

| Fix | Widens the bottleneck so... |
|---|---|
| **1** | …fewer handshake RPCs fail in the first place |
| **2** | …the failures that do happen are **transient** rather than fatal |
| **3** | …even worst-case stuck batches still finalize in bounded time so master accounting stays consistent |

## Module

- [x] Transfer Engine (`mooncake-transfer-engine`)
- [x] Mooncake Store (`mooncake-store`)
- [ ] Mooncake Conductor (`mooncake-conductor`)
- [ ] Reshard (`mooncake-reshard`)
- [ ] Mooncake EP (`mooncake-ep`)
- [ ] Mooncake PG (`mooncake-pg`)
- [ ] Integration (`mooncake-integration`)
- [ ] P2P Store (`mooncake-p2p-store`)
- [ ] Python Wheel (`mooncake-wheel`)
- [ ] Common (`mooncake-common`)
- [ ] Mooncake RL (`mooncake-rl`)
- [ ] CI/CD
- [x] Docs

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] New feature
- [ ] Refactor
- [ ] Breaking change
- [ ] Documentation update
- [ ] Performance improvement
- [ ] Other

## How Has This Been Tested?

- **Workload:** vLLM serving Kimi K2.5 (NVFP4, MLA), 8 × GB200 nodes, `DP=32 × EP=32`, Mooncake P2P-handshake (`device_name=mlx5_2`), 4 transfer engines per node = 32 engines = ~1000 pair-wise handshakes per cold start.
- **Bench:** vllm-bench multi-turn (`mt_k25_mooncake.json`, 1000 prompts × 5 turns, total 5000 requests).
- **Master-side metrics (after fix vs before):**
  - `master_batch_put_end_total`: 0 → **9,328** (commits)
  - `master_batch_put_revoke_total`: ~1 / run → **0** (rollbacks)
  - `master_key_count`: stayed near 0 → grows to **~320 k** committed keys mid-run
- **vLLM side:**
  - `vllm:external_prefix_cache_hits_total / queries_total`: 0.00 % → **64.41 %**
  - Total token throughput: 21–35 k tok/s → **79,382 tok/s**, 0 failed requests / 5000.
- **Smaller scales:** ran 2-node and 4-node DEP recipes both before and after; no regression — both still hit ~66 %.
- **HCA-counter forensics on the unfixed baseline** (used to rule out cluster-side issues before identifying the three code bugs): cluster-wide `port_xmit_data` delta over a 15-min run was ~105 MB, vs. the ~100 GB expected if PUTs worked — i.e. transfers genuinely never posted to the wire, not a network drop / RDMA work-completion failure.
- **Build:** clean `cmake -DUSE_HTTP=ON -DUSE_ETCD=OFF -DUSE_REDIS=OFF -DWITH_STORE=ON -DBUILD_UNIT_TESTS=ON && make -j` on the GB200 cluster.

**Test results:**
- [ ] Unit tests pass
- [ ] Integration tests pass (if applicable)
- [x] Manual testing done (describe below)

This PR is verified end-to-end on a multi-day vLLM serving run rather than via unit tests. A reproducible Mooncake-only scale test that simulates the 32+ peer thundering herd would be a natural follow-up; happy to add one in a separate PR if reviewers prefer.

## Relationship to other work

- **Complementary to #1959** (`[TE]: Fix possible dead lock in RDMA transport connection setup`). #1959 eliminates the 3-way circular deadlock between listeners that nest into `getSegmentDescByName`. This PR addresses the orthogonal **scale** problem: even with the deadlock gone, the listener can still saturate, single-shot RPCs can still fail transiently, and per-future timeouts can still compound.
- **Does not change the master-side accounting for partial replicas.** Fix 3 keeps the existing all-or-nothing semantics in `WaitForTransfers` — it just adds a hard ceiling on total wait. A separate quorum / partial-success rewrite is a logical follow-up.

- [x] I have performed a self-review of my own code
- [x] I have formatted my code using `./scripts/code_format.sh` (clang-format 20.1.8, clean)
- [x] I have updated the documentation (`MC_HANDSHAKE_WORKERS` in `docs/source/design/transfer-engine/index.md`)
- [ ] I have added tests to prove my changes are effective (see note above)
- [ ] For changes >500 LOC: I have filed an RFC issue (N/A, ~230 LOC)

## AI Assistance Disclosure

- [ ] No AI tools were used
- [x] AI tools were used (specify below)

Claude Opus 4.7 helped with the original investigation and implementation; Kimi Code helped address the review feedback. Every changed line has been reviewed by the human submitter, who can defend the change end-to-end.

title: [Bugfix] Pad NoF client I/O to the namespace block size
body:
# NoF client: unaligned buffer lengths and addresses (issue #4029)

## 1. Root cause

`TransferSubmitter::submitSpdkNofOperation()` in
`mooncake-store/src/transfer_task.cpp` gated every NoF request behind a hard
alignment check:

```cpp
if (block_size == INVALID_BLOCK_SIZE ||
    handle.buffer_address_ % block_size != 0 || size % block_size != 0 ||
    reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(ptr) % block_size != 0) {
    LOG(ERROR) << ... << " is not aligned to block size " << block_size;
    return std::nullopt;
}
```

The request was then turned 1:1 into a single `SpdkNofTask` of
`size / block_size` blocks reading/writing straight out of the caller's
buffer.

NVMe commands are addressed in whole logical blocks, so the *length* of the
I/O genuinely has to be a block multiple and the *disk* offset genuinely has
to start on a block boundary. But neither of those is true of the caller's
memory: upstream users (LMCache, SGLang) hand in logical object sizes such as
513 B on a 512 B namespace, and buffers whose virtual address is not a
multiple of the block size. The client had no way to build a padded, block
aligned I/O out of such a request without reading or writing past the ends of
the caller's buffer, so it simply refused the request and the put/get failed
with `TRANSFER_FAIL`.

## 2. The fix and why

Split the problem into "what I/Os does this request expand into" (pure
arithmetic, testable) and "issue them" (SPDK specific).

**New module `nof_io_layout.{h,cpp}`.** `BuildNoFIoLayout()` maps
`(block_size, disk_offset, buffer_address, size)` onto a list of block aligned
`NoFIoSegment`s, each either

* `kDirect` — DMA runs straight against the caller's buffer, or
* `kStaged` — DMA runs against a block sized bounce buffer whose first
  `payload_size` bytes mirror a range of the caller's buffer.

The tiers follow the strategy sketched in the issue, limited to what the
current single-buffer `SpdkWrapper::SubmitRequest()` can express:

| caller's request | layout |
|---|---|
| block aligned address, block multiple length | one `kDirect` segment (unchanged, zero copies) |
| block aligned address, partial trailing block | `kDirect` prefix + one `kStaged` trailing block (at most `block_size - 1` bytes copied) |
| unaligned address | one `kStaged` segment covering the padded length |

A misaligned *disk* offset is still rejected: the object's first byte would
not be addressable by an NVMe command and the client cannot repair a
master-side allocation.

**`submitSpdkNofOperation()`** now builds the layout instead of rejecting, and
for the staged cases allocates the bounce buffers with
`SpdkWrapper::Alloc(bytes, block_size)` (`spdk_zmalloc`, i.e. DMA capable *and*
zero filled). On write the valid bytes are copied in and the padding stays
zero, so the caller's buffer is never read past its logical end. On read the
padded blocks land in the bounce buffer and only `payload_size` bytes are
copied back, so the caller's buffer is never written past its logical end. The
fully aligned path still submits a single task with no copies at all.

All bounce buffers are allocated *before* the first task is queued: once a task
reaches the worker pool its completion callback is guaranteed to run, so
bailing out halfway would leave the shared state waiting forever.

**`SpdkNofStagedOperationState`** (in `transfer_task.h`) joins the parts. It
owns the bounce buffers (RAII via `SpdkNofStagingBuffer`), counts the
outstanding parts down, ORs their failures together, performs the read
copy-backs, and only then publishes the single result the existing
`TransferFuture` waits on. `SpdkNofOperationState::set_completed()` became
`virtual` so the worker pool keeps calling it unchanged.

The logical object size, the returned length and any checksum computed over
the caller's buffer are untouched — only the on-wire I/O length is padded.

## 3. Files changed

| file | change |
|---|---|
| `mooncake-store/include/nof_io_layout.h` | new — `NoFIoSegment` / `NoFIoLayout` / `BuildNoFIoLayout()` |
| `mooncake-store/src/nof_io_layout.cpp` | new — layout construction and its bounds/overflow checks |
| `mooncake-store/src/transfer_task.cpp` | `submitSpdkNofOperation()` builds and issues the layout instead of rejecting unaligned requests |
| `mooncake-store/include/transfer_task.h` | `SpdkNofStagingBuffer`, `SpdkNofStagedOperationState`; `SpdkNofOperationState::set_completed()` made virtual |
| `mooncake-store/src/CMakeLists.txt` | compile `nof_io_layout.cpp` (unconditionally, it has no SPDK dependency) |
| `mooncake-store/tests/nof_io_layout_test.cpp` | new — unit tests for the layout |
| `mooncake-store/tests/CMakeLists.txt` | register `nof_io_layout_test` |

## 4. Risk and uncertainty

* **Depends on master-side padding (PR #4024, still open).** Writing a padded
  trailing block overwrites the bytes between the logical end of the object and
  the end of its last LBA. That is only safe if the allocator reserved those
  bytes for this object, which is exactly what #4024 does ("use the namespace
  block size as the minimum allocation unit for NoF"). Until #4024 lands, a
  master that hands out byte-granular NoF offsets will also hand out offsets
  that are not block aligned, and `BuildNoFIoLayout()` rejects those — so the
  padded write path is effectively unreachable before #4024. Reads are safe
  either way because the extra bytes are discarded. This ordering should be
  stated in the PR: **merge #4024 first**.
* **No SGL/iovec path.** `SpdkWrapper::SubmitRequest()` only takes one
  contiguous pointer, so the "direct SGL with a separate padding descriptor"
  and "TCP `readv`/`writev`" tiers from the issue are not implemented here;
  they need new `spdk_nvme_ns_cmd_readv/writev` wrapper entry points and NVMe
  SGL-capability probing. This change keeps the common cases cheap (fully
  aligned: zero copies; aligned address with a partial tail: at most
  `block_size - 1` bytes copied) and falls back to full staging only when the
  buffer address itself is unusable. The byte-granular-SGL case the issue calls
  out (don't copy just because the address is not 4-byte aligned) still copies
  here — it is the follow-up that the wrapper work unblocks.
* **Bounce buffers are allocated per request** via `spdk_zmalloc`. For the
  tail-only case that is one block; for the full-staging case it is the whole
  padded object, which for a large object with an unaligned address is a real
  allocation plus a full memcpy on the submit path. A pooled/chunked staging
  allocator would bound this and is worth a follow-up if unaligned addresses
  turn out to be common.
* **Unverified against real hardware.** `USE_NOF` is `OFF` by default and needs
  SPDK/DPDK plus an NVMe-oF target, neither of which is available here, so the
  SPDK-facing code path was not compiled or executed against a device. See
  below for what was verified instead.
* `set_completed()` becoming virtual adds a vtable dispatch per NoF completion;
  negligible next to the I/O itself.

## 5. How I verified it

* `mooncake-store/tests/nof_io_layout_test.cpp` — 9 tests over 512 B and
  4096 B namespaces: aligned requests stay direct with zero staging; a 513 B
  object becomes a direct 512 B block plus a 1 block staged tail carrying a
  single payload byte; sub-block objects and unaligned addresses are fully
  staged; the segments always tile the caller's buffer exactly (`covered ==
  size`, no segment claims more payload than its blocks hold); misaligned disk
  offsets, zero block size, zero length, and block-count overflow are rejected.
  Built and run standalone (the repo's full build needs etcd/RDMA deps that
  are not installed here):

  ```
  g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -fsanitize=address,undefined \
      -I<fused-gtest> -Imooncake-store/include \
      mooncake-store/tests/nof_io_layout_test.cpp \
      mooncake-store/src/nof_io_layout.cpp gtest-all.cc gtest_main.cc -lpthread
  ```

  → `[  PASSED  ] 9 tests.`, no warnings, clean under ASan/UBSan.

title: TENT: add a segment warmup primitive
body:
## Description

The first transfer towards a freshly opened segment pays for connection setup. On RDMA that is the endpoint and queue-pair bootstrap: 42 – 56 ms for a single NIC pair on the hardware below, and around a second when a whole NIC set has to come up. The classic engine grew `warmupEfaSegment()` for the same reason; TENT had no equivalent, so benchmarks and latency-sensitive callers either ate the stall on their first real transfer or hand-rolled a dummy one.

Adds `TransferEngine::warmupSegment(handle)`, routed to every installed transport through a new optional `Transport::warmupSegment()` that defaults to `NotImplemented`.

- RDMA pre-establishes endpoints from every enabled local context to every RDMA NIC the target advertises, skipping pairs that are already ready. Bootstrapping also brings up the notification queue pair that rides on the same endpoint.
- `NotImplemented` means both "this transport does not warm" and "it has nothing to warm towards this target" — a non-memory segment, or a peer that advertises no RDMA NIC. Neither is a failure, which is how the classic `warmupEfaSegment()` answers the no-devices case too.
- A transport that genuinely failed is reported even when another succeeded. The caller asked for the setup cost to be paid up front, and returning OK would hand back a target whose first transfer still stalls, with only a log line to say why. The failure leaves that transport on its lazy path, so the target stays usable either way.
- `LOCAL_SEGMENT_ID` is a successful no-op that reaches no transport: local transfers take the in-process path and have no connection state.
- C API: `tent_warmup_segment()`.

Only RDMA implements warming. TCP's data path runs on a worker pool, and the RPC agent that owns the connection pool is `thread_local`, so a connection warmed on the caller's thread is not one a transfer would use. Warming it usefully needs its own change, and is left out rather than shipped as a call that looks like it does something.

## Module

## How Has This Been Tested?

**Test commands:**
```bash
cmake -G Ninja -DUSE_TENT=ON -DUSE_HTTP=ON -DBUILD_UNIT_TESTS=ON ..
ninja && ctest --output-on-failure
```

**Test results:**
- [x] Unit tests pass
- [ ] Integration tests pass (if applicable)
- [x] Manual testing done (describe below)

`warmup_segment_test` pins the routing and aggregation contract with fake transports: the local segment reaches no transport, every installed transport is offered the target, `NotImplemented` is not a failure, a real failure surfaces alongside another transport's success, and the first of several failures is the one reported. Each case was checked against its own negative control — with the aggregation rule reverted, `AFailureIsReportedEvenIfAnotherTransportSucceeded` fails.

The RDMA implementation needs a NIC and a peer, so it is not covered by the unit tests. It was exercised separately, below.

Manual testing on a server with RDMA hardware (8×H20, 5×RoCE). Full TENT suite 31/31. A standalone harness opens a segment between two engines on the same host and times the first 4 KiB write, pinned to a single NIC, three rounds:

| | first write |
| --- | --- |
| cold, no warmup | 42 – 56 ms |
| after `warmupSegment()` | 0.57 – 0.75 ms |

`warmupSegment()` itself took about 45 ms for that one NIC pair. An independent run on a different day measured 42.4 – 49.0 ms cold, 0.44 – 0.56 ms warm and 41.4 – 43.5 ms for the warmup — close enough that the figures look like a property of the path rather than of one afternoon.

A second harness run without pinning a NIC warms every local context against every NIC the target advertises; that costs around a second, because the per-pair cost is what scales. Those numbers are not quoted here: the third round of that run was disturbed by unrelated load on the shared fabric (both cold and warm first-writes at 3.7 s, warm slower than cold), and the run is reported only for completeness.

The setup cost moves into the explicit call rather than disappearing; that is the point of the primitive. The absolute figure depends on the fabric and is not portable. What the runs establish is that the first-transfer stall is a stable structural cost rather than an occasional hiccup, and that it is gone once the segment is warmed.

title: [Store] Optional Intel ISA-L acceleration for object checksum
body:
## Description
Follow-up to #3922 (slicing-by-8 CRC-64). This adds an **opt-in, default-off**
build option `WITH_ISAL` that swaps `CrcChecksum::Update`'s compute path from the
portable slicing-by-8 table lookup to Intel ISA-L's `crc64_ecma_norm_by8`
(PCLMULQDQ carry-less folding). It is a pure performance option:

- **Output is bit-identical.** ISA-L uses the `rem = ~seed` / `~rem` convention,
  so we negate on both ends (`~crc64_ecma_norm_by8(~crc, buf, len)`) to preserve
  `CrcChecksum`'s own convention (init 0, no trailing negation). The existing
  `crc_checksum_test` — which checks against an independent bit-at-a-time
  reference and the CRC-64/ECMA known vector — passes unchanged under both
  configurations.
- **Default `OFF` means zero risk to existing builds.** With `WITH_ISAL=OFF`
  (default) nothing changes: slicing-by-8 remains the sole path, no new
  dependency, no assembler required. `WITH_ISAL=ON` requires the `nasm`
  assembler (>= 2.14.01); the source is fetched via `FetchContent` at a pinned
  tag (`v2.32.1`).
- **slicing-by-8 stays as the fallback**, not replaced. It is the default path
  and the landing spot if a user turns `WITH_ISAL=ON` on an unsupported
  toolchain/arch and reconfigures back to `OFF`.

### Honest scope of the benefit

We benchmarked this end-to-end (RDMA Put/Get on a Xeon 8350C, checksum enabled).
The takeaway a reviewer should weigh:

- ISA-L helps **low-concurrency / large-object** workloads, where a single or
  few client threads cannot saturate the NIC with slicing-by-8. Example (read,
  aggregate MiB/s, NIC line rate ~12 GB/s):

  | clients x value_size | slicing-by-8 | ISA-L (by8) |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 1 x 1 MiB | 1215 (16% of line) | 5248 (68%) |
  | 4 x 1 MiB | 4764 (40%) | 11389 (95%) |
  | 8 x 1 MiB | 7265 (61%) | 11981 (100%) |

  Per-byte CRC cost on a single stream drops from ~0.65 ns/B (slicing-by-8) to
  ~0.05-0.09 ns/B (ISA-L).

- At **high concurrency** (>=16 clients on multi-MB objects) slicing-by-8
  already saturates the NIC, so ISA-L yields **no additional aggregate
  throughput** there. This is expected: the checksum is memory/NIC-bound in that
  regime, not ALU-bound.

So this is a latency / single-stream-throughput optimization for
few-client large-object access (e.g. one client fetching a multi-MB KV-cache
entry), not a blanket speedup.

### Why hardcode the `by8` variant (no multibinary, no AVX-512)

ISA-L ships wider variants (AVX2, AVX-512 `by16_10`) behind a runtime multibinary
dispatcher. We deliberately link only `by8`:

- `by8` needs only PCLMULQDQ (present on every x86-64 CPU since 2010), so a
  hardcoded call cannot fault with an illegal instruction — safe for a wheel
  shipped to heterogeneous machines, without pulling in the dispatcher.
- Micro-benchmarks showed AVX-512 (`by16_10`) is ~40-60% faster than `by8` only
  while the working set stays L3-resident; once the aggregate working set
  (concurrency x value_size) spills L3 the memory wall makes all variants
  converge. In the concurrency this store actually runs, `by8` already saturates
  the link, so the extra dispatcher machinery and AVX-512 downclocking risk are
  not worth it. This can be revisited as future work if a clear
  low-concurrency + AVX-512 deployment emerges.

### Why x86-64 only (AArch64 deferred)

Only the x86-64 `by8` path is wired up. ISA-L does ship an AArch64 PMULL
implementation (`crc64_ecma_norm_pmull.S`), so adding ARM later is a matter of
build wiring, not reimplementation. We deferred it here because we could not
build or validate an AArch64 binary on our x86 hardware, and we did not want to
commit unverified arch-specific build glue into a correctness-critical path. To
avoid a confusing "missing symbol" link error, `WITH_ISAL=ON` on a non-x86-64
processor fails fast at configure time with an actionable message pointing back
to `-DWITH_ISAL=OFF` (which is correct on every platform). Happy to add the
AArch64 path in a follow-up if CI has ARM runners to validate it.

title: [TE] Fix transfer byte accounting races and completion caching
body:
## Description

- Status queries can read transferred bytes before observing slice completion, returning `COMPLETED` with a stale byte count that the batch cache then retains.
- Batch queries treat the completion flag as proof that cached bytes are ready. Polling can publish this flag before the bytes, while event completion sets it without populating the cache, allowing zero-byte results or failed batches to be reported as successful.
- HCCL overwrites the accumulated byte count with the current slice's length after `markSuccess()`, losing bytes from earlier slices.

## Fix

- Acquire the completion counters before atomically loading transferred bytes in 17 transports (21 query sites) and the `MultiTransport` fallback.
- Add a separate cache-valid flag and publish it only after storing the aggregated byte count. Batch queries use this flag so completion events cannot expose an unpopulated cache or bypass failure checks.
- Remove HCCL's post-`markSuccess()` assignment, preserving the byte total accumulated by `markSuccess()`.

## Module

- [x] Transfer Engine (`mooncake-transfer-engine`)

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix

## How Has This Been Tested?

Tested on two NVIDIA H20 nodes with four RoCE HCAs each, using Release/CUDA builds with event-driven completion enabled and disabled, covering bidirectional CPU/GPU reads and writes over peermem and DMA-BUF. Earlier RDMA tests observed byte undercounts despite correct data. After the fix, all 128 cases (64 GiB, 131,072 requests) passed byte-count and payload checks, including 2,048 batches queried after completion events. Repeated cache queries, success/failure ordering checks, selected existing unit tests, and TCP loopback tests also passed. HCCL and other vendor-specific backends were not hardware-tested.

title: [EP] Enable MACA legacy EP with shared P2P and IBGDA device paths
body:
## Description

Enable Mooncake's legacy low-latency Expert Parallelism (EP) `Buffer` API on MetaX MACA devices by reusing the existing CUDA/MUSA EP and mlx5 IBGDA paths. The public legacy EP API remains unchanged: users construct `Buffer`, then call `dispatch` and `combine` with BF16 or FP8 payloads.

### Motivation

MACA deployments need both intra-node P2P EP and GPU-initiated RDMA EP. The shared Mooncake transport already contains the required QP lifecycle, WQE, doorbell, signal, remote atomic, and CQ logic. This change supplies the MACA compiler/runtime integration and device-ordering adaptations needed on C500 hardware, without introducing a second EP implementation or an MXSHMEM-specific kernel.

### Implementation

#### MACA build and runtime integration

- Compile the legacy EP device kernel with the MACA SDK cu-bridge `nvcc`.
- Link the EP extension and PG device worker against the MACA runtime.
- Exclude the elastic EP kernel from the MACA target because it contains NVIDIA-specific PTX and is outside the legacy `Buffer` API.
- Add the CUDA-runtime compatibility aliases required by the shared host code.

#### Shared IBGDA path

- Reuse the common mlx5 QP/WQE/doorbell/CQ implementation used by CUDA and MUSA.
- Use MACA system-scope fences and atomics for release publication and QP mutex ownership.
- Publish GPU-produced payload data before posting the corresponding IBGDA WQE, which is required for NIC visibility of MACA fine-grained memory.
- Serialize the two MACA sub-warp leaders that can contend for one QP channel during legacy combine posting.
- Keep the shared QP table at 256 entries and derive all-to-all metadata shape from the runtime local-QP vector.

#### Legacy EP protocol

- Remove the native phase-ACK kernels and API. The Python phase fence remains the synchronization boundary for MACA split SEND/RECV launches.
- Preserve MACA split SEND/RECV behavior and avoid passing the unsupported native `async_finish && return_recv_hook` combination.
- Zero-initialize packed receive counters before dispatch.
- Enable MACA FP8 conversion through the SDK's `__maca_fp8_e4m3` type.
- Remove zero-copy arms from the correctness matrix because zero-copy is not a supported path for this feature.

### Scope

This PR targets the legacy EP `Buffer` API. The newer elastic kernel is not compiled for MACA in this change. Performance tuning beyond the validated functional path, including QP sharding and active-QP auto-tuning, remains a follow-up.

## Module

- [x] Mooncake EP (`mooncake-ep`)
- [x] Mooncake PG (`mooncake-pg`)
- [x] Transfer Engine (`mooncake-transfer-engine`)
- [x] Python Wheel (`mooncake-wheel`)

## Type of Change

- [ ] Bug fix
- [x] New feature
- [ ] Refactor
- [ ] Breaking change
- [ ] Documentation update
- [ ] Performance improvement
- [ ] Other

## How Has This Been Tested?

Validation focused on MACA C500 devices and the actual legacy EP communication paths. The tests use the standard workload shape where noted (`tokens=128, hidden=7168, experts=288, top-k=8`) and exclude zero-copy.

**Test commands:**

```bash
# Official legacy EP correctness test, P2P path
PYTHONPATH=$ROOT/python python3 -u python/tests/ep/test_mooncake_ep.py

# Official legacy EP correctness test, pure IBGDA path
# The test harness passes disable_p2p=True and selects the allocated HCAs.
PYTHONPATH=$ROOT/python python3 -u python/tests/ep/test_mooncake_ep.py

# Native eight-rank MACA EP correctness/performance workload
PYTHONPATH=$ROOT/python python3 -u mooncake-ep/benchmarks/legacy_buffer_perf.py
```

**Test results:**

- [x] Manual testing done: two-rank MACA P2P correctness passes for BF16 and FP8 dispatch/combine, including hook and non-hook paths.
- [x] Manual testing done: two-rank pure-IBGDA correctness passes for BF16 and FP8 with fine-grained payload allocation, explicit HCA selection, split SEND/RECV, and the Python phase fence. Native phase ACK is disabled.
- [x] Manual testing done: eight-rank fixed-routing MACA correctness passes on the reduced formal smoke workload (`tokens=8, hidden=7168, experts=8, top-k=1`) with zero maximum error. A matched native run reports approximately `667--760 us` dispatch+combine latency.
- [x] Manual testing done: the formal eight-rank pure-IBGDA workload (`tokens=128, hidden=7168, experts=288, top-k=8`, P2P disabled) passes dispatch and combine correctness on all ranks with `max_abs_error=0`. The native loop reports approximately `2.09--2.11 GB/s` dispatch+combine effective bandwidth and `13.9--14.0 ms` average latency. NCCL/MCCL is used for device metadata and a separate Gloo control group supplies the MACA phase fence.
- [x] Manual testing done: the formal two-rank workload also completes pure IBGDA dispatch/combine correctness for BF16 and FP8. This is a functional bootstrap check; the performance data below is from the eight-rank workload.
- [x] Manual testing done: the MACA allocator requirement and HCA selection were validated independently. Fine-grained payload memory is required for GPU-produced IBGDA data; invalid HCA selection fails at IBGDA initialization rather than silently falling back to P2P.

For context, the prebuilt MXDeepEP low-latency benchmark on the same MACA family reports approximately `12.3 GB/s` per-rank effective dispatch+combine bandwidth for the formal eight-rank workload. From the human author's perspective (@UNIDY2002), Mooncake's `2 GB/s` per-rank result is already close to saturating the two 100-Gbps data-plane ports: `2 GB/s * 8 ranks = 16 GB/s`, versus `2 * 100 Gbps / 8 = 25 GB/s` of raw link bandwidth. The same calculation applied to the MXDeepEP number gives `12.3 GB/s * 8 ranks = 98.4 GB/s`, which appears to exceed that RDMA limit.

Codex's interpretation is that this comparison is too high because the printed figures are per-rank effective all-to-all rates and can count overlapping or duplicated traffic; they are not aggregate wire-rate measurements. The MXDeepEP result is therefore retained as a useful baseline, while the apparent 98.4-GB/s aggregate should not be read as physical link utilization. Mooncake's current native MACA result is a functional baseline; QP/CQ scheduling and communication overlap are follow-up performance targets.

## Compatibility and Operational Notes

- MACA IBGDA payloads must use fine-grained allocation. Set `MOONCAKE_EP_MACA_ALLOC=fine` for the pure-IBGDA route; the default allocator remains unchanged for ordinary P2P users.
- Set `MOONCAKE_EP_DEVICE_FILTER` to the actual InfiniBand device names for the allocated node (for example, `mlx5_10,mlx5_11`). Do not use a network bond name or the plural `MOONCAKE_EP_DEVICE_FILTERS`; verify the selected HCA in the `[EP IBGDA] Initialized on ...` log before interpreting results.

title: fix(ubshmem): preserve FabricMem handles on HDK 25.5
body:
## Problem

Mooncake UBShmem FabricMem registration and teardown call
`aclrtMemRetainAllocationHandle()` to reverse-lookup a driver handle from a
virtual address. On the tested A3 HDK 25.5.1.1 / CANN 9.0.0 nodes, the symbol
is present in `acl_rt.h`, but the runtime returns `207000`. This prevents
normal UBShmem local-buffer registration on those nodes.

## Cause

Mooncake owns the physical handle when it allocates a VMM buffer, but the
handle is discarded. Registration and free then try to recover it from the VA
through an API that is unavailable on HDK 25.5.

## Fix

- Preserve `VA -> aclrtDrvMemHandle` records for direct VMM allocations.
- Add explicit record/forget hooks for handles crossing the store/transport
  mount boundary.
- Export the preserved handle in `UBShmemTransport::registerLocalMemory()`.
- Reuse the preserved handle in `freePinnedLocalMemory()`.
- Retain imported Fabric handles in remap entries and release those exact
  handles during teardown.
- Route UBShmem Fabric allocation through direct VMM allocation, with the
  existing `MC_UBSHMEM_FABRIC_ALLOC_KIND=device|host` selection.
- Keep reverse lookup only as a compatibility fallback for externally-owned
  virtual addresses.

## Validation

- `git diff --check` passes.
- Built `ubshmem_transport_test` with `USE_UBSHMEM=ON` on an A3 HDK 25.5.1.1
  node.
- Focused owned-host VMM smoke passed: register -> unregister -> free, one
  test, 649 ms, with no `aclrtMemRetainAllocationHandle -> 207000`.
- Full cross-node transfer validation is still pending; this PR is draft for
  that reason.

title: [Store] Fix 32-bit host-pointer offset overflow in SPDK NoF transfers over 4 GiB
body:
## Description

In the SPDK NoF worker (`mooncake-store/src/transfer_task.cpp`, `SpdkNofWorkerPool::workerThread`), the host buffer offset for each sub-I/O was computed as:

```cpp
int lba_off = task->lba_count - task->remaining_lba;   // int
...
void* submit_ptr = reinterpret_cast<char*>(task->ptr) + lba_off * block_size;
```

`block_size` is a `uint32_t`, so `lba_off * block_size` is evaluated in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic. Once the running offset reaches 4 GiB (`lba_off * block_size >= 2^32`) the product wraps around and `submit_ptr` points to the wrong part of the buffer. The DMA for the tail of a >4 GiB transfer then reads from / writes to the *start* of the user buffer instead of the intended region, silently corrupting data.

The device-side address one line below — `uint64_t submit_lba = task->lba + lba_off;` — is already 64-bit, so only the host pointer offset was left narrow.

This is reachable for any sufficiently large transfer: a single `SpdkNofTask` is created with `lba_count = size / block_size` for the whole request and there is no size cap at the submit site (`submitNofTransfer` only checks block alignment), so `lba_off` walks from 0 up to `lba_count` as the task drains. It is the same >4 GiB scenario that was fixed for SSD offload in #2570.

The fix widens `lba_off` to `uint64_t` so the offset arithmetic stays 64-bit, matching the already-widened `submit_lba`.

## Module

- [x] Mooncake Store (`mooncake-store`)

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix

## How Has This Been Tested?

The SPDK NoF path is behind `USE_NOF` and needs SPDK + NVMe-oF hardware, so I could not build or exercise it locally (no native SPDK toolchain on this machine). It is verified three ways:

1. **Standalone reproduction of the arithmetic.** Mirroring the exact types (`int lba_off`, `uint32_t block_size`) and picking the first `lba_off` whose byte offset crosses 4 GiB for a 5 GiB transfer with 4096-byte blocks:

   ```
   lba_count=1310720 lba_off=1048576 block_size=4096
   expected byte offset      = 4294967296
   buggy (32-bit) offset     = 0
   fixed (64-bit) offset     = 4294967296
   buggy pointer wrong by    = -4294967296 bytes
   RESULT: OVERFLOW CONFIRMED (buggy != fixed)
   ```

   The 32-bit expression wraps to 0 (off by exactly 4 GiB); the 64-bit expression is correct.

2. **Parity with #2570**, which fixed the same 32-bit-overflow-on-a->4 GiB-size class in the SSD offload path and was accepted as a code-only change.

3. `clang-format` clean on the file.
